Raised by the review of `BL-109` and routed here rather than fixed there, because that item is
about what the app tells a reader and this one is about whether the vendoring run gave it grounds
to say it. `BL-109` infers "upstream has no record of this" from an item arriving in a curated
order with no metadata, on the premise that a curated order is the output of a completed run so
every item in it has already been looked up. The first half is true and the second did not follow,
because the run discarded which answer it got.

The vendoring run's lookup loop caught every error from the lookup identically and only warned, and
the item was then built from whatever the metadata map held, so it landed with every field null.
Four unlike outcomes reached that catch: a 404 from the non-ok throw at
`scripts/lib/fetch-json.mjs:68`, a 429 or 5xx that outlived the retry budget from
`scripts/lib/fetch-json.mjs:76`, a lost connection, and a body that would not parse. Those are
exactly the two kinds `BL-109` exists to separate, and the import path applied none of the test the
runtime path applies at `src/js/hydrate.js:72`.

The consequence is worse at import than at runtime, because it is unrecoverable. A refusal is
dropped from `pendingIssueIds`, therefore from `hydrationOrder`, and the hydrator is the only
caller of the issue lookup in the app, so nothing ever asks again and the one writer that clears
the flag never runs. The reader is then told the snapshot has no record of an issue the snapshot
would hold. Nothing stopped it, either: the run warned once per failed lookup and then wrote the
file anyway, and no check ever counted how many items came back empty, so an outage that lost thirty
issues left thirty warnings scrolled off a build log and an artifact that looked correct.

Not live today, and measured rather than assumed. 69 items across the fourteen shipped orders fail
`hasMetadata`, and they are two unlike things the app already counts apart. Six are placeholders in
the two X-Men orders, rows the vendoring run built deliberately for checklist lines Marvel has no
record of at all: a synthetic negative id, `placeholder: true`, and no lookup ever attempted. The
other 63 came back from a lookup, they are all in the two Ultimate files, and four of them were
checked against the live API on 2026-08-15 and answered 404, so the premise holds for the data that
ships. It is also not a regression: import forced `hydrated: true` before `BL-109`, so a transiently
lost item was already excluded from the queue. What changed is that the exclusion is now permanent
and carries a positive claim, which is what makes the soundness of the inference worth buying rather
than reasoning about. Evidence: `scripts/lib/lookup-issues.mjs:49`, `scripts/lib/fetch-json.mjs:30-36`,
`scripts/vendor-orders.mjs:258-264`.

**The item's own premise was checked rather than inherited, and the check was worth running.** The
block above rests on four issues having been asked about. All 63 lookup-derived empties were put to
the live API instead, and all of them answered 404, so the premise holds completely for the data that
ships, which is a stronger statement than the item makes. Those 63 items are 34 distinct issues, a
thing `BL-109` had already established and this run confirmed rather than discovered: the Ultimate
trades order re-lists what the singles order already carries. 34 is the number of lookups a tracker
holding both orders would otherwise spend, and it is the number that came back refused.

Shipped as a three-way reading of each lookup where there had been one. `scripts/lib/fetch-json.mjs`
now throws a `FetchError` carrying the HTTP status, and `scripts/lib/lookup-issues.mjs` sorts each
outcome into answered, refused or indeterminate. A rejection is a refusal only when
`err?.status === 404`, which is the same test `src/js/hydrate.js:72` already applies at runtime. The
status is a field on the error and not a parse of its message, and a lost connection or an
unparseable body produces an error carrying no status at all, which is exactly right: neither can
pass the test, so neither can pass for an answer.

**The review found the half of that agreement the first pass missed**, and it is the shape this
repository keeps relearning: the most dangerous code in a change is the code added to stop data
loss, because it runs only once something has already gone wrong. Classifying rejections alone left
a lookup that *resolved* with an unusable body counting as answered, so it built an item with every
field null and no `detailsRefused`, which is precisely the unrecoverable outcome this item was
bought to prevent, reached by the one route the new tests did not cover. The runtime path had always
guarded it, declining to upsert a falsy body so the issue stays pending for the next run; the import
path has no next run, so its only guard is declining to write the file. The fix applies the app's own
`hasMetadata` to the resolved body as well, at `scripts/lib/lookup-issues.mjs:43-44`, imported from
`src/js/lib/model.js:88-90` rather than restated, because a producer holding a second copy of the
rule can drift from the consumer without anything going red.

Measured before adopting that test rather than assumed, because a predicate that rejects a real
answer would make an order unvendorable. Across the fourteen shipped orders 1,404 items pass
`hasMetadata` and 69 fail, the 69 are exactly the empties and placeholders already known, and not one
of them carries a cover, a series name, an on-sale date, a description, a page count or a creator, so
the test separates exactly the items a lookup produced nothing for. Reverting the guard reddens 3 of
the 4 tests added for it. The survivor is the one holding a body with a series id and no digital id to
still being an answer, and it passes either way by design: all 1,404 answered items carry both ids,
so no shipped datum is in that shape and nothing derived from the data would notice the rule being
narrowed to `digitalId` alone. Narrowing it reddens that test and nothing else in 957, which is the
whole of its job.

A second review round found three prose claims the code does not support, and no gate caught any of
them. The comment beside that survivor test said plenty of real issues carry no digital id, which the
1,404 refute. This block said the old run warned only when the item count differed from the plan, when
in fact it warned once per failed lookup and then wrote the file anyway, which is both the true
statement and the more damning one. And writing `detailsRefused` only when true was described as
leaving an unchanged order byte for byte, which no re-vendor ever is, because `generatedAt` is a
fresh wall clock on every run. That claim is now scoped to the per-item payload, which is what the
conditional write actually buys.

Every one of those figures was then measured a third time, because this branch was rebased onto two
X-Men orders that landed on `main` while it was open and a measurement is about a tree rather than
about a claim. The rebase is where the numbers moved: 12 orders became 14, 751 items became 1,473,
688 answered became 1,404, and 63 failing the predicate became 69. One sentence in this block
survived that rebase as a silent falsehood, saying every empty item was in the two Ultimate files
when six of them had just arrived in the X-Men orders, and `git` reported no conflict on it because
the two branches had edited different lines of the same paragraph. The shape of every claim held: 0
of the 1,404 carry one id without the other, and 0 of the 69 carry any upstream evidence.

The re-aiming that rebase forced also produced a citation whose end read `null` where a number
belongs, because the end of the range fell inside a changed hunk and no arithmetic could place it.
That is not a citation the anchors gate recognises, so it was not reported as drifted or lost; it was
silently dropped from the corpus, and the range it should have named shrank from three lines to none.
What caught it was a test in `test/check-sizes.test.js:164-179` asserting that the lock still holds a
sentence stating a file's size, which stopped being true the moment the entry vanished. A malformed
anchor is therefore worse than a wrong one, because a wrong one drifts and a malformed one
disappears, and the only reason this one was visible at all is that an unrelated test happened to
depend on the entry it removed.

The abort is inside `lookupIssues` rather than in the caller, and that is a shape choice rather than
a placement one. A run that met an outcome it could not classify never gets its results back, so
"nothing is written" is a property of the function rather than of the order two statements happen to
be in, and no future caller can reintroduce the bug by reading the return value first. The message
names every unclassifiable id rather than the first, because a run that lost thirty issues to an
outage and reports one has told you the least useful true thing it could.

`detailsRefused` is written onto the item only when it is true. An order with nothing refused
therefore re-vendors with no per-item change at all, so the field costs nothing in ten of the twelve
shipped files and the change is legible as a diff in the two where it matters. Not byte for byte,
which is the tempting way to say it and is wrong: `generatedAt` is a fresh wall clock on every run,
so no re-vendor produces an identical file and an empty diff is not the thing to check a run against.

A new build-time module rather than a guard on the existing one. `scripts/vendor-orders.mjs` calls
`main()` unconditionally at module load, so a test cannot import it, and the obvious fix of guarding
that call behind an entry-point check would put `npm run vendor` one subtle path difference away
from doing nothing at all while reporting success. That is the failure this whole item is about, so
buying a testable seam with a copy of it would have been a poor trade. Extracting the logic gives
the seam with no entry-point risk, and the tests drive the real fetcher through it rather than a
stand-in, which is what caught the gap below.

Each of the six decisions was reverted in turn and the tests watched to redden. Making every
failure a refusal reddens 6, handing failures back to the caller instead of aborting reddens 9,
truncating the report to the first id reddens 2, dropping the status from the non-ok throw reddens
2, dropping it from the exhausted-retry throw reddens 1, and storing whatever the lookup resolves
with reddens 3. The abort figure is 9 rather than the 6 measured before the review, because the
three tests added for the resolved-body guard assert a rejection and so notice that revert too; it
is re-derived here rather than carried forward. The first of the two status reverts
reddened only 1 before the seam test existed, because every other test in the file builds its own
error object and would have gone on passing against a producer that had stopped carrying the status.
That gap is the reason one test drives the real fetcher.

The two Ultimate orders were re-vendored against the live API rather than edited, and the diff was
read rather than trusted: `detailsRefused: true` on 34 items in the singles order and 29 in the
trades, the snapshot timestamps, and one payload key the producer has always written since that
file was last built. No other per-item field moved, so the upstream metadata is byte-identical to
the snapshots these replace, taken on 2026-08-05 for the singles order and 2026-08-08 for the
trades, and this change is visibly additive.

What is left, deliberately. `refusedOnArrival` still infers a refusal from emptiness, and removing
it would have been the tidy-looking mistake: `coerce` re-normalizes every stored issue on load, so a
tracker imported before the field existed would have had those items pushed back into the hydration
queue to relearn 34 404s, which is the cost `BL-109` was bought to avoid. The inference is now the
legacy path and the recorded outcome is the primary signal, and the comment above it says so. The
order-gap counts still key on absent metadata rather than on the new field, which is correct
unchanged: they count what a reader is missing, and an issue is missing its cover whether upstream
refused it or nobody has asked yet.

**BL-127: Add an X-Men reading order spanning the Silver Age and the Claremont era**

- [x] Resolve every issue the reader's outline names against Marvel's metadata
- [x] Decide where the ranges the outline states twice should be read
- [x] Ship it as a group of two, the spine and the spine plus the optional reading
- [x] Say on the card what is not in the order, and why

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Filed and shipped from a reader request, supplied as an outline of Comic Book Herald's Silver Age
origins and Chris Claremont era guides. The catalog held 12 orders and not one of them was about the
X-Men. Nine were events, two were a creator run and two an era; there was no character run at all,
so the type existed in the code and in the filter chips with nothing behind it. The longest order in
the catalog was 219 issues.

The two orders ship as a group: 318 items in the spine and 404 in the one that adds the outline's
two optional sections, the Silver Age guest appearances and the modern retellings. 400 unique issues
resolved, every one of them with a `digitalId` and cover art, so nothing in either order renders
with the pending badge. That is the reason this went in as a vendored order and not as an import:
the mirror covers 1963 to 1987 as completely as it covers the present.

Four departures from the outline, all deliberate and all recorded on the card. The outline lists
Uncanny #199-210 and X-Factor #1-9 as runs and then lists six of those same issues again, interleaved
with Thor, Power Pack and Daredevil, as the Mutant Massacre. A list holds an issue once, so one of the
two readings had to win: `scripts/vendor-orders.mjs:311-313` warns that a repeated id will collapse on
import. The crossover won, and the runs before it stop at #209 and #8. Uncanny #214-220 and New
Mutants #45 were filled in, because the outline skipped them and both runs are otherwise unbroken.
Giant-Size X-Men #1 was added ahead of Uncanny #94, since starting at #94 as the outline does
introduces Storm, Nightcrawler and Colossus by having them already on the team.

X-Men #67-93 are not in either order. All 27 are reprints of #1-66, which both orders already carry
in full, and the mirror holds no record of them at all: series 2258 runs #1-66 and then resumes at
#94, which is exactly the reprint years and nothing else. They could only have shipped as 27 rows
with no cover, no link and no issue behind them, so they are left out and the omission is stated in
the description rather than left for a reader to notice.

Four issues do ship without a link, as placeholders. Power Pack #27-28 are chapters of the Mutant
Massacre sitting between X-Factor #10 and #11, so dropping them would have moved the issues around
them out of the order the crossover is meant to be read in; the mirror is missing Power Pack #27-34
and #36. X-Men Annual #1-2 are absent for a different reason, that series 2100 begins at #3, and they
appear only in the complete variant.

The section titles are bold paragraphs rather than Markdown headings, which looks like a formatting
preference and is not one. A level-2 heading in a checklist is vendored as `collectedIn`, and any
order with one is then described to the reader by the count of them at
`src/js/lib/catalog.js:381-386`. Uncanny #129-138 is a story arc, not a book anyone can buy, so
headings here would have put "5 collected editions" on a card where no collected edition exists.
Both orders vendor with `collections` at 0, which is the check that this worked.

The order stops at X-Factor #23 because the outline it follows did, partway through X-Factor's second
year. Fall of the Mutants, Inferno, Excalibur, X-Force and everything after are absent, and the
description says so rather than implying the Claremont era ended there.

**BL-128: Correct the provenance record's description count and record its placeholder shape**

- [x] Re-derive every figure the provenance record states and correct the one that disagrees
- [x] Describe the record shape the inventory never mentions
- [x] Keep the six placeholders distinct from the 63 bare records

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The provenance record is the document the publication decision rests on, so a stale figure in it
costs more than its size suggests. It stated the description count three times. Two said 798 and one
said 508, which is what the figure was when the tree held twelve orders rather than fourteen.
BL-127 added the other two and re-derived nine figures across the file, and this was the tenth. The
one that survived is inside the list of questions a legal review would have to answer, which is the
worst of the three places to be wrong: there the number is part of the question rather than part of
a description, and nobody reading the answer would know to check it.

The inventory also said every record copies thirteen named fields from upstream, and six records
copy none of them. Two in the Claremont order and four in its complete variant stand for checklist
lines the mirror holds no issue for at all, so nothing was ever fetched for them: they carry
`placeholder: true`, no url, and an id generated locally by hashing the order and the title and
negating the result so it can never be read as Marvel's. BL-126 already recorded that split as
delivery evidence. What it had never done is reach the document written for a reader outside this
project, and that document is the one that has to stand on its own.

Recording it needed care in one direction. The same file says 63 items carry nothing beyond an id, a
title, a number and a marvel.com link, and that number is exactly right as written: all 63 sit in
the two Ultimate universe orders and every one of them has a real Marvel id behind a real link. The
six placeholders fail the opposite way, with no link because no lookup was ever attempted. Added
carelessly they would have turned a correct 63 into an apparent 69, so the two now sit next to each
other with the difference stated rather than left for a reader to reconcile.

Filing this item moved five stated ranks, which the counts gate named and which were written back
from the values it derived. It also surfaced a sixth figure the gate does not read. The WSJF case
for BL-026 said it was outranked by forty-five items, twenty-eight of them cheaper, where the table
gave forty-six and twenty-nine before this change and forty-eight and twenty-nine after. Both had
been one behind since some earlier item was filed above it, and the neighbouring claim about
unlabelled items was correct, which is what made the pair worth checking rather than assuming. They
are re-derived here rather than shifted by two, because carrying a wrong number forward is exactly
how it survived this long.

Three further claims of that kind sit in the appendix that argues against re-sorting the table, and
no gate reads any of them. It counted the table at 102 rows where it held 103, said five rows carry
`Ready` where four do, and said a stable sort by score moves 39 rows where it moves 40. All three
were already wrong before this change, and the row total is the only one this change moved again, to
105. Six sentences carry them, so a reader meeting the figure a second time meets it wrong twice.
The appendix instructs its own reader to re-derive such a figure whenever a row's status changes,
and the item filed above it did not. The governance record states the same kind of derived figure,
of 108 detail blocks and 104 constraint checks, and a test does read that one: it failed on the
first run after the two rows here were added, which is the whole difference between a figure that is
checked and one that is only written down.

**BL-129: Collect the publication-conditional statements into a runbook**

- [x] List the statements that are true only while this repository is private, and record the search that finds them
- [x] Separate the live statements from the historical ones that must not be rewritten
- [x] Record the settings that become available on the day, and the one review that gates them
- [x] Link it from the entry points a maintainer would actually reach it by

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Twenty-one passages across ten files are true only while this repository is private, and they were
written that way on purpose: a security policy that describes a reporting route nobody can use is
worth more than one that pretends the route is there. The cost is deferred rather than avoided.
Publication falsifies all twenty-one in the same moment, none of them is a `path:line` claim, and so
no gate will notice. The publication gate and the surface gate both pass on a tree full of them,
because what they check is history and what the remote advertises rather than prose.

The list was wrong twice before it was right, and the second miss is the more instructive. The first
enumeration matched single lines against a pattern requiring the word "repository", so a passage
carried over two lines was invisible to it, and it missed both of `CHANGELOG.md`'s released notes
about protections that cannot be switched on yet. The second read passages rather than lines, and
still keyed every sweep on the private side of the phrasing, so it missed every passage written from
the public side. That is how a file quoting GitHub's own "make this repository public to enable this
feature" stayed off a list that already cited a block pointing straight at it.

So this no longer offers a count as its evidence. The runbook names every passage it holds, states
the rule for membership, and carries the search that finds them, whose recall was measured at
twenty-one of twenty-one with two false positives, both of which are sentences about the list rather
than members of it. A count is a claim a reader cannot check. A list with the search beside it is one
they can, and this item is the second time that difference was paid for rather than argued.

Ten of the twenty-one are in this file and two are in `CHANGELOG.md`. Eleven of those twelve sit
inside blocks recording what was true when a piece of work was delivered. Rewriting those would
corrupt a record to tidy a document, so the runbook marks them as history and leaves them alone. The
twelfth, in this file's introduction, is a live claim about which acceptance items cannot currently
be met, and that one does have to change.

Three settings are the actionable half: secret scanning with push protection behind it, private
vulnerability reporting, and branch protection on `main`. Each is free on a public repository and
refused on this one today, each was checked against the API rather than assumed, and each already
has an item recording the refusal. The runbook adds the ordering, since push protection is accepted
without secret scanning and then does nothing, which is the failure most likely to be mistaken for
success on the day.

None of it is enforced, and the runbook says so in its own last line rather than implying otherwise.
A gate for prose that is deliberately conditional would have to know when the condition changed, and
the only thing that knows that is the person changing it.

**BL-130: Shrink the open licence question before publication**

- [x] Produce the data tree without Marvel's description text, and measure what the app loses
- [x] Ask the upstream project what its stated licence is meant to cover
- [ ] Record both answers in the provenance document beside the questions they answer
- [x] Leave the review itself to BL-099, which this item does not close

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

BL-099 asks for a legal review and cannot be closed without one. This item is about the other
variable, which is the size of the question that review has to answer. Nothing here is a legal
opinion and nothing here decides anything. It makes the ask smaller and the answer cheaper, and
those are the only two things this side of the boundary controls.

The sharpest item is severable, and it was measured on 2026-08-15 rather than estimated. 798 of the
1,473 curated records carried a Marvel description, 151,840 characters in all, and the provenance
record already named that field as the one to look at hardest because it is Marvel's own prose
reproduced verbatim rather than a fact about a publication. Everything else in a record is an id, a
title, a number, a date, a series, a link or a creator credit.

Removing it costs one sentence on one screen. The field reaches the interface through exactly one
consumer at `src/js/main.js:2346`, and the function behind that line already answers for its
absence: `synopsisFallback` at `src/js/main.js:2534-2543` returns a sentence saying no synopsis is
recorded, for a record that was hydrated and came back without one, and a test already asserts it.
Catalog search does not read the field either, because the description it searches at
`src/js/lib/catalog.js:154` is the order's own one-line summary, written in this repository. So this
is a data change with a shipped fallback already waiting for it rather than a feature to build.

Drift: the field no longer reaches the interface at all. BL-134 closed the last path that could put
one into saved state, so `normalizeIssue` stopped carrying it and there is nothing left on a record
to read. The consumer named above is still the only one and still decides what a reader sees, but
what it now receives is a synopsis fetched for the session and held in memory. The sentence stands
as what this item shipped believing, and the count of screens it costs is now zero rather than one.

It is also reversible, which is worth establishing before anyone deletes anything. The upstream API
is still answering: the contract check ran on 2026-08-15 and 33 of 33 assumptions held across 17
requests. The descriptions can be fetched again by the vendoring script if the review comes back
permissive, so this is a decision that can be taken back rather than a one-way loss.

The second task is smaller and settles something this repository cannot answer from inside itself.
The third of the four open questions asks whether a licence stated in a README, with no licence text
and a package declaration scoped to a source directory, conveys anything for the two reading orders
vendored from that project's `data/` directory, which is outside it. Only the upstream maintainer
knows what was meant. The answer does not unblock publication either way, because that project does
not hold Marvel's rights and so cannot pass them on, but it replaces an inference with a statement
in a document whose whole purpose is to avoid inferring.

The first task shipped on 2026-08-15. All 798 descriptions are `null`, the key stays present on
every record so nothing downstream changes shape, `scripts/vendor-orders.mjs` writes `null` instead
of the fetched value with the reason in a comment beside it, and `test/licence-boundary.test.js`
fails if any returns. What the app loses, measured rather than predicted, is one sentence on one
screen: the 675 records that already carried no description render an absence today, 606 of them
through the sentence saying no synopsis is recorded and 69 through the sentence saying the snapshot
holds no record at all, and the 798 now join the first group. The contract check is deliberately
left asserting the field upstream, because that assertion is the evidence the change is reversible.

That first pass was incomplete, and how it was incomplete matters more than the shortfall. It read
`src/data/catalog.json`, walked the fourteen files listed there, and stopped. `design/mockups/mock-data.js`
is a generated projection of one of those orders, no catalog names it, and it held 41 more
descriptions totalling 7,193 characters, all 40 distinct values byte-identical to ones shipped under
`src/data/`. The guard test inherited the same blind spot, because it read the same catalog, so it
passed on a tree that still shipped the prose. Both now walk the tree rather than a list, and the
widened test was proven to fail on the un-stripped mockup with exactly 41 offenders. The provenance
document had never named `design/` either and now carries a subsection for it. This is the defect
shape the anchors gate's own header warns about, an enumeration somebody has to keep complete, met
in a second place.

One thing the strip does not reach, found while doing it and worth stating plainly rather than
leaving for someone to discover after publication: git history. 243 of the 246 commits then on
`main` carry the prose, and a clone of a public repository carries the whole history, so 455
distinct descriptions and 89,460 characters remain recoverable from it. The distinct figures run
below the 798 and 151,840 because the same issue sits in more than one reading order. Both figures
are raw character counts, measured the same way, which is worth saying because the first version of
this paragraph reported 89,558, the length after JSON escaping, and compared it to a raw count.
Rewriting history would reach it, this repository has never been public and has no forks so the cost
of doing so will never be lower, and publication is the moment that window shuts. That is a decision
for the owner and it is deliberately not taken here.

Drift: the first clause of that sentence is false, and the measurement that falsifies it is recorded
under BL-131. Rewriting history does not reach this prose, because the forge does not collect what a
force-push orphans and serves the orphans through the pull request refs among other doors. The
sentence stands as what this item shipped believing, which is the treatment this document gives a
superseded measured statement; what it asserts does not stand.

The obvious objection to this whole item is that other comic sites display this same prose, and it
was put on 2026-08-15 rather than left unasked. Answering it needed the terms the first hand
published, which can no longer be read from Marvel because the portal closed, so they were read from
an archived snapshot taken three weeks before it did. They separate the two acts this item turns on:
a licence to use the content inside an app, against an express refusal of the right to sublicense
it, to redistribute it outside an app, or to cache it indefinitely, with ownership stated to stay
with Marvel throughout. The two sites nearest this app's purpose display the prose and each forbids
anyone copying it back out, which is the same separation seen from the other side. That is evidence
bearing on the first of the four open questions rather than an answer to it, so it went into the
provenance document beside those questions, with the archive links and the date they were read, and
BL-099 is still the item that closes.

Shipped, with the third task deliberately left open, because it cannot be done yet and that is not a
gap in the work. The second task was completed on 2026-08-16 by asking the upstream project in the
open, at [emreparker/marvel-comics#2](https://github.com/emreparker/marvel-comics/issues/2), rather
than by private mail: the answer is citable that way, and it is useful to everyone else who vendored
from the same two checklists. The third task records the answers, and there are none yet. It stays
open until the maintainer replies, and this item is not reopened when they do; recording the reply is
a paragraph in the provenance document, not a change to anything the app does.

What the ask can achieve is bounded, and the bound is worth stating beside the item rather than
discovering later. It reaches the third of the four open questions and no other. The maintainer holds
nothing over Marvel's own material, so the friendliest possible answer conveys nothing about the
issue metadata, which is the first question and the one this item's own removal work was aimed at. A
reply is not permission, and this item does not become BL-099 by receiving one.

**BL-131: Decide the publication route, because a force-push cannot clean the history**

- [x] Decide, on the record, whether the description prose is to be removed from git history
- [x] Measure what a rewrite of the published branches would and would not reach
- [x] Verify the rewrite by re-running the evidence anchors gate and the full suite on the result
- [x] Choose a route that reaches what a force-push cannot, because pushing here does not
- [x] Record the chosen route and its reason in the publication runbook either way

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

This exists because BL-130 removed 798 Marvel descriptions from the working tree and that is not the
same as removing them from the repository. Measured on 2026-08-15: 243 of the 246 commits then on
`main` carry item description prose in the vendored orders, and 455 distinct descriptions totalling
89,460 characters are recoverable from them. The distinct figures sit below BL-130's 798 and 151,840
because the same issue appears in more than one reading order. A clone takes the whole history, so
what BL-130 achieved is that the app serves none of it and a checkout contains none of it, which is
most of the value and not all of it.

The reason this is not a note inside BL-130 is that it expires, and nothing else in this backlog
does. The repository has never been public and has no forks, so a rewrite today invalidates nobody's
clone and breaks nobody's fork. The moment it is published, both of those stop being true and the
prose is out irretrievably. That is the whole of the time criticality score, and it is why an item
worth 6.8 sits above things that will still be worth doing next year.

Neither answer is recommended here. A rewrite is destructive, it changes every commit id in the
repository, and it would invalidate `docs/anchors.lock.json` wholesale, so it is not a thing to do
casually or on an agent's judgement. Accepting the history is a legitimate answer too, and it is the
cheaper one. What is not legitimate is arriving at it by not noticing, which is what this item
prevents.

One thing to not misread on the way. `npm run publication` also scans history, and what it reports
is true of what it looks for, which is personal and credential-shaped content and the ignore rules
that keep session evidence local. It says nothing about third-party prose and was never meant to.
Its own header sets out both halves of its population at `scripts/check-publication.mjs:7-13`. A
green run there is not an answer to this item.

That paragraph was written while the gate still signed off with the words "the history is clean",
which is why it was needed. The wording was corrected in the same change, because the sentence was
accurate about the population and wrong about the reader: the one person most likely to run this
gate is the one about to publish, and this item is the thing they would take a green run to have
settled. The gate now names what it looked at instead of pronouncing on the history. The paragraph
stays because a document that only stops being wrong when someone reads the source is still wrong.

The owner decided on 2026-08-15 that the prose is to go, pending permission from a third party.
Acting on that decision turned up the thing this item had wrong, and it is the second task above
rather than the third because it had to be measured before anything could be chosen.

**A force-push does not reach it.** The forge does not collect what a force-push orphans, and its own
guidance names three places the commits survive one: clones and forks, cached views addressed
directly by their SHA-1, and any pull request that references them, retrieved 2026-08-16 from
`docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/removing-sensitive-data-from-a-repository`.
So the pull request refs below are the easiest door onto the residue rather than the cause of it, and
a repository with no pull requests at all would not be cleaned by a force-push either. This one has
116, and a forge serves every one of them a permanent `refs/pull/<n>/head` that the owner cannot
rewrite, delete or force past.
Those refs are not branches, so a clone does not receive them and the publication gate does not scan
them, but they are readable by anyone the moment the repository is public. Measured on 2026-08-15 by
fetching all 116 into a scratch clone: 85 of the heads are already unreachable from `main`, 32 blob
versions under them carry item prose, and what they hold is 455 distinct descriptions totalling
89,460 characters. Those are not similar to the figures in the paragraph above. They are the same
two numbers, so on the evidence a rewrite of the published branches removes none of the exposure it
was supposed to remove.

The check that settles it needs no rewrite to run. Four pull requests here were closed without
merging, their branches are long gone, and their heads are still fetchable today carrying between
396 and 508 descriptions each. That is the post-rewrite state already visible in the present tense,
which is why it is quoted rather than predicted.

What the refs hold is not what the discussions hold, and the difference bears on the route choice.
Scanning every pull request title and body here, 116 of them, together with the 44 issue and review
comments the forge returns for this repository, finds none of the 455 descriptions reproduced in
full. The one hit is a deliberately truncated 60-character excerpt in this branch's own pull request
body, quoted there to show what was being removed. So the exposure sits entirely in the code the
refs point at rather than in anything a person wrote, which makes losing the discussions a cost of
the new-repository route rather than a second leak that route would have to clean up. That scan also
re-derived the set it was searching for, taking it from the pre-strip `main` rather than from the
refs, and got 455 distinct descriptions totalling 89,460 characters: the same two numbers again, from
an independent direction.

The rewrite itself was built and verified anyway, because every route that does work needs it. It
replays history through git plumbing rather than `filter-repo`, which needs a Python this machine
does not have. Across 251 commits it rewrote 248 and left 3 untouched. That 248 is not the 243 of
246 above with this branch's commits added, and an earlier draft of this paragraph reconciled them
that way: a rewrite changes the object id of every commit from the first one it touches onward,
whether or not that commit carries prose, so 248 counts descendants where 243 counted carriers. The
comparable figure at the branch tip is 244 of 251 carrying prose, and the 3 untouched are the only
common ground between the two counts. Commit subjects, authors and dates are identical either side.
Two properties make it checkable rather than merely finished: applied to the
branch tip, which BL-130 already stripped, it reproduces that tree byte for byte, and applied to
`main`, which it had not, it produces exactly the 839 changes BL-130 made. No reachable blob in the
result carries prose.

That first property also retires a cost this item warned of. The paragraph above expects a rewrite
to invalidate `docs/anchors.lock.json` wholesale, and it does not: the lock fingerprints the content
at a path and a line, no commit id appears in it, and a rewrite that leaves the tip tree identical
leaves every one of the 809 anchors untouched. The expensive half of the fear was the wrong half.
The rewrite is cheaper than this item thought and reaches less than it thought, and only the second
of those changes the decision.

One risk in the new-repository route was hypothesised and then tested rather than left standing. The
lock holds 9 anchors targeting `src/data/` or `design/mockups/`, so a rewritten `main` could
plausibly have landed with a red gate on its first day. Two qualifications, both measured, and the
first corrects an earlier draft of this paragraph which called those nine exactly the files the
rewrite edits. They are not. The rewrite edits 14 files and only 2 of the 9 sit on one of them: the
mockups' generated data file at its first line, and the New Ultimate Universe trades order at its
first ten. The other seven cite a catalog file, two order notes and two mockup pages, none of which
carries an `items[]` description or is ever opened by the transform. Second, nothing moves in any
case, and that is a property of the transform rather than luck: it replaces each description value
with `null` in place instead of deleting the entry, so every file keeps its line count. Measured on
the file likeliest to break that, the mockups' generated data file is 1,215 lines before the rewrite
and 1,215 after. Do not read that across to the shipped strip on this branch, which is 1,219,
because BL-130 also replaced a one-line provenance header with five; the transform accounts for none
of those four lines. Run
against the rewritten `main` all seven gates are green: 0 drifted anchors, 963 tests passing, and
lint, counts, sizes, contrast and the publication gate clean. Note the 963 rather than 966, which is
main's own suite before this branch adds three, and note that it passes on a stripped tree, so
nothing on `main` asserted the prose was there.

So the remaining choice is not whether to rewrite but where to push the result, and it is the
owner's. Pushing it to this repository leaves all 455 behind the pull request refs. Pushing it to a
new repository leaves them behind in a repository that is never made public, and costs the pull
request discussions, which do not travel; the code history does, intact, including the six tracked
working artifacts. Asking the forge's support to purge what is left was described here as the only
route that keeps both, and that was wrong on both halves. Its published policy on the page cited
above says it will not remove non-sensitive data, and will assist on sensitive data only where the
risk cannot be mitigated by rotating a credential; third-party marketing prose is neither, so on the
published terms the route probably does not exist. The same page says the removal takes the internal
references that render pull request diffs with it, so even granted it would cost the diff view on
every closed pull request, which is most of what the route was supposed to preserve. What is genuinely
unknowable in advance is not the shape of the residue, which `git ls-remote origin 'refs/pull/*/head'`
enumerates today, but whether support would exercise discretion against its own published policy.

The scores stay as they are. The time criticality that put this at 6.8 was always about the moment
of publication, and that has not changed: it has moved from the last moment a rewrite is free to the
last moment the choice above is available at all.

**Resolved on 2026-08-16: accept.** The owner chose to leave the 455 descriptions in history and
behind the pull request refs, and to publish this repository as it stands rather than rebuild it
somewhere clean. Three things made that the cheaper answer. What is exposed is a third party's
marketing copy rather than anything private, so the harm it can do is a licensing question rather
than a security one. The working tree, the app and every checkout are already clean of it under
BL-130, so what remains is reachable only by someone who goes looking through the object store. And
the only route that would have removed it costs all 116 pull request discussions, which are most of
the record of how this repository was built. The rewrite is kept rather than discarded, because it
is what makes the decision reversible in the one direction that matters: if the rights holder ever
asks, the repository can be made private again and the new-repository route run then, on a transform
already proven to reproduce the tip byte for byte. What is not reversible is the exposure between
publication and that moment, and that is the risk being accepted rather than a gap in the plan.

**BL-132: Measure what the day-of rewrites cost the anchors gate, before they are made**

- [x] Count the citations pointing into the files that carry the publication-conditional passages
- [x] Separate the ones that break whatever is written from the ones that break only on a line shift
- [x] Prove the separation by experiment rather than by reading the gate
- [x] Record the cheaper method in the runbook, above the edits rather than below them
- [x] Check whether any test defends the prose, so a red suite is not mistaken for one that does

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

BL-129 collected the twenty-one passages publication makes false and said what each one asserts. It
did not say what rewriting them costs, and the answer is not small: nine files carry the ten live
passages, and 54 citations point into those nine. Left alone that is a 53 anchor round, run on the
night of the flip by whoever is also turning on three settings and reading a table of twenty-one
passages.

The useful part is that 39 of the 53 are avoidable. A citation sitting after an edit in the same
file breaks only when the replacement has a different line count from the passage it replaced, so
matching the count confines the round to the 14 that overlap a passage and cannot be saved. That is
a constraint on prose being rewritten anyway, which is what makes it worth stating rather than
merely true.

It was proved rather than reasoned, because reasoning about this gate has gone wrong here before.
The security policy's publication-conditional paragraph is six lines, and that file carries a
citation ninety lines below it. Replacing the six with six drifted two anchors, both overlapping the
paragraph. Replacing the six with eight drifted three, the third being the distant citation that no
edit had gone near. The experiment also corrected this item's own first count: classifying citations
by whether they begin before the first edit called a range running from line 29 to line 42 safe,
when it contains the paragraph and in fact breaks in both arms. Overlap is the test, not the start
line, and the figures above are the corrected ones.

The last acceptance item is there because a large red round invites the assumption that something
real broke. One assertion does pin this prose, and the first pass missed it by reading the test that
holds it and stopping at the wrong line. `test/intake-config.test.js:109-115` requires the security
policy's fallback sentence as well as the blank-issues setting, and that sentence is inside the
first rewritten passage. Matching every assertion in the suite against all ten passages returns that
one and nothing else, which is the check that should have been run in place of the reading.

**BL-133: Turn on the three settings publication unlocks, and make the conditional prose true**

- [x] Enable secret scanning, confirm its alerts endpoint answers, then enable push protection
- [x] Enable private vulnerability reporting and verify it by reading the setting back
- [x] Set branch protection on `main` and verify the rules by reading them back
- [x] Rewrite the ten live passages publication makes false, each to its own line count
- [x] Close the acceptance tasks those settings were blocking, without rewriting their records

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The repository was published on 2026-08-16, which is the event BL-129 wrote the runbook for and
BL-132 costed. Three settings that had been refused outright became available. All three were turned
on and then read back rather than assumed to have taken: secret scanning and push protection both
report `enabled`, private vulnerability reporting answers `{"enabled":true}`, and the branch rules
read back with three required checks. Secret scanning found nothing, which is the answer a
repository whose history was examined at length in BL-131 wanted to hear.

The order the runbook insisted on was real rather than cautious. Push protection was left alone
until the alerts endpoint stopped answering 404, and it answered with an empty list once scanning
was on. Asking for push protection first is accepted and changes nothing, and that trap is still
written down in the security policy, because it stays true for anyone forking this repository even
though it is no longer true here.

Branch protection needed a decision the task had left open, because "the intended reviews and
checks" cannot both be had. The checks are documented: `GOVERNANCE.md:44-49` says the maintainer
does not merge past a red gate, so the three continuous integration contexts are required, taken
from a real run rather than derived from the workflow file, which is where a matrix job's name is
easy to guess wrong. A required review is not documented anywhere and cannot be satisfied here:
there is one collaborator, GitHub never asks a pull request's author to approve it, and the rule
would either block every merge or be bypassed by the same person it was meant to constrain. It is
refused for that reason rather than omitted. Force pushes and branch deletion are refused outright,
which is the part that matters most to a repository that decided in BL-131 to keep its history. The
endpoint that answered 403 on two measured days now answers 404 "Branch not protected", which is
what a readable and unset endpoint says, so the wall BL-098 recorded is down rather than moved.

BL-132's advice held. Every one of the ten replacements was written to the same line count as the
passage it replaced, so no citation downstream of an edit moved and the round stayed inside the
overlapping few. The tenth was not on the runbook's list: its search had found the sentence in
`README.md` that points at the runbook and had filed it as a false positive, "a sentence about the
list rather than a member of it", when it also asserts in the present tense that the repository is
private and that three settings cannot be switched on. A review found it; the search had already
found it and let it go. The eleven passages the runbook marks as history were left exactly as they
are, including the three that still read in the present tense about settings that are now on, because a
delivery record says what was true when the work was delivered. What changed instead is four
acceptance boxes, which are live status rather than narrative: BL-089's scanning, BL-096's private
route, BL-098's branch rules, and BL-039's long-open task to make the run required before merge,
which is the same setting arriving from a different direction.

A review found that distinction drawn too narrowly. Three of those four blocks also say in prose
that the box is unticked or the task is open, and that is not a claim about what was measured on a
past date but a claim about the document a reader is holding, so it went false the moment the box
was ticked. Each of the three now carries a dated closing line recording what publication changed,
appended rather than written over the paragraph, because all three of those paragraphs are cited
from the runbook's history list and rewriting one would falsify the citation. BL-039's equivalent
sentence is cited by nothing, checked against the lock rather than assumed, so it was corrected in
place instead. The rule the four cases share is that a delivery record may say what was true then,
but not what is true now about its own ticks.

One thing the runbook did not anticipate about itself. It exempts itself from its own list, on the
grounds that a runbook is spent by the event it describes, and that is right about its prose and
wrong about its citations: the nine rows name passages by `path:line`, the gate holds those claims
live whether the document is spent or not, and rewriting the passages changed what those lines say.
Leaving it alone would have meant blessing "private reporting cannot be turned on here" onto a line
that says it was turned on, which is the corruption the gate exists to prevent rather than a pass.
The document is stamped as executed and its table header put into the past tense instead, which is
cheaper than rewriting it and keeps every row true as a record of what the passage used to say.

**BL-134: Fetch a synopsis at read time instead of shipping one**

- [x] Close every path that writes an issue synopsis to saved state
- [x] Keep the prose out of both caches, and empty the one that already holds it
- [x] Fetch a whole reading order on request, sequentially, behind a provenance disclaimer
- [x] Prove each promise with a check observed to fail without its fix

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

BL-130 removed 798 Marvel descriptions from the vendored data and measured the cost as one sentence
on one screen. That measurement was honest and it was also the whole of what the app then offered:
every curated issue now answers "No synopsis is recorded for this issue", including the 798 that used
to say something. This item is the other half of that trade. The prose is fetched from the same
service the app already asks for covers and reader links, it is shown, and it is never written down.

The four promises are structural rather than procedural, which is the only reason they are worth
believing. `normalizeIssue` no longer carries the field, and both `upsertIssue` and `coerce` reach
saved state through it, so there is one gate rather than a rule to remember. `SynopsisRunner` at
`src/js/synopsis.js:89` writes only to a `Map` and never calls `store.update`, so the promise holds by
construction. `withoutSynopsis` at `src/js/api.js:34` strips the field before the response cache is
written, and every request now carries `cache: 'no-store'` at `src/js/api.js:95` and again on the
reader launch path, which fetches the same endpoint from a different module.

The browser's own cache is the store the plan missed and the critique found. It is on disk, it is
written by the same fetch, and the settings screen's button to clear cached metadata cannot reach it.
Without the directive the memory-only promise would have held in every store except the one a reader
has no way to inspect, which is the worst place for it to fail.

Two more critique findings were quiet failures rather than visible ones. `ResponseCache.clear` used to
return nothing and swallow its errors, so `purgeStaleCache` at `src/js/main.js:655` would have recorded
a purge that never ran and left thirty days of unstripped prose sitting there with the app believing it
gone; the clear now reports, and the marker only advances on success. The marker is merged from storage
at write time rather than from the settings snapshot, because settings are read once at boot and
written whole, so a tab left open across the upgrade would have erased the marker on the reader's next
theme toggle.

The run is sequential with a lookahead of eight, which was the owner's decision and turned out to
match a shape the hydrator already had. Extracting it as `lookaheadPriority` at
`src/js/lib/model.js:831` exposed a defect in the original: it sliced the first nine ids and then
filtered, so a reader resuming a list whose first issues were already answered got a group of nothing
and a run that stopped. Applying the predicate first is a behaviour change to hydration as well, made
deliberately, because eight useful answers is what the number was always for.

The disclaimer at `src/js/main.js:2881` is shown every time a run starts rather than once and
remembered, by owner decision, and the reading order is captured before the dialog opens so a reader
who switches list while it is up does not start a run against the list they left.

Ten mechanisms were each reverted on their own and every one named the tests that defend it, which is
a sharper measurement than reverting the modules and watching the suite go red. The proof script had
to be repaired before it proved anything: its first run reported five of the ten as skipped, because
its anchors were written with Unix line endings against a tree checked out with Windows ones, so it
matched nothing and said so in the same shape as a pass. That is this repository's rule about checks
never seen to fail, met one level above the checks.

What this does not do is make the app work offline or faster. A run competes with hydration for the
same twenty requests per ten seconds, so "a synopsis in seconds" is the best case rather than the
promise, and the first session after upgrading is slower because the cache is emptied once. Both are
recorded in the changelog rather than left for a reader to report as a fault.

Two independent reviews of the change found nine defects between them and all nine were fixed in it.
Three were the same class of fault, a claim the interface makes that the code cannot support: a run
in which every lookup failed still announced that all synopses were fetched, an issue the service had
just answered "no synopsis" for still read as not yet fetched, and the disclaimer named one service
by hand while the reader is free to point the app at another. The remaining six were quieter. A
response landing after a cancel was recorded before the guard that was supposed to stop it, so prose
appeared that the "stopped after n of m" count had already excluded. `synopsisOrder` queued
already-read issues ahead of unread ones, against its own comment. Nothing capped the length of a
fetched synopsis once `normalizeIssue` stopped carrying the field that used to. `ResponseCache.clear`
reported success from a transaction that could still roll back, which is the same false success the
purge marker exists to prevent. Changing the service address left the run still asking the old one.
And saved state that already held prose from before the upgrade was cleaned in memory on every load
and never written back, so it sat on disk indefinitely; it is now rewritten once, on the load that
finds it. Seven of the nine are proven by reverting the fix alone and naming the test that goes red,
and the other two by driving a real browser.

A third review, this one aimed only at the nine fixes, found one defect they had left behind and
confirmed the rest. The partial ending stopped a finished run claiming answers it never got, but the
same count runs through the stopped ending too, and `done` is incremented for a refused request
exactly as for an answered one. So a reader who stopped a failing run was told it had fetched what it
had in fact failed to reach, next to a hero still saying no synopsis is recorded. The count now
subtracts what could not be reached and names it, as the finished ending already did. Extracting the
line as `synopsisStatusLine` is what makes that testable: it was inline in a renderer that needs a
document, so the visible half of the earlier fix had been proven only in a browser while its spoken
half had a unit test. Both halves of this one are proven by reverting each in turn.

That review also found the transaction fault's own test weaker than it looked. The double that stands
in for IndexedDB did not roll back an aborted transaction, so the test could assert only the returned
value and not the thing the value describes, which is that the prose is still in the store. The
double rolls back now and the test says so, and removing the rollback turns exactly that assertion
red. A fake that cannot express the difference between two contracts cannot tell you which one you
have.

A fourth review, aimed at that fix, found the same counter read a third time and left unsubtracted:
the line shown while a run is going. The arithmetic there was no more wrong than it had been, but
fixing two of the three reads is worse than fixing none, because the three had at least agreed with
each other before. Measured against the real runner on a run losing two of its first three, the
reader watched the number climb to 3 and pressing stop rewrote it to 1, so the count appeared to go
backwards at the one moment it was being looked at. The running line now subtracts and names the
failures exactly as the two endings do, so the number a stop leaves behind is the number that was
already showing. It also holds still while a wholly failing run works through its queue, which reads
as stalled and is the honest report, so the failure count beside it is what shows the run is moving.

That review also noted `synopsisStatusLine` was exported without the guard its only caller applies,
so calling it before a run had started returned the sentence for a run that had finished. It returns
nothing for that case now, which is what the renderer has always done with it. Both are proven by
reverting each alone, and the harness that proves them was itself wrong first: it filtered for a TAP
failure line against a runner that prints the spec reporter, so it reported every mechanism green
including ones that were genuinely broken. It reads the fail total back as a cross-check now.

A fifth review found the change's own record overstating it. The commit and the pull request both
said the browser check had gained three assertions, and the committed browser check had gained none:
the assertions were real and had been watched failing, but they lived in a script outside the tree,
which is the arrangement `scripts/browser-check.mjs:3-7` was written to end. Seven of them are the
committed check's sixth journey now, driven against a service that refuses every request on a delay,
and what they carry is the claim this round was about. All four ways the fix can be undone were run
rather than reasoned about, and they do not agree. Taking the whole series back to the shapes it
started from turns four of the seven red and prints no pair. Reverting the running line's subtraction
alone turns two red, and the second of those is the one that prints both lines beside each other, a
run showing one fetched followed by a stop reporting none. Reverting both subtractions turns two red
and prints no pair, because the stopped line then agrees with the running one. Taking the running line
all the way back to its pre-series shape, which drops the clause naming what could not be reached as
well as the subtraction, turns three red and prints the same pair. The wait that gets the scenario to
that point counts refusals in the harness rather than reading them off the status line, because a
scenario that waited for the line to name a refusal could only ever be satisfied by the behaviour it
exists to be able to find missing, and on a broken build it would time out instead of naming the claim
that failed. The rest of this feature's browser evidence is still out of tree, and is BL-138.

A sixth review then measured that sentence and found the revert it named producing a different number,
and three later passes found, in turn, that conclusion wrong, the first account of why it was wrong
wrong as well, and one clause of the second account wrong after that. The sentence said reverting the
subtraction turns three of the six red and prints the pair. Reverting the subtraction alone turns two,
and the sixth review concluded that three was a figure no revert produced. That conclusion contradicted
the paragraph above it, which already recorded the running line's pre-series shape at three red, and it
mis-assigned the figure besides, saying the larger count belonged to the full revert, which reddens
four. So the gap was never an unrun revert. It was a red count nobody read back against the conclusion
drawn a few lines below it, and a pair nobody looked for on the build that carries that count. The
sixth review had found the pair on the subtraction-alone build and recorded it; what nobody checked was
whether the three-red build prints it too, and it does, in the same run, so the sentence was
reproducible and its fault was naming the subtraction for a revert of the whole line. Recording it that
way rather than keeping the tidier version, in which the earlier round had simply not looked, is the
same rule this series exists to enforce, applied to the series. The sixth review also found the stopped
line's failure clause unguarded, which is why the journey now carries seven assertions rather than six:
deleting the clause this series began by adding left every other assertion green, so the first fix of
the series was the one part of it nothing watched. The full revert reddens four rather than three
because of that seventh.

The mutation aimed at this scenario was replaced in the same round, and that stands on its own
evidence rather than on the disputed sentence. It had made the metadata service answer instead of
refuse, which starved the wait and reddened only the harness's catch-all row, so
`npm run browser:prove` recorded that the scenario could break without recording that any claim in it
could fail. It now rewrites the running line to report attempts rather than answers, which is the
miscount the scenario exists to catch, and it reddens two named claims and prints the side-by-side
pair as its own evidence. The pair was reproducible before by reverting the tree by hand, which is a
thing a reader has to be told to do and has to do correctly; it is printed by a committed check now.

**BL-135: Refuse an issue synopsis at the boundary that writes, not only at the one that reads**

- [ ] Reject issue prose where saved state is written, rather than where each writer builds its value
- [ ] Reject it again where a backup is exported, so a copy cannot carry what state may not
- [ ] Prove the guard fires by writing prose past `normalizeIssue` and watching it refuse

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

BL-134's promise that no synopsis reaches saved state holds today, and it holds by enumeration. Five
places write `state.issues`; four reach it through `normalizeIssue`, which no longer carries the
field, and the fifth is a cache read whose single caller strips it first. That was checked rather
than assumed, and finding no live defect is why this is an enabler rather than a fault. But an
enumeration is a list somebody has to keep complete, which is the shape of defect this repository's
anchors gate exists because of, and a sixth writer added later would breach the promise silently.

A guard at `Store.update` and at `exportBackup` turns the promise into one that cannot be broken by
adding code elsewhere. `exportBackup` copies the map verbatim at `src/js/lib/model.js:1120`, so it is
the second boundary rather than a duplicate of the first: a backup written before the guard existed,
restored after it, would otherwise reintroduce exactly what the guard refuses.

The open question is what refusing should mean. Throwing turns a licensing promise into a crash on a
path readers depend on; stripping silently keeps the app working and hides the bug that a test would
otherwise catch. Stripping plus a console warning is the likely answer, because the promise is about
what reaches disk and nothing about the reader's session needs to end for it to be kept.

**BL-136: Decide what happens to the prose in copies kept for recovery**

- [ ] Say in one place whether a recovery copy is rewritten, left alone, or discarded
- [ ] Apply that decision to the pre-restore copy and to every salvage copy
- [ ] Prove the decision by observing a copy taken before the upgrade and read after it

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The load path now rewrites saved state once when it finds descriptions left over from before
BL-134, which closes the ordinary case. It does not touch the copies kept so that a failed restore
or an unreadable state can still be recovered. The pre-restore copy is written from the raw prior
value at `src/js/storage.js:547`, and the salvage copies are the same shape, so any of them taken
before the upgrade still holds the prose that the main key no longer does.

Rewriting them is not obviously right and that is the whole of this item. These are the copies that
exist because something already went wrong, they are the least exercised paths in the app, and a
rewrite that fails leaves a reader with neither their state nor the copy of it. Discarding them
outright is worse. Leaving them is defensible: they are transient, the pre-restore copy is cleared
on the next successful restore, and nothing displays their contents.

So the deliverable is a decision written down and applied consistently, not a change of behaviour
chosen in advance. Whichever way it goes, the promise BL-134 makes should say what it means for a
copy taken to survive a failure, because at present it is silent and a reader would reasonably read
it as covering everything on disk.

**BL-137: Close the window a tab left open across the one-time purge is writing into**

- [ ] Stop a tab loaded before the upgrade from writing unstripped responses into the shared cache
- [ ] Stop it from rewinding the purge marker the new tab has already advanced
- [ ] Prove both by driving two contexts against one cache

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The one-time purge at `src/js/main.js:661` empties the response cache once, so the prose cached
before BL-134 goes. A tab that was already open when the upgrade landed is still running the old
code, still caching unstripped responses into the same shared store, and still holding the old
settings snapshot, so its next write can move the purge marker back and buy the next session a
second purge.

Neither consequence is severe, which is why this ranks where it does. The stale tab's own writes are
bounded by how long it stays open, the marker rewind self-heals as one repeat slow session, and both
require the reader to have left a tab open across a version change and then used it. It is recorded
because the cost of finding it later, from a report of the app being slow twice, is far higher than
the cost of writing it down now.

The likely shape is a version stamp the cache carries, so a write from code that predates the purge
is refused by the store rather than by the writer. That is the same reasoning as BL-135: a guard at
the boundary holds without every writer having to remember, and here the writer is a tab that cannot
be updated because it is already running.

**BL-138: Bring the rest of the synopsis browser evidence into the committed check**

- [ ] Port the four consent assertions: the disclaimer opens before any request, names the service and the promise, nothing is fetched before consent, and declining starts no run
- [ ] Port the five durability assertions: every issue request carries `no-store`, no saved issue, no `localStorage` key and no IndexedDB store holds fetched prose after a run, and a reload loses every synopsis
- [ ] Port the four service-change assertions: the new address is saved, prose from the previous service is dropped, the disclaimer names the address just typed, and the next run asks it rather than the one before
- [ ] Port the two legacy assertions: prose saved by an older build was really there to begin with, and is rewritten out of storage rather than only out of memory
- [ ] Port the ten that are none of those: the import, the two button affordances, progress being reported at all, the stop button replacing the fetch button while running, the current issue landing inside the first nine asked for, a stop halting further requests, what a cancel says is kept for the tab, a synopsis being displayed, and an issue the run asked about no longer saying it is unfetched
- [ ] Aim a mutation at each ported group, so `npm run browser:prove` records which scenario each one reddens

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

BL-134 shipped with its browser evidence in a script outside the tree, which is the exact shape
`scripts/browser-check.mjs:3-7` exists to end: verification that was real and that a clean clone
could rerun none of. Seven of those assertions came in with the fix to the running count, because
they were that change's own evidence. Twenty-five did not.

Most of the twenty-five carry the part of the promise the ported seven do not touch: that nothing is
fetched before the reader consents, and that nothing fetched is ever written down. Ten are neither,
and the fifth bullet above exists because an earlier draft of this block described all of them as
consent and durability, which a review measured and found false. Its own figure of nine did not
survive being re-derived either: the four groups and the remainder are counted out in the bullets now
so the split adds up in the open rather than resting on a number nobody can check. They are the
ordinary furniture of the journey, and they are worth porting for the same reason as the rest.

That is the argument for the item rather than against the split. Prose that never reaches storage is
the whole claim of BL-134, and the only committed check of it is a unit test against a double. A
browser holds the real IndexedDB, the real `localStorage` and the real page, so it is the one place
the claim can be checked rather than argued.

The port is not a copy. The out-of-tree script runs a single long journey against a stub of its own,
while the committed harness gives each scenario its own browser context and installs its stub before
the app loads, so each ported group has to stand up as a scenario on its own. Three mechanics are
already known from porting the first seven: the stub has to answer from `preparePage`, because one
installed after load is a stub the app has already gone past; a refusal has to be delayed, because an
immediate one empties the queue before a click on stop can land; and a mutation aimed at a ported
group has to break a named assertion rather than starve a wait, or the prove pass records that the
scenario can fail without recording that any claim in it can.

**BL-139: Let the browser install the tracker, so it has a window and an icon of its own**

- [x] Serve a web app manifest, with every path in it origin-relative
- [x] Draw the app icons from a source anyone can read, rather than committing an opaque image
- [x] Check each manifest claim against the file or origin it claims about
- [x] Say in the README that installing does not remove the need to start the server

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 4 is the one worth stating: the icon
generator is a build script that runs on a maintainer's machine, uses only `node:zlib`, and adds
nothing to `package.json`. Nothing new reaches the browser except three static files: the manifest
and the two icons it names.

The app was a tab you had to find again, which is a poor home for something opened most days. A
manifest is what lets a browser offer to install a page, and it costs one link element and three
static files. Nothing about how the app runs changes: the installed window is the same origin, so
`mrt.state.v2` is the same key and the reading progress is the one already there, which is what
Constraint 5 makes the deciding question for any change to how the app is opened. The two paths
that decide where an installed window lands, at `src/manifest.webmanifest:6-7`, are origin-relative
for exactly that reason. An absolute address
would have pinned an installed window to 8787 and quietly emptied the app for anyone running on
another port, which is the same defect the README's warning about the address is written against.

The icons were the part with a real decision in them. Chromium will not offer an install unless the
manifest names PNG icons at 192 and 512 pixels, so the inline SVG the tab icon uses cannot serve
here, and a committed PNG is a file no reviewer can read and nobody can regenerate. So the mark is
written as geometry at `scripts/build-icons.mjs:29-37` and the bytes are produced from it, which
makes the two images a build output with a source in the same way the vendored indexes are. The
test redraws both and compares pixels rather than file bytes, because the compressed form depends
on the zlib the build ran against and the suite runs on two Node versions, so a byte comparison
would go red for a reason that has nothing to do with the picture.

A maskable icon was considered and refused. It exists so Android can crop an icon to whatever shape
the launcher uses, and this app cannot run on a phone at all, because the page is served by a
program running on the same machine. Shipping one would have been a third file, drawn to a padding
rule nobody here can check against a device.

Both new checks were proved able to fail before they were trusted. Removing the manifest link from
the page turns one red, and widening the glyph stroke in the generator without regenerating turns
the pixel comparison red, which is the case that matters: it is the one that catches a committed
icon quietly ceasing to be the icon the source describes.

The two insertions moved 68 citations of `src/index.html` and `package.json`. Both shifts were
derived twice, once from the diff hunks and once by searching each file for the head the lock
already held, and the two agreed on all 68. No range spanned an insertion point in
`src/index.html`; four spanned it in `package.json`, all of them whole-file or whole-block ranges
whose end moved and whose start did not.

**BL-140: Give the tracker a file a non-engineer can double-click to start it**

- [x] Add a launcher for each of the two desktop platforms this app is used on
- [x] Make each one work from wherever the project was unzipped, not from wherever the shell was
- [x] Say what to do when Node.js is missing, in the window, rather than closing it
- [x] Leave the address alone, so a launched app is the same app with the same progress
- [x] Test the contract, because the reader of these files cannot diagnose them

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 5 is the one this item is most able to
breach and the one its tests are built around: a launcher that set `MRT_PORT`, or that opened
`localhost`, would put a reader on an origin their reading progress is not filed under, and the
symptom is an empty app rather than an error.

BL-139 gave the tracker an icon, and an icon is a promise that clicking it opens something. What it
did not do was remove the terminal, and the terminal is where the audience for all of this stops
reading: "open a terminal, change directory, type a command" is three instructions, each of which
can fail in a way that produces a message written for somebody else. The file a person opens by
double-clicking it is the whole feature, and there is almost nothing to it.

Almost nothing, but not nothing, and the parts that are not nothing are all failure modes that
happen on a machine nobody here is sitting at. A double-clicked script does not start in the
project folder, so both files move there first and both tests check the move happens before the
server is started. A `.command` with Windows line endings is refused by the kernel before its first
line runs, with a message naming an interpreter the reader never typed, so `.gitattributes` pins
the endings of both extensions and a test reads the blob as git holds it rather than as this
machine checked it out. The executable bit is recorded in the git index for the same reason: a
clone that loses it produces a permission error rather than an app.

The Windows file is written as one-line statements and gotos rather than parenthesised blocks. That
is not a style preference. `cmd.exe` has never parsed a multi-line block reliably in a file with
Unix line endings, and the reader this is for arrives by "Download ZIP", where the endings are the
archive's decision rather than this repository's. The pinning above makes CRLF likely; writing the
file so it does not care makes it certain, and a test holds that shape by refusing any line that
ends in an opening parenthesis.

Every one of the 8 checks was proved able to fail, by eleven single-change mutations applied one at a
