time and each reverted before the next. Nine were edits to the two launchers and to `.gitattributes`:
removing either directory change, setting a port, naming localhost, opening a parenthesised block,
removing the address for Node.js, removing the pauses, misspelling the server file, and unpinning the
endings. The remaining two checks are about how git holds the file rather than what is in it, so no
edit reaches them and the mutations are index operations: untracking the macOS launcher, which turns
both of those checks red, and clearing its executable bit, which turns one. All eleven named the test
that defends them. Two earlier drafts of the suite did not: one assertion read the file with its
comments left in and so was satisfied by a paragraph describing the command rather than by the
command, and it was rewritten before it was trusted.

The Windows launcher was then run for real. The server printed its startup banner and `curl`
returned 200 for the page, the manifest and the 192 pixel icon. The macOS file is the same contract
in bash and is checked by the same tests, but it has not been run on a Mac by anyone here, which is
stated rather than implied.

**BL-141: Let the installed window open when the server is not running**

- [x] Keep a copy of the app in the browser, so an installed window has something to open
- [x] Take that copy on the first visit, which is the visit somebody installs the app on
- [x] Ask the network first every time, so nobody running the server is served a stale page
- [x] Store nothing from another origin, so no comic image byte can enter the copy
- [x] Make a failed store impossible to turn into a failed page
- [x] Prove the whole thing in a real browser, with the server genuinely stopped

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 1 is the one a service worker is most
able to breach, because caching whatever the page asks for is the obvious way to write one and
cover images are exactly what the page asks for most. It is answered structurally rather than by
care: the worker declines to answer any request for another origin at all, covers come from Marvel's
CDN and issue metadata from the third-party service, so neither can enter the store even by
accident. The browser probe below read the store back and found nothing in it from another origin.

BL-139's own record said the install "does not start the app for you", and that an installed window
opened with nothing running "will simply say the site cannot be reached". That was true and it was
the defect. An icon that works only when a terminal is already running is an icon that is wrong most
of the time, and the reader has no way to tell a stopped server from a broken app: both are the same
browser error page.

Network first, cache second, and never the other way round. While the server is running every
response comes from it, so an edited file is seen immediately and the no-cache and ETag behaviour in
`server.mjs` keeps working exactly as written. The store is consulted only when the fetch fails,
which is the case this exists for. A cache-first worker is the shape people reach for and it is
worse in the one way that is hardest to notice: it works perfectly until somebody edits a file, and
then it serves yesterday's copy with nothing on screen to say so. A deliberately cache-first version
of this worker passed every other test in the suite, which is why the test that catches it exists.

Nothing is precached. A precache is a list somebody has to keep complete, which is the same defect
class `scripts/check-anchors.mjs` refuses to enumerate for, and it is the one that goes wrong
silently. The shell is instead asked of the browser: `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')`
already knows every URL the page fetched, so the list describes itself and cannot fall behind the
files it names. The page re-fetches that list once, on the first visit only, and every answer goes
through the worker on the way back. The browser probe recorded 31 stored entries after one visit,
which is the whole app.

The first visit is the whole difficulty, and the first version of this item got it wrong. The worker
is registered after `boot()`, so the document, the stylesheet and all 26 modules of the first visit
had already been fetched before any worker existed to see them, and the app makes no further
same-origin requests afterwards. `clients.claim()` did take control, which made the mistake easy to
miss, but taking control of a page that has stopped asking for anything stores nothing. Measured in
Edge on a cleared profile: one visit left **0 entries**, and stopping the server then gave "can't
reach this page" from the installed icon. That is the exact failure this item exists to prevent, and
it would have hit the reader most likely to hit it, the one who installs the app the moment the
browser offers to. The warm-up closes it, and it is gated on the page having arrived uncontrolled so
it is paid once rather than on every visit forever.

The most dangerous code here is the code that stores things, and it is dangerous in the direction
this repository has been caught in twice: the protection taking away the thing it protects. A cache
write can be refused, for quota or for a partial response, and an uncaught refusal would turn a page
that had just been fetched successfully into a failed load. So the store is best effort and its
catch is the point of the function rather than decoration, and only a status of exactly 200 is
offered to it. Removing that catch turns a test red, which is how it is known to be load-bearing.

The store is also kept off the reader's path and out of everybody else's cupboard. It is handed to
`event.waitUntil` rather than awaited, so a healthy server's response is not held behind a disk
write on every navigation, stylesheet and module, and the clone is taken before returning because
the browser consumes the body it is given. The read is scoped to this worker's own cache by name:
`caches.match()` searches every cache on the origin, activation deliberately leaves caches this
worker did not create alone, and `127.0.0.1:8787` is an address anything on the machine may have
used, so the unscoped form could have answered a reader with a page this app has never seen.

Verified in Edge, twice, with the tree changed between the two runs. With the worker present: the
registration activates, the page is controlled and its shell stored on the **first** load, 31
same-origin entries and none from any other origin, and then with the server killed a fresh tab
opened at the manifest's `start_url` returns 200 and renders the whole app, 12 catalog cards and
all. With `src/sw.js` stashed and nothing else changed: nothing registers, nothing is stored, and
the same fresh tab shows `ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED` and Edge's own "can't reach this page", which is
the exact sentence the README used to promise. That pair is the item.

Every one of the 25 checks was proved able to fail. Twenty-six single-change mutations of the
worker, its registration and the server were applied one at a time, each reverted before the next:
dropping the origin guard, dropping the GET guard, caching a non-200, removing the quota catch,
deleting caches this worker did not create, precaching on install, answering from the cache first,
fetching without storing, never consulting the store when the network fails, answering a total
failure with a reply of our own, registering with a root-absolute path, letting a failed
registration reject, assuming service worker support exists, attempting an origin the browser does
not trust, serving JavaScript as plain text so registration is refused, searching every cache on the
origin, awaiting the write in front of the response, dropping the same-origin filter from the shell
list, leaving the document out of it, keeping fragments in it, letting one failed fetch abandon the
rest, warming with no worker in control, never waiting for control, waiting for control the page
already had, never warming, and warming on every visit. All twenty-six turned a named test red. The
last two are the same line read both ways, never warming and always warming, and each turned exactly
one test red: that line is the whole of whether the first visit is stored, so it is worth knowing
which check would notice if it were ever changed back.

What this does not do is make the app work offline in any wider sense. Issue details and covers come
from other origins and are deliberately untouched, so an offline launch shows what you have already
seen and what you have already saved, and says nothing new. The metadata service being unreachable
is a state the app already handles and already reports. Two things are left for later and neither
blocks this: the stored copy is not counted in the "cache usage" figure under About, which measures
a different store entirely, and a worker registered by this version would outlive the deletion of
`src/sw.js` if that ever happened, because nothing here unregisters one.

**BL-142: Add twelve reading orders compiled from Comic Book Herald guides**

- [x] Compile a Captain America order, a Doctor Doom primer, a Spider-Man order, a Thor order and a
  Scarlet Witch order
- [x] Compile the seven Avengers orders that together run from 1963 to the Fresh Start era
- [x] Resolve every issue against Marvel's own metadata rather than against the guide's prose
- [x] Name every row that could not be resolved, in the file, rather than dropping it quietly
- [x] Credit the guides for what was actually taken from them, and no more

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 4 is the one a batch this size invites a
breach of, because twelve orders is where somebody reaches for a scraper library. Nothing was added
to `package.json`: the generators are throwaway scripts that ran outside the tree and are not
committed, and the only thing committed is their output. Constraint 2 is answered the same way. No
page on `marvel.com` or `read.marvel.com` was fetched by anything here; the guides were read by a
person, and every issue behind them was resolved from the metadata mirror the repository already
uses.

Twelve orders, 1,178 items, 1,151 distinct issues drawn from 87 series. Every one resolved: no
placeholders, no missing digital ids, no missing covers, and no record that came back empty. That
last figure is not luck. The latest on-sale date anywhere in the twelve is 2020-02-12, comfortably
inside the window the retired developer portal covered, so none of them land in the gap that leaves
63 bare records in the two Ultimate orders.

The debt to Comic Book Herald is real and it is narrow, and BL-106 is the precedent for saying so
carefully. What was taken is the selection and the grouping: which runs are worth reading and which
arcs belong together. What was not taken is the issue-level sequence, which the guides mostly do not
give, or the identifiers, or the metadata. Those were resolved here, issue by issue, and in one case
the resolution contradicted the guide outright. So the credit line reads "Compiled for this project
from Comic Book Herald's guide" and links to the page, which says both halves: the guide chose the
shape, this repository built the contents.

The resolution rule was settled once, in advance, rather than row by row, because the alternative was
forty separate judgement calls made in the dark. Marvel's metadata wins wherever a guide's volume
label disagrees with it. A nested range ships once, as the containing range. A row with no issue
numbers resolves to the whole run. Sections keep the guide's order. And anything genuinely
unresolvable is named in the file's own header, never guessed at and never silently dropped.

That last clause did most of the work. Nine rows are named as unresolvable, and they fall into three
honest kinds. Two are not issues at all: `Triumph & Torment` is a trade paperback in the metadata and
`Marvel Graphic Novel #27` is a graphic novel, so neither has an issue record to link. One is absent
from Marvel's series index entirely, the 1994 `Scarlet Witch` mini. And one is a hole in the mirror
rather than in the guide: `Astonishing Tales (1970) #8` is missing while #7 and #9 to #24 are
present. That last pair took the whole Cynthia von Doom section of the Doom primer with them, which
is recorded in that file rather than papered over, because a section that quietly shrank to nothing
is worse than a section that says why it did.

The single most dangerous row was the one that looked easiest. The Spider-Man guide lists "Coming
Home" as `Amazing Spider-Man #30-35`, and there is an `Amazing Spider-Man #30-35` in the 1963 volume:
six real issues, published 1965, about the Cat Burglar. The arc meant is the 1999 relaunch. Nothing
in the guide's text distinguishes them and both resolve cleanly, so this is the kind of error that
ships looking correct and is found by a reader years later. It was caught by checking each resolved
issue's on-sale year against the era the section claims, which is now the reason that check exists.

Two smaller traps were found the same way. Marvel numbers point issues inside several of the named
ranges, and they are real issues rather than artefacts: `#699.1`, `#6.5`, `#1.5`, `#12.1`, `#21.1`,
and `#1.1` through `#4.1` of Avengers (2016). All are included and all are recorded, and the last
four are the entire reason the All-New All-Different order holds 92 items where the arithmetic on the
guide says 88. Separately, the mirror carries four genuine duplicates, two ids for one issue, in
Avengers/Invaders #2, Savage Avengers #1, and Avengers (2016) #5 and #1.1. Those are deduplicated to
the lower id, which keeps the rule BL-135 set down: a list holds an issue once.

Every count was reconciled against hand arithmetic before it was accepted. Ten of the twelve matched
first time; the two that did not were both diagnosed to a cause rather than adjusted to fit, which is
how the point issues and the duplicates were found at all. A count that disagrees is evidence, and
the temptation is to trust the machine and move on.

**BL-143: Shelve the catalog in reading order rather than in the order the manifest happens to list**

- [x] Record when each order's reading starts, as a fact about the order rather than a guess
- [x] Leave an order that ranges across the timeline out of the sequence instead of forcing it in
- [x] Sort once, where the catalog is parsed, so every view of it agrees
- [x] Keep grouped variants of one order together

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Twelve new orders turned a shelf you could read into a list you had to search. The order they
appeared in was the order the manifest happened to list them, which is the order they were added,
which is no order at all: Essential Avengers, which opens in 1963, sat below an order that opens in
2023.

The year is recorded rather than derived, and that is the decision worth defending. Deriving it from
the earliest on-sale date in the file gives the wrong answer for exactly the orders that need it
most: a best-of that opens in 2004 and then works back to 1966 would sort to 1966, where nobody
looking for it would think to look. Deriving it from `type` is worse, because the type does not carry
the distinction. A creator run can sit squarely on the timeline and a character run can range across
the whole of it, so the field would be answering a different question from the one asked.

So the absent value means something specific: not "unknown", but "this order ranges across the
timeline instead of sitting on it". Seven orders are undated on that basis and all seven are
retrospectives. The other nineteen carry a year, each checked against the on-sale year of the first
issue in its own pinned file.

The sort is stable, which is load-bearing rather than incidental. Six orders share a year with
another, and three of those pairs are the same event at two reading depths. An unstable sort would
separate the pair that the catalog groups and renders as one card with a depth toggle. Ties keeping
manifest order is what holds them together.

It is applied inside `parseCatalog`, at the single point where the catalog becomes data the app can
use, rather than at each place the app renders it. The home page shows only the first few cards, so a
sort applied at render time in one place and not the other would have produced a home page whose
"first" orders were a different set from the catalog's first orders. One call site cannot disagree
with itself.

Two judgement calls are worth flagging, because each is a one-value change if the reading is wrong.
The Essential Avengers order was retyped from a character run to an era and dated 1963, so that it
heads the Avengers spine the seven new orders form. The Claremont X-Men order was left undated,
because it is a single title's retrospective rather than a place in the story. Neither is enforced by
anything; both are editorial and recorded here so they can be argued with.

One thing was deliberately not done. The new Civil War Avengers order could be folded into the
existing Civil War group as a third reading path alongside the full event and the essentials, and
there is a case for it. It was left out because it is a different question from the one asked, and
grouping is a decision about how a reader chooses between orders rather than about where they sit.

Reversed in part on 2026-08-22, on the first of the two judgement calls above. Essential Avengers is
back to a character run and carries no year. The invitation to argue with it was taken up, and the
argument is this item's own rule rather than a new one: an absent year means the order ranges across
the timeline instead of sitting on it, and a best-of the Avengers' whole history is exactly that.
Dating it 1963 also walked into the failure this item names two paragraphs earlier, since 1963 is the
on-sale year of its first issue and the order works forward from there rather than belonging to the
Silver Age. The record above stands as what was decided at the time; what changed is the reading of
it. The order does not become harder to find as a result: the catalog now has a screen for character
spotlights, which is where it lands, and the reading path it used to head still lists it as the first
stop. The second judgement call, leaving the Claremont X-Men order undated, is untouched and still
reads correctly.

**BL-144: Shelve one card per story, and let the reader pick a reading path inside it**

- [x] Read the grouping the catalog already carries, instead of shelving each reading path
- [x] Fold the Civil War Avengers order in as a third path, which BL-143 left open
- [x] Group before the twelve-card cap, so folding frees a slot rather than wasting one
- [x] Count stories wherever the app says how many orders there are
- [x] Keep the choice off the shelf card, and put it where the reader has already decided to look

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Twelve new orders made a problem visible that had been latent since the second reading depth was
added. The catalog carried `group`, `groupName` and `variant` on every entry that is one way of
reading a story someone can read more than one way, and the home shelf ignored all three. So the
shelf showed twenty-six cards for nineteen stories, and seven of the twelve cards it had room for
were three stories: Civil War three times, House of M twice, Secret Invasion twice. A reader
scanning for something to read met the same title three times before meeting the second story.

Reading them is the whole change. Folding the six groups leaves nineteen stories, so the twelve
cards on the landing page are now twelve different stories rather than eight. The grouping happens
before the cap rather than after it, which is what makes the freed slots useful: fold after the cap
and the shelf shows nine cards, fold before it and the shelf shows twelve.

Where the app said how many orders there are, it now counts stories. That is not cosmetic. The
filter chips, the "Showing 12 of 19" line, the "See all 19 orders" link and the threshold that
decides when the search box is worth offering all counted rows, and a reader told there are
twenty-six things and shown nineteen has been given a number they cannot check.

**Where the choice goes was the expensive part, and the first answer was wrong.** The chooser
shipped on the shelf card, as a row of pills under the title. Measured in Edge at 1280x900 with
storage cleared, against the identical page built from the tree before the change: the grid went
from 1149px to 1458px, the tallest card from 293px to 445px, the spread between the tallest and
shortest card from 29px to 181px, the focusable controls in the grid from 24 to 33, and the
speaking surfaces from 65 to 77. A card offering a choice averaged 399px against 331px for one that
did not, and the chooser alone was 123px of a 277px card. The labels are authored prose of 17 to 46
characters and the card column is about 28, so every one of them wrapped to two lines. They were
also pill-shaped and grey, which is exactly what the filter chips 100px above them look like.

The fix is to ask the question once, where it is being asked of somebody who has already decided
they are interested. The card says only that there is a choice and how many ways there are, in one
quiet underlined line reading "3 ways to read this", and pressing it opens the same preview dialog
the card's own button opens. The dialog is full width, so both pills fit on one line, and it lists
the issues right underneath, so choosing a path shows you what you just chose. Re-measured on the
shipped tree: the grid is 1188px against 1149px before any of this, the tallest card 309px against
293px, the spread 45px against 29px, the focusable controls 28 against 24 and the speaking surfaces
68 against 65. The four extra controls and the three extra surfaces are the four cards that now say
there is a choice, which is the whole of the cost.

The catalog keeps its visible pills, and the difference is the column width rather than a second
opinion about the design. A catalog row is the full width of the pane, both labels fit on one line,
and the reader arriving there is comparing orders rather than scanning a shelf.

Three things in the implementation are worth naming because each is a defect that was designed out
rather than found. The chooser is built once when the dialog opens and never inside the repaint,
because rebuilding a radio group destroys the radio holding focus and a group that loses its
focused radio silently hands focus, and the appearance of the selection, to its first one.
Ownership is written into the labels a chooser already has, for the same reason, rather than the
group being rebuilt when an order is added. And the radio `name` carries the surface it is on, so
the catalog pane and the dialog, which are both in the document at once, cannot join into one group
in which choosing a path in one unchecks the other.

Library identity stays per reading path rather than per story, which means the mark reading "in
your library" is information and not prevention. Keeping both the main series and the complete order
is a reasonable thing to want, and nothing here deletes or replaces a list a reader already has.

Verified with 1,093 unit tests passing, 16 of them new, and forty browser checks in Edge at
1280x900, all passing, two of which were proved to fail on the tree without their fix: removing the
re-render that carries a dialog choice back to the card failed exactly one check, and removing the
in-place ownership update failed exactly one other. The first of those checks had to be rewritten
before it was worth anything, because the first version imported an order in the same journey, and
an import re-renders the grid on its own and carried the choice back whether or not closing the
dialog did.

**Review of the pull request found four defects, and the worst was again in the code written to be
careful.** Focus restoration after a repaint matches on `data-key`, and the preview button carried
the key of the list rather than of the story. Choosing a different path rebuilds the card around a
different list, so the key the repaint captured no longer exists, and the miss falls through to the
card's primary action, which is Add. A reader who opened the preview, changed path and pressed
Escape landed on a control that imports an order, one Enter away from importing it. The ways button
was already keyed by the story, so the two routes into the same dialog behaved differently, which is
why nothing caught it: the route that was tested was the safe one. Keying both by the story fixes
it.

The other three are smaller and all of a kind. The lift that holds the ways button above the
full-card preview overlay sat on the paragraph wrapping the button rather than on the button, so an
85px by 29px strip of empty text column was raised with it and took clicks meant for the card;
`.ocard-foot .btn` in the same stylesheet was already doing it the right way. Every chooser in the
catalog pane carried one identical literal legend, and three stories offer radio labels that match
word for word, so six choosers announced as one name repeated; the dialog's chooser now takes the
story's name. Promoting each row title from a `div` to an `h3` answers the six group headings this
change had removed, which had left the pane with none at all. And `.ocard-desc` sets
`display: -webkit-box`, an author declaration that outranks the user agent's rule for `[hidden]`, so
a card whose description was absent would have shown an empty clamped box; unreachable from the
bundled data, reachable through the manual entry form.

Twelve further browser checks cover the four fixes and all twelve pass. Nine of them fail on the
tree without the fixes, each reproducing what the review observed rather than merely going red:
focus landing on the Add button, the raised strip resolving to the paragraph instead of the button,
six choosers with no name, no headings in the pane, and a hidden description still laid out.

**BL-145: Ship the tracker to Windows as one archive that needs nothing installed**

- [x] Put the app and a Windows Node runtime in one archive, so the reader installs nothing
- [x] Make the launcher prefer the bundled runtime and still work for anyone who has their own
- [x] Carry the runtime distribution's whole licence file, rather than a summary of it
- [x] Publish the archive as a release asset, so one link replaces the download instructions
- [x] Leave the address alone, so an unzipped app is the same app with the same progress
- [x] Test the packaging contract, because the person this is for cannot diagnose it

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 4 is the one to argue with, because it
says runtime dependencies stay at zero and this ships a runtime. The reading taken is that the
constraint governs what the browser loads and what npm resolves, and the archive changes neither:
the dependency count stays at zero and the binary sits beside the app as a delivery vehicle rather
than as something the code imports. Constraint 5 is the one most able to break this quietly, exactly
as it was for BL-140. An archive whose launcher sets a port, or opens localhost, hands the reader an
empty app rather than an error.

BL-140 removed the terminal. What it did not remove is everything that comes before the terminal,
and that is now the whole of the difficulty: install Node.js from one website, find the project on
another, choose the right item from a menu written for programmers, wait, find where the archive
landed, extract it, open the folder, and only then double-click. The audience for this app is one
person who does not program, and every one of those steps is a place they stop.

Everything below was measured rather than assumed, on 2026-08-16 and 2026-08-17.

The machine this is developed on is ARM64 and its Node reports `arm64`. Copying that binary into an
archive would produce something that runs for the author and fails for nearly everyone else, which
is the worst shape a distribution fault can take, because the only person able to diagnose it is the
one person who cannot reproduce it. The x64 build is the one to ship: it runs natively on an x64
machine and under emulation here, so a single archive serves both and the author still tests what
the reader receives.

The size is unremarkable, and it was measured by building the archive rather than by adding up
parts. Staging the x64 `node.exe` beside `src/` and compressing produced 35,270,705 bytes, near 34
MiB. The runtime is nearly all of it: that binary compresses to 31 MiB inside the published
`node-v24.19.0-win-x64.zip`, itself 37,304,352 bytes, while the app adds 3.6 MiB across 94 files
before compression, of which 3.0 MiB is vendored order data. Retrieved from
<https://nodejs.org/dist/v24.19.0/> on 2026-08-17. A download near 34 MiB is ordinary and needs no
explaining. The shipped build came out at 35,308,148 bytes across 100 files on 2026-08-18, the
difference being the launcher's new branch and the short text file the reader is meant to open
first. The upstream figure was confirmed byte for byte by the build, which is the half of the
estimate that had to be exact.

The version to bundle is chosen by the test matrix, not by the engines floor alone.
`package.json:37-39` asks for Node 20 or newer, which every current line satisfies, so the floor
narrows nothing. `.github/workflows/ci.yml:40` does: the suite runs on 20 and 24 and on nothing
else, so bundling any other line would hand the reader a runtime this project never runs its own
tests against. That picks 24, which is also the newest LTS line and the one the app is developed on.
An earlier draft of this item said the floor had already settled the question and named 22. The
floor does permit 22, and the matrix is the reason not to ship it.

The licence is larger than one word. The runtime's own grant is MIT, but the file that travels with
the distribution names dozens of bundled components, OpenSSL and V8 and ICU among them, each
carrying its own attribution terms. Writing MIT beside the binary would under-attribute what is
inside it, so the archive carries that whole file. This repository already treats a licence question
as first-class, and BL-130 exists to close one before publication, so the record should not be the
thing that sets the bar too low.

Two figures were taken here and they disagree, which is worth recording rather than tidying away.
The estimate above was 157,606 bytes naming 44 components, read from the v24.x branch on 2026-08-17.
The file the built archive actually contains is 160,552 bytes and names 47, counted from the
`LICENSE` inside `node-v24.19.0-win-x64.zip` on 2026-08-18. Neither reading was careless: they are
different files, a moving branch against a pinned release, and the branch had moved on. The shipped
number is the one the code and its tests state, because the only licence that can be wrong is the
one in the reader's hands.

The obvious alternative was built rather than argued about. Node can produce a single executable and
one was made, with an embedded asset read back correctly at runtime and the experimental warning
suppressed, so its output was clean. It measured 77 MiB, and that number needs the same care as the
paragraph above demands: it is an ARM64 build, because it was injected into the ARM64 binary this
machine runs. A single executable is its base binary plus the injected payload, and the x64
`node.exe` is 92,825,416 bytes by itself, so the artifact a reader would receive is nearer 89 MiB.
It was rejected either way, and the reason is narrower than the first draft of this item claimed.

That draft said the executable meets a warning and the archive meets none. Half of it was wrong, and
the running guide says so at `docs/RUNNING.md:41-55`, where the reader is already told their
computer may ask them to confirm because the file arrived from the internet. So it was checked. A
zip was marked the way a browser marks a download, `ZoneId=3`, then extracted through the same shell
interface File Explorer drives, and the extracted launcher carried the mark through, referrer and
all. The archive warns too. Extracting with the PowerShell cmdlet instead drops the mark, but a
reader who reaches for that cmdlet is not the reader this item is for.

What separates the two is the signature, not the number of files. The upstream `node.exe` is
Authenticode signed and verifies as valid, by the OpenJS Foundation. Injecting a single-executable
payload into it breaks that signature, which is why the built file reports `NotSigned` and why
Node's own recipe for this ends in a signing step. So the choice is between shipping a binary whose
signature is intact and shipping one whose signature we destroyed. The first meets the confirm
prompt the README already documents; the second meets the reputation check, which is the harsher
dialog and the one whose default button declines to run it. The certificate that would settle it
costs money every year and still needs reputation before it takes effect.

Two things this deliberately does not do. It does not help the reader who never downloads anything
at all: that reader wants a link, a link means hosting, and hosting moves the origin and takes the
reading progress with it. And it does not cover the Mac, although BL-140 shipped a launcher for
both. Every measurement above is a Windows one, and the Mac is the harder case rather than a copy of
this one, because a binary that arrives quarantined there without notarization is refused rather
than merely questioned. `docs/RUNNING.md:46-55` already carries a workaround for the milder version of
that. Sizing this at 3 is sizing the Windows archive alone, so the Mac needs its own item with its
own measurements rather than a line in this one.

**BL-146: Put a way out of the capped landing grid where the reader runs out of it**

- [x] Give the reader something to press at the end of the grid, not only above it
- [x] Say the same thing in both places, so neither can go stale against the other
- [x] Derive "is there more" once, rather than from two expressions that happen to agree
- [x] Keep the cap, because a wall of cards is not a landing page

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Reported as "the dashboard displays only 12 reading orders and there is no way to scroll or load
more". Nothing was broken, which is what made it worth measuring rather than arguing about. The
landing grid caps at twelve by design, states the shortfall underneath, and offers `See all` in the
section header. All three worked. The reader was still right.

Measured in Edge at 1280x900 against the 19 orders bundled today, with storage cleared. The grid
ends at y=1526. The only control sat at y=134, so a reader who had scrolled to the last card was
1,392px past it, more than one and a half viewports. Scrolling to the end of the grid put the header
button off screen and left exactly one thing in view: a sentence reading "Showing 12 of 19 reading
orders." with nothing to press. An affordance that is never on screen when it is wanted is
indistinguishable from one that does not exist, and the report was the honest reading of what was
there.

The cap is kept. Its stated reason is that the page stays one you can take in at a glance however
far the catalog grows, and that reason gets stronger as orders are added, not weaker: the ask that
prompted this was for many more lists, and the answer to a hundred of them is not a hundred cards on
the landing page. The catalog view already takes the whole catalog with no cap, and it has the
facets and the search box for going deeper. What was missing was the door, not the room.

So the same action now sits under the grid as well, 44px below its last row, and the two labels are
generated from one call rather than written twice. After the change, a reader scrolled to the end of
the grid has the control on screen and the header one off it, which is the exact inversion of the
measurement above; pressing it arrives at the catalog with all 19 rows.

The label names the whole number rather than the remainder. `See all 19 reading orders` describes
where the button goes; `Show the other 7` would describe an append, which is a different interaction
from the one it performs.

One thing the first version of the test got wrong, recorded because the mistake is the reusable
part. The check for "the count and the action never disagree" swept matched counts 0 to 40 with
`shown` set to `min(matched, 12)`, and under that sweep a rule written against the cap and a rule
written against the shown length give the same answer for every input. Mutating the code to the
cap-based form left it green. It needed the case the sweep cannot construct, nineteen shown out of
nineteen, before it could fail. A test that cannot distinguish the fix from the defect is not
evidence, however many inputs it runs.

Removed on 2026-08-22 by BL-189, which took the cap away. The paragraph above argues the cap is
kept because the answer to a hundred orders is not a hundred cards on the landing page, and the
owner has since decided the opposite: the jump from cards to rows at the door was worse than the
long page behind it. With no cap there is no shortfall to state and nowhere for the door to lead,
so the sentence, the button under the grid and the one in the section header all went with it. The
measurement above stands as what was true of the capped page; what changed is that there is no
longer a capped page to measure. Nothing this item shipped survives, which is why its evidence
column now records an absence rather than a line of code.

**BL-147: Stop the startup failure messages naming a tool the download does not carry**

- [x] Say nothing about npm, which the packaged download does not contain
- [x] Stop offering a different port as the way past a busy one
- [x] Say what a different port would cost, rather than only refusing it
- [x] Cover the port being held by something that is not the tracker
- [x] Keep every line inside the width the console window opens at

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 5 is the reason this is a defect at all:
the origin is load-bearing, and the message was recommending that the reader move it.

Found while verifying the archive BL-145 ships, by starting it against an occupied port rather than
by reading the code. The launcher handled it correctly and the server printed this underneath:
`Otherwise start it on another port:  set MRT_PORT=8788 && npm start`.

Two things are wrong with that line, and the second is the serious one.

There is no npm in the download. The archive carries a runtime, the app and the launcher, and no
`package.json`, which is the whole point of it: the reader it was built for has installed nothing.
Extraction of the built archive confirms it, 100 files and no `package.json`. The advice was sound
when a clone was the only way to run this, and it survived into a distribution where it cannot be
followed.

Worse, following it loses the reader their reading. Progress is saved by the browser against the
exact origin it was saved at, so a reader who moves to 8788 opens an app with nothing in it while
everything they have read sits at 8787 where they cannot see it. That reader has just been told
their port is busy, which is not the moment they are best placed to work that out. The repository
already knew this: `test/launcher.test.js:77` forbids the launcher from setting `MRT_PORT` on
exactly these grounds. The rule was enforced on the launcher and not on the advice the server
prints beside it.

The message now refuses the port change and says what it would cost, and it covers the case that
prompted the original report: the port held by something that is not the tracker at all, where
"open the address instead" answers `Not found`.

Both messages moved out of the error branch and into `server.mjs:214-235`, returned as lines rather
than printed, which is the same reason `browserCommand` is a table: a branch that only runs when a
socket is taken is a branch nobody reads. `test/startup-messages.test.js` reads the words without
binding a port.

Five of its seven assertions were run against the shipped strings and fail on them, which is the
evidence that they test the fix rather than describe it. The remaining two are honest regression
guards: the address line was always correct, and the width check earns its place by having caught
the replacement copy at 88 characters before it was committed.

**BL-149: Read the Marvel Unlimited book id off an address the reader pastes**

- [x] Take the book id from a read.marvel.com address given to the hand-entry form
- [x] Store it, so the Read button opens the reader instead of falling back to a catalogue page
- [x] Say which of the two outcomes happened, rather than reporting both the same way
- [x] Tell the reader in the form which address does the work, and why
- [x] Refuse a lookalike host, a zero and anything that would build a link to nothing
- [x] Answer schemes the way the two sibling checks already do, and stop at the length the launcher will accept
- [x] Keep a pasted reader address out of the detail link, so Info does not become a second name for Read
- [x] Point the address field at the hint that explains which of the two addresses does the work

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 7 is the one this had to be written
around: it forbids awaiting a lookup before opening the window, and this change removes the need for
the lookup rather than moving it.

The metadata service this app hydrates from stopped on 2025-10-29. Asking it for 2026 returns a
total of zero. That is not a lag that will catch up: Marvel's own API was withdrawn without notice
or replacement, and the service is a mirror of a mirror of it.

The hand-entry form already existed for exactly this, and the form's own hint has said since 2025
that anything newer has to be added by hand. What it could not do was make such an issue openable.
The Read button sends the issue to `/open.html`, which resolves the digital book id from the
metadata service, and for an issue the service has never heard of that lookup can only fail. The
launch then degrades to the marvel.com catalogue page, which is honest and is not reading the comic.

The fix is that the id was already on the reader's screen. A subscriber reading a book in Marvel
Unlimited has `https://read.marvel.com/#/book/129648` in the address bar, and that number is the
digital book id the launcher wanted. Pasting it needs no key, no account, no request to anyone and
no agreement with any third party. The form already accepted the host, because `isSafeMarvelUrl`
has always allowed `read.marvel.com`. Nothing read the number out of it, so the entry fell back to
a synthetic negative id and lost the one field that would have made it work.

This is worth stating plainly because it bounds what any amount of further work can achieve. Five
candidate catalogues were checked on 2026-08-18, and not one records Marvel's digital book ids:
Comic Vine, Metron, the Grand Comics Database, Wikidata and the Marvel Fandom wiki. The id is
generated inside Marvel Unlimited and the only machine-readable sources that ever carried it were
Marvel's own API and the two mirrors that cached it, all three of which are frozen or gone. There is
a second floor beneath that one: Marvel adds an issue to Unlimited about three months after print,
so an issue published last month has no digital id anywhere, including at Marvel. A subscriber
pasting an address is therefore not a workaround for a missing integration. It is the supply.

Availability is deliberately not touched. An issue added this way still reports `unknown`, because
the Unlimited date is a separate field and nothing in the pasted address carries it. Saying so in
the confirmation is the point: the two outcomes used to read identically, and whether Read will
reach the reader is the one thing the row does not show afterwards.

The parser is stricter than the host check that precedes it. It parses the address rather than
matching a pattern over it, so `read.marvel.com.evil.com` is rejected on the hostname and cannot
smuggle a chosen number into the launcher. It rejects a marvel.com issue address outright, because
that carries an issue id, and reading one as the other would open a different comic with no sign
that anything was wrong. Zero and anything beyond the safe integer range are refused for the same
reason `readerUrl` refuses them: a Read button that goes nowhere is worse than one that is absent,
because it looks like it worked.

Three further refusals were added after a review rather than before it, and none of them was
reachable, which is the reason worth recording. This module's own host check and the private copy of
it in the reader module both refuse anything outside http and https, and the parser did not: probed
with crafted addresses, ftp, file, javascript and data URLs naming the reader host each yielded a
book id here while being rejected there. The caller gates on the sibling first, so nothing could
reach it, but two functions answering the same question differently is a contract waiting to be
relied on. The length bound has the same shape. The launcher will not build a reader address from
more than twelve digits, so a longer id was storable here and refused there, which is exactly the
dead Read button this function's comment claims to rule out.

The pasted reader address is deliberately not kept as the issue url. It would satisfy the detail
check in the reader module, which accepts that host, so the row's Info link and the hero's Info
button would both appear, name themselves after marvel.com, and open the very reader the Read button
already opens: one destination offered twice under two names, one of them wrong. With no url and a
synthetic negative id there is no detail link at all, which is the honest answer, because nothing
here knows a marvel.com page for an issue this new. A www.marvel.com address pasted instead is kept,
because that one is a detail page.

The address field points at its hint through `aria-describedby`, the first use of that attribute
anywhere in the page. It is recorded rather than slipped in, because it changes the page's own
convention: every other field here explains itself through its label. This one cannot, because which
of the two accepted addresses yields a working Read button is a paragraph rather than a label.

The parser sits in this module beside `issueIdFromUrl` and `isSafeMarvelUrl` rather than in the
reader module beside `READER_PREFIX`, and the reason is direction of travel. This module reads ids
out of addresses; the reader module builds addresses out of ids. Filing a reader with the builders
would have split three parsers across two files to keep one pair of related constants together.

Checked by removing the pieces rather than by running the whole thing, one line at a time, because a
revert that takes out a whole module only tells you the suite noticed something. Withdrawing the
parser's answer turns four tests red. Removing the scheme check on its own turns exactly one red,
and it is the one written for it. Removing the twelve digit bound on its own turns exactly one red,
and it is the one written for that. Returning the pasted address to the issue url, which is the
whole of the Info decision, turns exactly one red. In the browser the same discipline holds: the two
mutations aimed at this scenario are each caught by it and redden nothing else.

**BL-150: Fill in what the metadata snapshot cannot, from the one catalogue a browser can reach**

- [x] Establish what the Marvel Fandom wiki can and cannot supply for a post-snapshot issue
- [x] Decide whether anything derived from it is used at runtime only or written into the tree
- [x] Weigh the share-alike obligation that vendoring its text would attach to this repository
- [x] Fill the hand-entry form from a lookup the reader asks for, and store nothing until they add
- [x] Take Marvel's own issue id from the page, and refuse it when the tracker already holds it
- [ ] Decide whether covers are worth widening the pinned image host for, or are better left out

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraints 1, 3 and 4 are the ones that will
decide the shape: no image bytes, no accounts, and no runtime dependency.

Of the five catalogues checked on 2026-08-18, the Marvel Fandom wiki is the only one a browser can
call at all. It answers with a permissive cross-origin header, needs no key and no account, and it
covers 2026: a June 2026 cover date category enumerates, and an April 2026 issue returns a fully
populated record with a page count, a release date and creator credits by role.

It also carries Marvel's own issue id, which is worth having because that id is what the rest of
this app is keyed on. The field is called `MarvelUnlimitedID`, and the name is
misleading enough to be a trap: it is not the digital book id. It was checked against this
repository's own vendored data twice. Amazing Spider-Man Vol 1 1 reports 6482, which is the issue
id; the digital book id for that issue is 1067. Ultimate Wolverine Vol 1 1 reports 121270, matching
the vendored issue id exactly, with a release date matching the vendored on-sale date. Anyone
reading that field as an Unlimited id will produce reader links to the wrong comics.

What that id cannot do is close the gap, and this was measured rather than assumed. An issue id
becomes a reader link only by way of `/v1/issues/{id}` on the metadata service, which is the lookup
the launch page performs. Asked for the April 2026 issue the wiki supplies, that service answers
404. Asked for 121270 and 6482 it answers 200, with digital ids 71158 and 1067. The chain breaks at
exactly the point the gap begins, and for the same reason the gap exists. So this item is scoped to
what a reader sees written down, not to what the Read button does. The reader link for a
post-snapshot issue has one measured route, which is BL-149, and it works precisely because the id
comes from the reader rather than from a catalogue.

Three limits are known before any work starts. There is no reverse lookup: three search forms that
would find a page from a Marvel issue id all returned nothing, so the wiki can be read forwards
from a title and not backwards from an id this app already holds. The content is wikitext and would
have to be parsed. And the text is share-alike licensed, so writing it into these files attaches an
attribution and licensing obligation to a repository that currently has none, which is the decision
in the second and third tasks rather than an implementation detail.

The reverse lookup is closed by the wiki's own configuration rather than by the search index alone.
Neither Cargo nor Semantic MediaWiki is installed, so there is no table to select a page from by
field value: `action=cargoquery` answers `badvalue`. Building an id to page index would mean
enumerating and fetching every page, which is a maintenance job rather than a lookup.

The forward route was measured on 2026-08-18 and it works. A typed title finds the page through the
ordinary search list, with the right page as the first hit for all three phrasings tried, including
one for a 2026 issue. Wikitext can be fetched for many titles in a single request rather than one
at a time. `Category:Comics Released in March, 2026` enumerates that month's comics, where the bare
year and month category mixes in television episodes. Every one of those calls takes `origin=*` and
comes back with a permissive cross-origin header, no key and no account.

Worth recording so the question is not reopened: those same five catalogues were checked on that day
for the digital book id, and not one of them holds it. Not Comic Vine, not Metron, not the Grand
Comics Database, which is CC0 and would otherwise be the ideal source, not Wikidata, which has
Marvel properties for characters and creators and none for issues, and not the Fandom wiki itself,
whose `MarvelUnlimitedID` is Marvel's issue id under a misleading name rather than the book id.
Price and review aggregators carry no such field either, and no public dump of the retired Marvel
API was found to have preserved it. The field appears to exist nowhere outside Marvel's own systems,
which is why BL-149 takes it from the reader's address bar instead.

Covers are a separate question from text and are listed apart for that reason. Fandom serves them
from its own host, and this app pins the cover host to Marvel's CDN in one constant and again in the
server's content policy. Widening that is a real change to a deliberate boundary and should be
decided on its own merits, not carried along by a metadata change. That task stays open: nothing
shipped here fetches an image from the wiki, and the pinned host is untouched.

Shipped on 2026-08-19. The hand-entry form has a lookup button, and pressing it is the only thing
that makes a request. The search is fuzzy enough that picking the top hit would routinely file the
wrong comic's date against the entry, measured: asking for `X-Men Vol 7 26` returns the series page
first and issue 25 second. So the matches are offered and the reader picks one, and even then
nothing is stored until they press Add issue. Filled from the page: the release date, the page
count, the credits by role, and the series and number when the page title parses as one. The title
box is overwritten with the page title so the box shows exactly what will be stored.

The second and third tasks resolved together, and in the only direction that keeps this repository's
licence position where it is. Nothing derived from the wiki is written into the tree. The parser
admits a field only if the field is named in an allowlist, so a page's quotation, its appearance
list and its story titles are dropped because they were never asked for rather than because
something excludes them, and a test asserts none of them can reach a caller. The fixtures are
synthetic wikitext written here with real field names and invented values, so no wiki text enters
the tree even as test data. Bare facts carry no share-alike obligation; prose would, and none is
taken.

The decision on Marvel's issue id was reversed during implementation, and the reversal is the more
interesting half of this item. The first decision was to leave the id alone, reasoning that an
entry carrying a real id would show a Read button that could not open anything. That reasoning was
wrong, and reading `src/open.js` is what showed it: a missing digital id is not an unhandled state
but a designed one, which says that the issue has no Marvel Unlimited link recorded and opens its
page on marvel.com instead. Every catalogue issue lacking a digital id already behaves that way.

Measured on 2026-08-19 with a browser user agent, because Marvel's CDN refuses a bare one: the
official page for the April 2026 issue whose id came from the wiki answers 200, and an invented id
answers 404, so the 200 is a real page rather than a soft failure. The metadata service still
answers 404 for that same issue, so the id reaches the comic's official page and never the reader.
That distinction is worth stating plainly wherever this is described, because overstating it would
promise a reader something this does not do.

Two things were found while checking that, and both make the id worth more than it first appeared.
A hand entry has no link to its own official page today, because the launcher refuses to build one
for a negative synthetic id, so adopting the id fixes an absence nobody had written down as a
defect. And the address needs no new construction: the launcher already builds exactly that page
for any positive id, so the whole benefit arrives through code that was already there.

The collision hazard is real and is guarded. `addIssuesToList` merges the incoming issue into
`state.issues` before it decides whether the list already held that id, so a colliding id overwrites
the held issue's title, series, release date, page count and credits even on the path that reports
nothing was added. The reader would be told the issue was already in that list and would not be
told that a curated issue's metadata had just been replaced by this form's. The snapshot's 2025
cutoff does not protect against this, which was the tempting argument and is false: the bound
applies to the catalogue, not to what a reader types, and the wiki page for Amazing Spider-Man Vol 1
1 reports 6482, which is in the vendored data.

The guard refuses the entry and names the lists that hold the issue, rather than adding it under a
synthetic id. That follows what this form already does when the list holds the issue, and it is the
recoverable choice: nothing is lost and the reader is told something true, where a second row for a
comic they already track would sit in their reading list permanently.

What the guard tests is the id that will actually be written, and it fires whenever a wiki match has
been accepted. The first shape of it tested the wiki's id instead, on the reasoning that an id read
from a pasted address names one issue the reader deliberately pointed at. That reasoning is still
right about the id, and it is still honoured: a pasted address with no lookup behind it merges
exactly as it did before, because no match is held and the guard does not run. It was wrong about
which id gets written. `issueIdFromUrl(url)` outranks the wiki id, while the accepted match's facts
are spread into the payload either way, so a lookup for one comic and a pasted address for another
put the first comic's facts onto the second comic's id, and that id had been examined by nothing.
Nothing withdraws an accepted match in that sequence either, because the withdrawal listener watches
the title box and `acceptManualMatch` sets that box programmatically, which fires no input event.
Measured on the unguarded build in real Edge: a held issue's release date became 2026-07-01, its page
count became 99 and its writer was replaced, while the reader was told the issue was already in that
list and that nothing was added. Found by review on a sibling branch, and the correction is the one
that review proposed: gate on the presence of the fuzzy-search facts rather than on the id's
provenance, so what becomes impossible is facts this code searched for landing on something already
held, which is the principle the first shape had stated and failed to implement.

Constraint 3 is what shaped the request itself. It is never automatic, it sends the words in the
title box and nothing else, it carries no cookie and no referrer, and it is disclosed beside the
button that fires it and in the three surfaces the privacy copy test holds to that standard, which
now enforce two further rules: that the lookup sends the typed title to this wiki, and that it
happens only when the reader presses the button. Constraint 4 is untouched: the two new modules use
`fetch` and nothing else, and the dependency count is unchanged. Constraint 6 is untouched because
nothing here writes the availability field, so all five states survive.

Verified: 1,152 tests pass and 0 fail, up from 1,122, with the 30 new ones proved to fail against
the unfixed tree. All seven CI checks pass. The browser check grew to 53 assertions across 8
scenarios from 43 across 7, and the new scenario drives real Edge through a lookup, a pick, an add,
a refused duplicate and a refused cross-id collision with the wiki stubbed. A further injected
fault was added and aimed at it, taking `npm run browser:prove` to 13 of 13 caught. The first version
of that fault hooked the write and turned nothing red, which is the harness reporting honestly: a
refused add performs no write, so there is nothing there to intercept. What it injects instead is the
hazard's own signature, the stored entry carrying the second answer's date, page count and writer at
the moment the reader is told nothing was added, and that reddens exactly one assertion and no other
scenario. The two assertions covering the cross-id route were proved the same way and more cheaply:
reverting the guard's condition alone, one line, reddens exactly those two and nothing else.

**BL-151: Carry a pasted reader address through export and back in again**

- [ ] Read the book id from a reader address met while parsing a checklist
- [ ] Give such a line an identity that survives being imported twice
- [ ] Keep it out of the hydration queue, which can only spend requests learning it is not there

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Exporting a list writes each issue as a Markdown link, and for a hand-added issue that link is
whatever address was pasted. So a list containing Marvel Unlimited addresses exports correctly and
re-imports as unresolved lines, because the checklist parser only recognises the marvel.com issue
shape. The reader is then offered a title search to resolve them, and for an issue newer than the
snapshot that search cannot succeed.

This predates BL-149. The hand-entry form has always accepted `read.marvel.com`, so the round trip
has always lost these. BL-149 makes it matter more, because the address now carries something worth
losing.

Deliberately not folded into BL-149. Importing raises two questions the hand-entry path does not.
An imported line needs an identity, and the synthetic id the form uses is minted from the clock,
which is not stable across two imports of the same file and is not even distinct between two lines
of one paste. And an imported issue enters the hydration queue, which excludes hand-added issues by
source and would otherwise spend the reader's request budget on ids the service cannot resolve.
Both are answerable, and neither is answerable by the change that ships BL-149.
**BL-152: Say which order to read after this one, for a reader who has read none of them**

- [x] Declare the sequence once, as data, beside the lists it names
- [x] Refuse a path naming an order that does not exist, doubling back on a story, or running to fewer than two stops
- [x] Say on each row which path it belongs to, where it sits on it, and what comes next
- [x] Say "Start here" on the first stop, because that is the question actually being asked
- [x] Prove no two stops overlap, at either reading depth a story offers
- [x] Print the start year the shelf was already sorted by but never showed
- [x] Measure the badge's contrast on the surface it actually renders on, not the one it borrows its colour from

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 8 shaped the path's end: it stops at the
last story the snapshot covers rather than gesturing past the boundary.

The catalog was shown to someone who wanted to start reading Marvel comics, and they could not. That
is not a discovery problem. All 19 stories were on screen, each with a name, a length and a
description, and the shelf had already been sorted into reading order by BL-143. What was missing is
that a shelf is a set and reading is a sequence, and nothing on it said any order followed any other.
Sorting them put them in the right order without ever claiming they were in one.

The evidence that they do connect was already in the data and had never been used. Ten of the
nineteen stories are the Avengers spine, from Essential Avengers to Fresh Start, 1963 to 2018. Every
pair of them was measured: 45 pairs across 671 issues, zero shared. So the shelf held a sequence that
no reader could see, and every stop on it is disjoint, which is the property that makes calling it a
sequence honest rather than a suggestion.

The first design was a `follows` field on each entry, and the plan critique killed it. Pairwise links
admit a cycle, admit two orders both claiming to follow a third, and have no answer to "where does it
begin" that is not a scan. A named ordered array has none of those failure modes by construction:
there is no cycle to check for, the next stop is the next element, and it starts where it starts. The
critique's two blocking findings were dissolved rather than answered, which is the better outcome and
took a smaller change to reach.

A step names an order id rather than a story key. Ids are already checked for uniqueness across the
manifest, so a typo fails the vendor run instead of resolving to the wrong story; naming the order
also records which reading of a story the source chose; and a story key is an internal shape that has
no business being typed into hand-authored data. The app resolves each step to its story, so naming
either reading of House of M places the House of M row, not one version of it. Measured against the
shipped data, all 10 stops resolve and the two grouped stops name the story rather than a reading.

At story level the safety measurement is wider than the pairwise one: 10 stories, 15 orders behind
them, 99 cross-story pairs, 821 unique issues, zero overlap. That measurement is a test rather than a
note, because it is the one property a path asserts that nothing else in the catalog does. Two orders
sharing an issue is legitimate everywhere else, so no validator can refuse it in general; what the
test refuses is two *stops* sharing one, which is the claim being made. Add an overlapping stop and it
fails with the pair named.

The line reads `Start here Ã‚Â· The Modern Avengers Ã‚Â· Step 1 of 10 Ã‚Â· Next: Avengers Disassembled` on the
first stop and `Step 3 of 10 Ã‚Â· The Modern Avengers Ã‚Â· Next: Civil War` in the middle. Two drafts were
thrown away against a screenshot of the real shelf. The first repeated the path's name in a badge on
all ten rows, which made the most prominent element on the shelf the one word that never changed. The
second printed "After Essential Avengers", and since the shelf is sorted by year, that restated the
row directly above it. What a reader cannot get by looking up is what comes next, so that is what it
says.

Amended on 2026-08-22 by BL-191, and the rejection above stands exactly as written. The reason it was
refused assumed every stop sits on one year-sorted shelf, and the catalog is now drawn across three
screens by kind of reading. Measured against the shipped data, the one bundled path crosses a screen
at two of its nine hops and stays put at the other seven, so the predecessor really is the row
directly above on seven of them and the redundancy the draft was refused for is real there. What the
split created is a case the original rule never had to answer: on the two crossing hops the previous
stop is on a screen the reader is not looking at, so a reader who lands mid-path has nothing above
the row to orient them.

That case was met with a different affordance rather than with the wording that was refused. A
backward stop link, "Previous: Essential Avengers" on the two crossing rows, was costed at about
fifteen lines and declined by the owner: it spends a new word on every row that carries it to say
what the row above already says, and it puts a second directional label on a line that already has
one. What ships instead is that the path's own name, already printed on every stop, becomes the link
to the first stop. It closes the same orientation gap and adds no visible word to any row, which is
why it was taken over the costed option. Both links obey the same boundary, so the name is a link on
9 rows and plain text wherever the first stop is already on the screen being drawn.
The forward half is what BL-191 ships alongside it: "Next" becomes a link on exactly the hops that
cross a screen, and stays plain text on the seven that do not, for the same reason the backward draft
was refused.

`sourceOrigin` is required on a path for the same reason it is required on a list. A path is a claim
this repository makes about how stories connect, and no upstream publishes one in this form, so the
shelf has to be able to say who compiled it and from what. Seven of the ten stops follow Comic Book
Herald's Avengers guide; the other three are placed by their start year, and the wording says so.

19 unit tests in `test/reading-path.test.js`, and every guard was proven to fail without its fix by a
mutation harness, 13 of them plus a control. Two browser journeys and four mutations were added to
`scripts/browser-check.mjs`, which now runs 53 assertions across 8 scenarios with all 14 mutations
caught by the scenario aimed at them.

Two of those proofs were false negatives before they were true ones, and both are worth recording
because both reported success. The first mutation reported that removing the duplicate-id guard broke
nothing: `else if (seen.has(id))` appears twice in `src/js/lib/curated.js`, once for entries and once
for paths, and a plain string replacement took the first. It really did break the entry check, which
these tests do not cover, so the run was honest about a guard nobody had asked it about. Occurrence
indexing fixed it. The second pair reported that removing a stylesheet rule broke nothing, because the
app sends `style-src 'self'` and the injected `<style>` element was silently dropped. Rewritten
through `insertRule`, both caught their target. A mutation that cannot reach the code reads exactly
like a scenario that does not test it.

A review of the pull request found a third check of that shape, and this one was green rather than
falsely red. The "Start here" badge reuses `.pill-ok`'s two values exactly, so reusing a measured
colour looked like reusing its measurement. It is not: the contrast gate carried `--green` against
`--bg` and `--card`, and a catalog row is neither, it is `--card-2`. The badge shipped on a surface
nothing had measured, and the CSS comment beside it said the opposite. The pair is now gated at
`scripts/check-palette.mjs:61` and measures 8.38:1 in the dark theme and 6.07:1 in the light one
against a 4.5:1 floor, so the badge was in fact legible and the claim was still unearned. The
assertion that should have forced the question lists which surfaces each foreground is measured on,
and it did not name `--green`; it does now, and removing the pair fails it. The gate's other
coverage assertion, that every declared surface has something rendered on it, passes on the broken
tree and always would have: it walks the three named surfaces the file composites by hand, and a
token background is not one of them, so a missing token pair was never inside its reach.

**BL-153: Stop collapsing the sidebar from blanking every pill in the catalog**

- [x] Scope the collapsed-rail pill rule to the rail
- [x] Keep the two status pills collapsing to dots as they were meant to
- [x] Hold the scope with a browser mutation, since no unit test draws a stylesheet

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Found while checking that the new "Start here" badge survived a collapsed sidebar. It did not, and
neither did anything else. `.railed .pill` was written for the two status pills in the rail's foot and
set `width: 10px` with `color: transparent`. But `.railed` is set on `#shell`, and `#shell` contains
`main`, so the rule reached every pill in the catalog. Measured in Edge at 1280x900 with the sidebar
collapsed: the depth label became 89px of transparent text, and the badge this change adds would have
become a 10px dot.

This shipped before the reading path existed and has been wrong the whole time, which is the argument
for fixing it here rather than filing it: the change that found it is the change whose new element it
breaks, and the fix is one selector. Scoping to `.railed .rail-foot .pill` fixes it; the rail's own
pill still collapses, measured 132px to 10px.

Two mutations hold it. One unscopes the selector back to what it was, and one deletes the width, so
neither the scope nor the collapse can be lost silently. Both were verified to redden the scenario
they were aimed at.

**BL-154: Shelve the events apart from the character runs, and say why the runs sit last**

- [x] Divide the shelf into events and character-focused reading, keyed on the order's type
- [x] Say what each section is for, in a sentence a new reader can act on
- [x] Keep the reading path intact across the division, since its stops span both
- [x] Leave the facet chips working, so a filtered shelf still says which section it is showing

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Asked for directly by the owner: the event orders should be separated from the ones that follow a
single character. The data already supports it. `type` has four values and all 26 orders carry one,
and the facet chips above the shelf already filter on it.

Two sections rather than four. `type` splits four ways, but the reading path runs through orders
typed `era`, `event` and `creator-run`, so dividing by all four would cut the sequence this change
just shipped into three pieces on three parts of the page. Events and eras read as one thing to a
new reader, and the character runs read as another.

That sentence named `character-run` when this item was written, and it was wrong. Measured against
the shipped catalog: the path's stops are typed `era`, `event`, `event`, `event`, `event`, `era`,
`era`, `creator-run`, `era`, `era`. No stop is a character run, and the one creator run is stop 8,
Hickman's Avengers. Filing creator runs with the character runs, as the original sentence implied,
would have taken a stop out of the middle of the sequence and put it in the half the sequence does
not run through, breaking this item's own third acceptance criterion. So `creator-run` sits with the
shared story, on the evidence rather than on the label. A test holds the division against the real
catalog, and reversing the one line that decides it fails both that test and the unit test beside it.

The third acceptance criterion is written on that same mistaken premise, and is left standing rather
than rewritten, because a criterion edited after the fact records nothing. Its "since its stops span
both" is false on the measurement above: no stop is a character run, so the stops span one section,
not two. It is ticked because the path is intact and wholly inside the shared story, which is what
the criterion was for. Had the premise been true, the same tick would have required the opposite
arrangement, and that is the reading of it this paragraph exists to prevent.

There is a second finding worth carrying into that change. All 7 character-run orders have no
`timeline` year, so the year sort already puts every one of them at the bottom of the shelf. A reader
sees the grouping and is told nothing about it. The sections would make an accident into a statement,
which is the actual value here rather than the reordering.

Key it on `type`, not on whether a year exists. Today those two produce the same split, but that is a
property of the data as it stands rather than a rule anything enforces, and a dated character run
would silently land in the events half.

Shipped as two headed sections, "The shared story" and "Character spotlights", each with a sentence
under it. Nothing is reordered: the year sort already put the boundary where it is, and the headings
only name it. A story belongs to the spotlights only when every one of its readings is a character
run, which keeps a story with any shared-universe reading on the side a path can run through. An
empty section is dropped rather than headed, so a facet or a search that narrows the shelf to one
kind still names the kind it is showing.

**BL-155: Draw the reading path as a path, instead of a badge on each row of a list**

- [ ] Show the whole sequence in one place, so its shape is visible without scrolling a shelf
- [ ] Mark where the reader has got to, using progress the app already holds
- [ ] Keep the shelf's badges, which answer the same question from the other direction
- [ ] Decide what a second path does to the view before adding one

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

BL-152 answers "what do I read after this" on the row a reader is already looking at. It does not
answer "what is the shape of this", because ten badges spread down a shelf are a sequence only to
someone who scrolls the whole thing and holds it in their head.

The original request was a timeline page, and this is the honest version of it: not a proportional
year axis, which would put 1963 and 2015 on one line and waste most of it, but a linear spine with
named stops, which is how continuityguide.net presents the same material and why it works. The stops
already have names, positions and start years.

It is ranked below the shelf sections because it is a new view rather than a change to one, and
because the badge already delivers most of the value for the reader who prompted all this. It is worth
doing when there is more than one path, since a view that draws exactly one thing is a page that could
have been a paragraph.

**BL-156: Make the Start here badge carry more weight than a colour change**

- [ ] Distinguish the first stop by something other than hue alone
- [ ] Say where to start above the shelf as well as on the row, for a reader who has not scrolled
- [ ] Keep the badge readable against `--card-2` in both themes, at the gate's 4.5:1 floor
- [ ] Leave the other pills alone, so "start here" does not drag "ok" and "warn" with it

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Direction from the owner, recorded verbatim because it is the whole of the requirement and nothing
else in this repository holds it: "I like the way it currently reads, I just wish the 'Start Here'
was more prevalent."

Measured, which is what makes the request actionable rather than a matter of taste. As originally
raised, the rule now at `src/styles.css:443-445` set two properties, a text colour and a border
colour, and both were the same two values `.pill-ok` already used. Everything that made a pill a
pill, the `.72rem` size, the inherited weight and the padding, was shared with every other pill on
the row. So the one element on the shelf whose job is to answer "where do I start" was the same size
and weight as a status chip, and differed from it only in hue. A reader scanning the page had nothing
to catch their eye, which is exactly what the owner reported.

Two changes are in scope and they answer different readers. Weight and fill on the badge itself
serve the reader already looking at the row. A line above the shelf naming the first stop serves the
reader who has not scrolled to it, and that reader is the one who prompted the original request,
since the complaint that started all of this was not being able to tell where to begin.

Hue alone is also the accessibility problem behind the same symptom, so the first criterion is not
only cosmetic: a reader who cannot separate the green from the muted grey currently has no signal at
all. That is why the criterion asks for something other than hue rather than for a stronger green.

It is filed rather than folded into BL-154 because BL-154 divides the shelf and this changes what one
row looks like, and this repository ships one feature per change. BL-154's conditional route sentence
is adjacent but is not this: it points at the badge when the badge is on screen, which presumes the
badge is already worth pointing at.

Partly overtaken on 2026-08-20 by BL-166, which had to touch this exact rule for another reason. The
badge now carries a tinted fill and a heavier weight rather than a text and border colour alone, so
it is distinguished by more than hue and it clears the floor on the surface it is drawn on. What
remains open is the second criterion, the line above the shelf that names the first stop for a reader
who has not scrolled to it. That reader is the one who prompted the original request, so the item
stays `Ready` rather than being closed on the part that was incidental to someone else's change.
