**BL-157: Show the catalog in the README instead of only describing it**

- [x] Put a picture of the shelf in the README, above the instructions for running it
- [x] Show the reading orders that can be imported, not the empty first-run home view
- [x] Guarantee no comic artwork is committed, rather than checking the frame by eye
- [x] Describe the picture in text, for a reader who cannot see it

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 1 is the one that bites and is treated
below. Constraint 10 caps the value: this is not an acquisition asset, and the score reflects that.

Direction from the owner: the README "needs something for users to visualize what they're getting
into", refined to a picture that "shows the reading orders one can add to their library". The second
sentence rules out the obvious shot. The landing view is the home panel, which on a fresh install is
mostly empty, and `docs/ux-artifacts/01-landing-firstrun-1280.png` already records what that looks
like. What answers the request is the catalog, because that is the screen the imports come from.

Constraint 1 forbids storing comic image bytes, and a screenshot is bytes, so a capture that catches
cover art breaches it no matter what the surrounding prose says. The page requests twelve covers from
`i.annihil.us` on load. Framing around them would be a judgement made by eye and would silently rot
the first time the layout moved, so the guarantee is made mechanical instead: the capture writes
`{"covers":false}` into the settings key before first paint, and the app then requests no cover at
all rather than fetching and hiding them. The run asserted both halves, zero image requests observed
and `document.images` empty at the shutter.

Switching covers off does not make the picture unrepresentative, which is the objection this answers.
The catalog draws no covers in either setting: captures taken with them on and off are the same
picture. So the file is the shelf as it ships, and needs no caveat in the README saying otherwise.

No capture script is committed. Producing the file needs `puppeteer-core`, which the browser checks
deliberately keep outside this repository, and committing a script that cannot run without it would
imply a dependency the project does not have. The cost is that the picture can go stale without
anything failing. That is accepted rather than overlooked: the alternative is either a dependency the
repository has refused, or a gate that cannot run in CI for the same reason.

**BL-158: Let the reader close the undo notice a deleted list leaves on every screen**

- [x] Give every message raised under the undo key a control that closes it
- [x] Spend the undo when it is closed, rather than hiding the words and leaving the buffer behind
- [x] Speak the way out, as the offer beside it is already spoken
- [x] Land focus somewhere honest when the button that held it is removed

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Nothing here touches the network, storage or the
origin; the buffer this ends is in memory and always was.

Reported by the owner, with a screenshot: a list deleted hours earlier still had its banner and its
button above every view. The expectation was a message that lasted five or ten seconds.

BL-035 held the offer for the whole session on purpose, and that decision is not reversed here. Its
reasoning survives re-reading: deleting the list you were reading moves you somewhere else, and a
clock that expires while the reader is still deciding takes the only way back at the worst possible
moment. What BL-035 missed is that a clock was doing two jobs. It ended the offer, which it was bad
at, and it ended the message, which nothing else did. Only the second job was ever wanted, so it is
given to the reader instead of to a timer: the words go when they say so, and the undo lasts exactly
as long as it did.

Closing spends the undo rather than only hiding it. A buffer still live behind a message the reader
has closed is an offer they can no longer see and cannot take, and it would not stay quiet: putting
the same order back from the catalog consults that buffer and raises a fresh message about a deletion
the reader had already finished with. That is the shape of defect this repository keeps finding in
its own recovery paths, so the dismiss runs `forgetDeleted()`, which is the same withdrawal a backup
restore and an erase already use.

All four messages under that key got the control, not just the offer. Two of them report something
that has already happened and offer nothing to do about it, so they are the ones a reader is most
likely to want gone, and they were the ones with no button at all. They are raised from a shared
record rather than written out at each call, and a test reads the source for every `notify` call
carrying that key and fails on any raised without one, or with one written into the argument before
it, because the defect was never in one message: it was in the key, and a fifth message added later
with no way out puts the reader back where they started.

The fourth is not settled, and it does not say "Dismiss". A restore that failed for want of space
can succeed once the reader frees some, so that message keeps its buffer and offers "Try again", and
the buffer is by then the only place the deleted list still exists. Closing that message throws it
away. "Dismiss" names clearing the screen, so on this one message it would be a destructive act
wearing the label of a tidy-up, pressed by a reader who has just asked for the list back. It reads
"Give up", which is the same withdrawal under the name of what it costs.

The way out is spoken as well as drawn. BL-035's own argument for announcing the undo was that a
button nobody is told about is a button a screen reader user cannot know to look for, and it reaches
this control for the opposite reason. This is the one notice that stays until it is closed, so a
reader who is not told it can be closed is the reader who keeps hearing it.

Dismissing destroys the button that was pressed, and a focused node leaving the document drops focus
to `<body>` at the top of the page, which is the silent landing BL-054 was filed for. The heading of
the current view is where `showView` already puts a reader, so that is where a dismissed notice puts
them too, and the code that does it is now one function serving both rather than two that can drift.
Inside an open dialog the page behind is inert and focusing it does nothing, so that case is left to
the browser, which keeps focus in the dialog.

Which of those two applies is asked before the click runs, not after. Closing the notice detaches the
button, and `closest` on a detached node walks up to null, so the same question asked afterwards
answers "not in a dialog" every time: the one case the guard exists to skip would be the one case it
could never see. The first draft of this asked afterwards. Nothing observable depended on it, because
an inert page ignores `focus()` anyway, but a guard that cannot return one of its two answers is a
guard in name only, and it was found by review rather than by any check here.

Dismiss is drawn as a second text button rather than a bare glyph, because the notice already holds
one text button and a word beside a word reads as a choice between two things. It loses its outline
until it is pointed at or focused, which is the whole of its being secondary: its colour is left
alone, since dimming text is the one way to say "secondary" that costs contrast, and this is the
control a reader is looking for when they want the message gone.

Thirteen tests were added, and every one of them has been watched to fail. Thirteen single-line
reverts were made in turn and each turned a named test red, with all thirteen tests appearing in
that list, so no test in the file is merely passing alongside the code it is meant to defend.
Raising the offer without the control, and raising the two withdrawals without it, each fail the
source scan, and so does handing the control to the action slot rather than the dismiss slot, which
the first version of that scan waved through. Drawing no control at all fails six tests, three of
them the ones about focus. Dropping `dismiss` from the spoken message fails two. Restoring the old
layout rule leaves a dismiss-only notice without the flex row that makes space for a button, and
applying the new one to every notice makes a message with nothing to press claim a button it has
not got. Closing the message without spending the undo, deleting the focus move, and asking the
dialog question after the click rather than before each fail the single test written for it.

None of those runs a browser, so the claim was also settled in one. A scenario in the committed
browser check drives installed Edge through the reported journey: import an order, delete it, read
the notice, carry it to another screen, close it, and then delete and undo a second time. Ten
assertions, all passing, within a check of ninety-one across twelve scenarios, and they cover the
two things the unit tests cannot see, which are that the message really does survive a change of
screen and that focus lands on the heading of the screen being read rather than on `<body>`. That
second one was worth nothing until this review. A synthetic click does not move focus, so the
button being removed could never have dropped focus anywhere, and the assertion passed on every
tree it could ever be run against. Focusing the button before pressing it, which is what a reader
does, makes it discriminating: it now reports `BODY` on a tree without the fix. Two mutations prove
the scenario can fail, and both are among the twenty the mutation run carries, all twenty caught.
Stripping the second control reproduces the notice exactly as it shipped and reddens three named
assertions before starving a wait; making the button hide the paragraph without spending the undo,
which is the tempting shape of this fix, now reddens two, the focus landing and the assertion that
the closed message does not come back on the next screen.

One path is left to the unit tests alone. The message shown when putting a list back fails needs a
storage failure to reach, which the browser check has no way to stage, so its wiring is pinned by
the test that reads the source and nothing drives it in Edge. That is a deliberate limit rather than
an oversight, and it is recorded here so nobody reads the browser figures as covering it.

**BL-160: Tell readers when a newer release is available**

- [x] Ask GitHub for the latest release at most once a day
- [x] Let the reader switch automatic checks off without disabling a manual check
- [x] Offer the stable release zip as the primary action and the release notes as the secondary link
- [x] Say that reading progress stays in the browser and that the old folder can be deleted
- [x] Drive that upgrade against two real installs, so the sentence is verified rather than asserted
- [x] Keep the browser harness deterministic by stubbing the release request and proving the scenario

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 3 is satisfied because the request asks
GitHub only for the latest release JSON and carries no reading data, no note and no identifier.
Constraint 4 is satisfied because no runtime dependency was added. Constraint 5 is untouched because
the app still serves the same 127.0.0.1:8787 origin. Constraint 11 is checked by the dash scan.

Readers previously had no in-app way to learn that a release existed. The distribution work done in
BL-145 made a zip easy to download, but the app still depended on the owner telling people to go get
it. This closes that gap without making the app a self-updater: the browser asks GitHub for the
latest release and, if the tag is newer than the running version, shows a notice. It never downloads,
extracts, installs or starts anything on the reader's machine.

The release logic is deliberately small and stateless. `src/js/lib/updateCheck.js:3-4` holds the
latest-release endpoint and the stable zip URL, and `src/js/lib/updateCheck.js:55-95` performs the
injected fetch, strips the leading `v`, compares dotted numeric versions and turns every failure into
a silent result. The unit test covers current, older, newer, malformed and missing tags, a rejected
request, non-200 and rate-limited responses, and the not-due path where the injected fetch count must
stay at zero.

The setting lives with the other reader preferences rather than with reading progress. The visible
switch is in the settings screen at `src/index.html:750-761`, and the manual button is in the About
screen at `src/index.html:881-884`. `src/js/main.js:768-784` applies and saves the switch, while
`src/js/main.js:870-907` lets the About button force a check even when the automatic one is off.
The stored record only gained fields, so the launch page that reads the same key for the API base
keeps seeing the field it already understood.

The notice copy is the important part of the feature, not decoration. `src/js/main.js:790-817` names
the new and current versions, keeps the download action pointed at the stable zip URL, adds the
release-notes link, says reading progress is saved by the browser, and tells the reader they can
delete the old folder once the new version opens. `src/js/main.js:847-858` starts the automatic
check without awaiting it, and `src/js/main.js:4991-5013` shows that the boot path continues into the
normal load, settings and render work without waiting for GitHub.

The browser harness had to change with the feature. Its request stub now intercepts the update endpoint
at `scripts/browser-check.mjs:2744-2751`, and the update scenario at
`scripts/browser-check.mjs:2361-2428` verifies the default current-release response, the explicit
About button, the newer-release notice, the off switch, and a release request that never settles.
The targeted run reported twelve update assertions passing. Five update mutations were added at
`scripts/browser-check.mjs:806-862`: one makes the default answer newer, one suppresses a newer
answer, one corrupts the download link, one removes the release-notes link, and one rewrites the
delivered module so boot waits for the update check.

The sentence telling the reader to delete the old folder was the one claim in the notice that
nothing exercised, and it is the one whose failure loses an entire reading history. `npm run upgrade`
drives it against two real installs. `scripts/upgrade-check.mjs:355-390` is the heart of it: after a
second directory takes the address the first was using, the check reads which build is being served,
that the saved order survived by identity and by issue order, and that the upgraded copy draws the
order and its progress. `scripts/upgrade-check.mjs:392-415` is the control, serving the same new copy
at a second address and requiring the progress to be absent there. Without the control the check
would pass just as happily if progress were being read out of the folder, which is the opposite of
what the notice claims.

`npm run upgrade:prove` broke five things on purpose, at `scripts/upgrade-check.mjs:46-83`, and each
one reddened the assertion it was aimed at: five of five. Freezing the new copy's
version number breaks only the claim that the new build is being served. Renaming the state key
breaks only the painting assertion, because the reader's data survives untouched under the old name
while their shelf comes up empty, which is the distinction between storage agreeing and a reader
seeing their progress. Discarding read state leaves the order in place but returns visible progress
to zero. Starting the upgraded copy on a different port breaks the survival assertions, and is the
one way a reader following this advice really can lose everything. Pointing the control at the origin
it is supposed to differ from breaks the control. Neither command runs in CI, for the same reason
`npm run browser` does not.

The first version of the check was itself the finding, and it is recorded at
`scripts/upgrade-check.mjs:253-265`. Navigating to a URL that differs only in its fragment is a
same-document navigation, so it swapped the served directory and then re-ran nothing: the modules in
memory were still the old copy's. It reported the old version after the upgrade while every storage
assertion passed, which reads as a serious finding about the app and was in fact a check that had
never once loaded the thing it was testing.

**BL-161: Redraw the app icon so it stops echoing Marvel's trade dress**

- [x] Replace the red-square-with-white-M mark in the inline favicon and in both PNG sizes
- [x] Keep the app's own identity dominant, so the mark identifies this app and not a publisher
- [x] Check the result against the palette gate rather than judging the contrast by eye

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 1 is untouched because an icon drawn
here is this project's own artwork and not comic image bytes. Constraint 4 is satisfied because
drawing an SVG adds no dependency. Constraint 11 is checked by the dash scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-20. A Node-only generator now owns the approved purple page mark, writes one
SVG plus the two install PNGs, and supplies the SVG to both the favicon and rail. The focused icon
suite binds all three generated files to that source and the palette gate reports no new
below-floor pair.

The replaced icon was a red rounded square carrying a bold white capital M. It was declared as an
inline data URI and as the two exported sizes under `src/icons/`. That was the construction of
Marvel's own logo, which is a red field carrying white letterforms.

The red is not the app's own colour either, which makes this cheaper than it looks. `#e23636` was
measured at 4.36:1 and 4.33:1 against the two jobs a single red would have to do, and retired from
the stylesheet for failing both, at `src/styles.css:107-110`. The icon kept it. So the mark is drawn
in a colour the product itself already rejected, and redrawing it settles no palette question that
has not been settled once already.

This ranks above the naming question, and it is worth saying why, because the intuition runs the
other way. Using a mark's word to describe the thing that mark names has a recognised defence. The
nominative fair use test set out in New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302
(9th Cir. 1992), asks first whether the product can be identified at all without the mark, and a
Marvel reading order cannot be. The second and third parts are where a borrowed logo fails: only so
much of the mark as is reasonably necessary may be used, and nothing may suggest sponsorship. The
court's own application of it turned on the defendant having used no "distinctive logo". A red box
with a white letter is not necessary to identify anything, so it takes the weaker half of the test
while adding nothing the word had not already established.

It also reaches past this repository. Microsoft Store policy 11.2 requires all content "and
associated metadata" to be originally created, appropriately licensed, used as permitted by the
rights holder, or used as otherwise permitted by law, and the section preamble defines that
metadata to include the product icon. Read from the [Store
policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/publish/store-policies), document version
7.19, on 2026-08-20. So the icon is assessed at certification whether or not anyone complains.

Sized 1 because it is one drawing and two exports. It is ranked first of the three because it is
the cheapest of them and the only one that needs no decision taken before the work can start.

**BL-162: Decide the published name before a store listing exists**

- [ ] Carry the decided name into the web manifest and the listing, so the two cannot disagree
- [ ] Keep the descriptive reference to Marvel in the description, where it does referential work
- [ ] Re-check the name is still clear immediately before reserving it, since a reservation lapses
- [ ] Say plainly which risk the decision accepts, rather than recording only the choice

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 10 is the live consideration: this is a
naming decision taken for legal exposure and not a market-facing one, and nothing in it proposes
segments, positioning or growth. Constraint 3 is untouched. Constraint 11 is checked by the dash
scan.

Partially implemented on 2026-08-20. The app, web manifest, package, backup label, Windows package,
current documentation, and repository adopt Recap Page. Microsoft Store name reservation and
listing remain intentionally separate, so this item stays Ready until the listing carries the same
name and the reservation-time clearance check is recorded.

Two documents bear on the name, and they are independent of one another.

The first is Marvel's own stated position. Section 5 of the Marvel API terms says a developer may
"not create derivatives of Marvel Property, or use the 'Marvel' name or any other Marvel Marks in
the title of your App without Marvel's prior written approval", read from the [2025-10-08 archive
snapshot](https://web.archive.org/web/20251008063626/http://developer.marvel.com/terms) on
2026-08-20 because the live page answers 403. That clause binds users of the Marvel API, and
`docs/DATA_PROVENANCE.md` records that this project never called it, so the clause is evidence of
Marvel's posture rather than a term this repository agreed to. It remains the clearest statement
Marvel has published about third-party naming, and it names the title slot specifically.

The second is Microsoft's, and it does not depend on Marvel at all. Store policy 10.1.1 requires
that a product "must not in any way attempt to mislead customers as to its actual features,
functionality, or relationship to other products", that a product title "must not contain marketing
or descriptive text, including extraneous use of keywords", and that a product "must not claim to
be from a company, government body, or other entity if you do not have permission to make that
representation". Same source and date as BL-161. A reviewer can decline the listing under any of
those three without Marvel being involved at all, which makes it the likelier of the two to be met
first.

What comparable apps are called is the most useful evidence available, because it records what
survived rather than what anyone argued. The established comic trackers take arbitrary names and
mention Marvel in the description instead: Comic Geeks, CLZ Comics, iCollect Comic Books and
ComicsTracker, listings read on 2026-08-20. Riot, TMDB and Letterboxd each publish a third-party
policy saying the same thing in their own words, which is to keep the mark out of the title, say
the product is unofficial, and keep the developer's own branding dominant.

The app already carries the disclaimer half of that pattern, at `src/index.html:790-794`, and it is
better written than most. It is the title slot alone that diverges.

Decided on 2026-08-20: the published name is Recap Page, and it does not lead with the Marvel mark.
A recap page is the page at the front of a comic that catches a reader up on the story so far, so
the name says what the app does in the reader's own vocabulary without borrowing anyone else's.

The clearance is the part worth trusting, rather than the name. USPTO's register returns nothing for
the phrase, on an exact-phrase search and on a both-words search, checked 2026-08-20. The bare word
RECAP is crowded in class 9, where Autodesk, the Free Law Project, Saluda Medical and Tangent
Systems each hold a live registration, and a crowded field narrows what any one owner can reach.
None of them is in comics, books or reading. The App Store returns nothing, npm holds neither
`recap-page` nor `recappage`, no Microsoft Store product carries the name, and `recappage.com`,
`.app` and `.io` were all unregistered.

What the decision accepts: a recap page is a term of art, so the name is descriptive and would be
weak to register as a mark. That is the trade. It buys freedom to use and gives up the ability to
stop anyone else using it, which is the right way round for an app that will never police a mark.

The candidate this beat is worth recording, because it failed for a reason that was invisible
without checking. Pull List is the term the audience actually uses, and Marvel Characters, Inc.
holds two live registrations for it: 6122684 in class 9 for downloadable media in the field of
comics, and 6122685 in class 41 for the service, both filed 2019-08-09 and registered 2020-08-11,
read from USPTO's own record on 2026-08-20. Class 9 is where a downloadable app sits, the field is
comics, and the mark is being actively maintained, since a combined section 8 and 15 filing was
received on 2026-07-09 to renew it and ask for incontestability. Choosing it would have moved this
project from a name Marvel objects to on principle to one Marvel owns outright.

The two candidates already in the tree were considered and set aside. `Reading Tracker`, the web
manifest's short name, is descriptive to the point of being unfindable, and Longbox, recorded in
`design/mockups/5-longbox-focus.html`, names a storage box rather than a reading order.

Registration is not a prerequisite for any of this. Microsoft reserves a store name first come,
first served and asks for no proof of rights, and the [name reservation
page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/publish/publish-your-app/msi/reserve-your-apps-name)
read on 2026-08-20 puts the obligation the other way round: do not use a name trademarked by someone
else, because they can report it and the app is pulled from the Store until every instance of the
name has been changed in the app, its content and its listing. That penalty is the reason the
clearance came before the choice rather than after it.

Sized 2 and ranked below the icon because nothing here is urgent while distribution is a zip on a
releases page. The exposure changes when a searchable storefront listing exists, not before.

**BL-163: Say where the metadata came from, instead of borrowing Marvel's API attribution**

- [x] Replace the API attribution string with one describing the chain the data actually came down
- [x] Keep an attribution to Marvel as the origin of the underlying facts
- [x] Check the replacement against `docs/DATA_PROVENANCE.md`, so the two records cannot disagree

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 3 is untouched because this is display
text that sends nothing anywhere. Constraint 11 is checked by the dash scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-20. Both short surfaces now read "Marvel metadata via
marvel.emreparker.com." The sentence names Marvel as the origin and the community endpoint as the
route, matching the detailed About copy and the provenance record.

Before this item shipped, the home screen rendered "Data provided by Marvel." with a copyright
line beside it. That is the wording Marvel's attribution page requires of API users, and
`docs/DATA_PROVENANCE.md` establishes in the same breath that this project never called that API:
the metadata was fetched from the third hand in the chain, under terms this repository is recorded
as never having agreed to.

Displaying it anyway was the cautious choice, and as a claim about origin it is defensible, since
the facts did begin with Marvel. The problem is narrower than that and runs the other way. The
string is the official one, so it reads as attribution given under an agreement, which is the one
impression the rest of this repository works to avoid. Under the endorsement question that BL-161
and BL-162 both turn on, borrowed official wording is a liability rather than a mitigation.

Two smaller things go with it. The required text is literally "Data provided by Marvel. Ã‚Â© 2014
Marvel", with the year hard-coded by Marvel and never templated, read from the [attribution
page](https://web.archive.org/web/20251008073256/https://developer.marvel.com/documentation/attribution)
on 2026-08-20, so the current line does not match the string it imitates in any case. And the
sources the data did come from are already named accurately further down the same screen, which is
where the replacement wording should take its lead rather than being drafted fresh.

**BL-164: Carry a rename without breaking the download link installed copies use**

- [x] Hold the release asset filename fixed across the rename, whatever the repository comes to be called
- [x] Change the three baked URLs together, or establish on evidence that they need no change
- [x] Leave the storage key alone, and say in the item why it is the one thing that must not move
- [x] Check an installed copy still finds the update afterwards, rather than assuming a redirect covers it

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 5 is the live one and it is not
breached: a rename touches neither origin nor port, and this item holds the storage key fixed
rather than proposing to move it. Constraint 11 is checked by the dash scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-20. A live installed-copy check reached release v1.2.0 from the new API route.
Old and new API, release-page, and fixed-asset URLs all answered 200 after redirects; old and new
clone routes resolved the same commit, and a clean clone completed a no-write fetch. The versionless
Windows archive filename and every `mrt.*` key remain fixed.

Renaming the repository is nearly free, and the one place it is not free is the place easiest to
miss. GitHub redirects a renamed repository, so an installed copy's update check survives.
Measured on 2026-08-20 against a repository that really was renamed, the API call answers 301 and
then 200 once the redirect is followed, and `checkForUpdate` passes no redirect option to `fetch`,
so it follows by default.

The download link does not have that property, because GitHub redirects repository names and not
asset names. Measured the same day: a release asset requested under its real filename answers 200,
the same asset requested under a renamed filename answers 404, and the repository page itself
answers 200. So the trap is not the repository name at all. It is `src/js/lib/updateCheck.js:4`,
which bakes the asset filename into the download URL. An installed copy would be told correctly
that an update exists and then sent to a 404.

The mitigation is to leave the asset filename alone. It never had to match the repository name,
nothing a user sees displays it, and renaming it to match a new project name is the single change
that would break the link while buying nothing.

One thing must not move under any circumstances. `src/js/storage.js:9` holds the key every reading
list is stored under, and the temporary, pre-restore and salvage keys are derived beside it.
Renaming those loses every user's progress silently, and the recovery paths that would otherwise
salvage it are keyed on the same prefix, so they would be looking in the wrong place too. The
prefix is internal and never displayed, so there is no reason to touch it.

The backup file records the project slug at `src/js/lib/model.js:1119`. Nothing reads it back:
import validates the shape of the payload and never compares that field, so it is a label rather
than a check. It can change or stay, and either way an older backup still imports. Worth knowing
before someone changes it defensively, or refuses to on the assumption it is load-bearing.

Sized 1 because the whole of it is one filename left alone and one key left alone. Ranked beside
the icon because it is cheap, and because getting it wrong is only discoverable after the rename
has shipped, when the users it strands are the ones who installed earliest.

**BL-165: Let the landing page use the desktop it is given, without stretching prose**

- [x] Widen the shell past the fixed measure it has carried since the first release
- [x] Hold every prose view at the width it already had, so reading is not made worse to make browsing better
- [x] Get more cards per row at a desktop width and again on an ultrawide one
- [x] Measure the result in a browser rather than deriving it from the stylesheet

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 5 is the live one and it is untouched:
this changes a max-width, not an origin or a port. Constraint 11 is checked by the dash scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-20. Measured in Edge against the running app: at 1280x900 the shell is 1028px
and the landing view 964px, giving 3 columns; at 2560x1080 the shell stops at the 1360px cap and the
landing view is 1296px, giving 4. The reading measure is 876px at both, unchanged. Neither width
overflows horizontally.

The shell was `max-width: 940px` with `1.6rem 2rem 3rem` of padding. That is the whole finding,
because `box-sizing: border-box` means the content box was 876px and not 940px. Anything that set
the new prose measure to 940 would have widened every prose view by 64px while claiming to have
left them alone, and nothing in the suite would have said so. So the reading measure is pinned at
876 and only the landing page is allowed past it, through one modifier class.

The catalog grid's own minimum deliberately did not move. `auto-fill` fits
`floor((available + gap) / (min + gap))` with a 14.4px gap, and at 260px that is already 3 columns
in 964px of space and 4 in 1296px. Raising it to 300px was considered and rejected on arithmetic:
it changes neither of the two widths this item is about, drops the 881px to 960px band from two
columns to one, and overflows a 320px viewport. A number that buys nothing at the sizes named and
costs something at the sizes not named is the wrong number.

Sized 2 because the width change is small and the checking is not: every view had to be looked at
at both widths, in both themes, and the failure mode is a prose column that silently got wider.

**BL-166: Move the app's identity off Marvel's red and onto its own purple**

- [x] Take the brand colour from the app's own icon rather than choosing one that looks close
- [x] Keep red for danger only, so a warning still reads as a warning
- [x] Give links, success and warnings each their own hue instead of overloading one
- [x] Measure every pair in both themes before shipping, and put none below the contrast floor

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 6 is the live one and it is honoured:
all five availability states stay distinct, and the availability badge is untouched apart from the
token rename behind it. Constraint 11 is checked by the dash scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-20. The palette gate measures 88 pairs across both themes and reports 0 new
below the floor. The five that sit below it are the five already recorded before this change, all of
them progress-bar tracks and one checkbox tick, none of them introduced here. One of the five did get
worse: the white tick on the dark teal fill fell from 2.30:1 to 1.93:1, and rather than inherit
BL-069's acceptance the justification in `scripts/check-palette.mjs` was re-derived on the new fill,
because a pair already recorded is the pair a later change can most easily worsen unwatched.

The brand colour was read out of the shipped icon rather than picked: decoding the 512-pixel PNG,
`#6d28d9` covers 69.41% of its opaque pixels, and the committed vector is byte-identical to it. That
is the light-theme accent. It cannot be the dark-theme accent, which is the part worth writing down:
measured against the progress track it is 2.14:1, and it fails five of its eight pairs on a dark
page. Mixing it 20% toward white gives `#8a53e1`, which is the least white that clears all eight, and
white on it measures 4.77:1 against a 4.5 floor.

Red is now danger and nothing else. The row you are reading used to be marked with the danger line,
which is why it carried a faint red wash; it now has its own accent line, because selection is not
danger. Blue carries links and focus, teal carries success and positive availability, amber carries
warnings and the one featured panel. Neutrals were rotated to hue 240 with saturation scaled to keep
them quiet, holding lightness rather than luminance, so ratios did move: across the 88 pairs 52 went
up, 30 came down and none crossed a floor in either direction. The largest movement of a pair with no
recoloured token in it is the dark secondary text on the page, 11.83:1 down to 11.28:1.

One bug was found by the owner during review and is worth recording because the shape of it recurs.
A filled badge cannot take a fixed foreground when its fill flips polarity between themes: the teal
token is light on a dark page and dark on a light one, so a dark glyph on it measured 9.55:1 in one
theme and 2.83:1 in the other. The fix is the tint pattern the stylesheet already used elsewhere, a
12% wash behind the theme's own text colour, which measures 7.16:1 and 6.02:1 on a card.

Review found two shipped surfaces the token rename could not reach, and both are worth recording
because the reason they were missed is structural rather than careless. The Marvel Unlimited launch
page is opened in its own tab and never loads the app's stylesheet, so `src/open.css` writes its
colours out as literals and was still carrying the retired red mark and the pre-rotation neutrals.
The web app manifest names the dark page colour twice, for the standalone splash and the browser's
own chrome, and it too was still `#0f1115`. Both are now the shipped dark values. The palette gate
reads `src/styles.css` alone, so neither file is measured by anything, which is why they drifted
without a gate saying so and why the launch page now states its four measured ratios in a comment.
Widening the gate to every file that paints a colour is filed as BL-168 rather than done here.

Sized 2 because the colours are one file and the checking is three: every pair measured in both
themes, every renamed usage read to confirm it was brand rather than danger, and the whole thing
looked at in a browser.

**BL-167: Answer "where do I start" on the first screen, with one order named**

- [x] Name one reading order on the first-run landing page, rather than offering nineteen equally
- [x] Say what the commitment is, in issues and in hours, where the decision is made
- [x] Choose it by a rule anyone can check, not by an editor's pick that nobody can audit
- [x] Withdraw the offer the moment the reader has said something more specific
- [x] Leave the returning reader's own progress exactly where it was

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 1 is the live one and it is honoured:
the panel shows the same cover URL the shelf already shows and stores no bytes. Constraint 11 is
checked by the dash scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-20. Measured in Edge: the panel is shown on a genuine first run and names
Avengers Disassembled; it is hidden while a search is typed, hidden once a facet is chosen, and
hidden once a single order has been imported, at which point the continue-reading panel is showing
and the library holds one list.

The rule is the beginner-friendly order with the fewest issues, ties broken by catalog order. That
is deliberately the smallest real commitment the data can offer, because "how much am I signing up
for" is the question a first-time reader is actually asking and an editor's pick answers a different
one. Against the bundled catalog it selects a five-issue event. The tie-break matters more than it
looks: without it two orders of equal length can swap places between renders, and the landing page
then offers a different starting point each time it is opened.

Withdrawal is the half that is easy to skip. A reader with a library has chosen before, and a reader
who is filtering or searching is choosing right now; in all three cases the panel would be answering
a question that has already been answered. Withdrawing the offer when it stops making sense is
cheaper than explaining it afterwards, and it is why the returning reader sees no change at all.

Sized 3 because the panel is new markup, new selection code and new tests, and because the failure
mode is quiet: a panel that keeps offering a starting point to someone who has already started reads
as the app not noticing them.

reachability test red and nothing else. The second exists because the destination is a data value

just described was one of them, which is the sharpest lesson of the round: its allow-list was
written by hand and held `library`, `settings` and `reading`, none of which are views, while
omitting `data` and `read`, which are. It would have passed the exact typo it was added to catch.

seen to fail on a wrong destination and on a wrong disclosure id, each alone. Second, the reading
ring lost the word "read" when it became a percentage over a count. The circle beside it is
`aria-hidden`, so those two spans are the entire spoken statement of progress, and it had come to
say "13%, 12 of 89" with nothing naming what was counted. The verb is back in the second line.

The third is older than this change and was fixed because this change rebuilt the pane it sits in.
The navigation pane is a scroll container, so a focus ring drawn outside a button is clipped at its
edge, and outlines do not scroll into view, so nothing reveals it. Padding the container cannot
help, because a rail button is full width and simply stretches to the new box: measured in Edge at
1280x900, the padded arrangement leaves the same 11 of 14 controls clipped as the unpadded one, and
the arrangement this change replaced clipped 13 of 13, so it was never a regression. The ring is now
drawn inside the button, at the shallowest offset that clears the edge, which is the ring's own
width.

Two recommendations from the review were deliberately not taken, and both are recorded rather than
silently dropped. The reading screen keeps all five list commands on the canvas instead of moving
four into an overflow menu, because a test exists to hold that line and says why. The absent-synopsis
line stays, because it is one of three distinct states and the code says so. A third, folding the
about screen into settings, is left open: the guidance prefers it, the routing and several tests
assume otherwise, and the gain is small.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Nothing here reads or writes anything off the
machine, no dependency is involved, and the fix is a stylesheet ordering question rather than a
change to what any screen says.

Found by review on 2026-08-22 while measuring the pane rebuilt in BL-187, and separated from it
because it is not that change's doing. The stylesheet asks for a stacked layout below 880px and does
not get one. The rule that sets `position: static` and `height: auto` is declared before the rule
that sets `position: sticky` and `height: 100vh`, at equal specificity, so the later one wins and
both of the narrow-width declarations are dead.

Measured in Edge at 880, 860, 700 and 640 pixels wide, each with one order on the shelf: the pane
computes to the full window width and 900px tall in all four, and the content begins at y=900 in all
four, which is exactly one screenful down. So on a window of 880px or narrower the app opens showing
navigation and nothing else, on every screen. The boxes do not overlap, which is worth stating
because it looks like overlap in a screenshot; the content is simply pushed below the fold.

Present on `main` as well, at the same four widths, so this is a long-standing defect rather than
one introduced by the rebuild.
