Progress was carried by a 36px ring whose only figure, `0 / 8`, was a tooltip on the ring's wrapper.
A tooltip is not available to touch, is not read out on focus, and takes a hover and a pause on a
mouse. The ring is now 44px and the count is text beside it: `0 of 8 read` with `8 to go Â· 0%` under
it. The `title` attribute is gone rather than kept as a duplicate, because two sources for one number
is how they come to disagree. The circumference constant moved with the radius, from 94.2 to 119.4,
and a test now asserts the two agree so a future radius change cannot silently leave the arc drawing
the wrong fraction.

The list-management row was five outlined pills of the same weight as the hero's own buttons. They
are now borderless until hovered or focused, inside a single bounded strip, so the row reads as one
group of secondary actions rather than five competing offers. Every button keeps its label, its
place in the DOM and its tab stop, and the border returns on `:focus-visible`, so keyboard use is if
anything clearer than before. Under forced colors the strip and each button take a system border,
which is correct: the demotion is a visual hierarchy the user's own colours are entitled to discard.

The current issue is marked in the full order by an accent outline rather than by a tint alone, and
that outline was for a while drawn on three sides. Rows are separated by a top border on every row
after the first, and both rules weigh the same, so the later one took the top edge of whichever row
it landed on. The current issue is the first *unread* row, so in any order with progress in it that
row is preceded by a read one and lost its top edge every time; only an untouched order, which is
what both gates imported, showed it whole. The separator now stands down for the rows that have
something of their own to say, and the browser check reads the four border colours of the current
row after marking an issue read.

This partly overtakes BL-165's second task, "hold every prose view at the width it already had". That
task was right about the landing page and about prose, and the reading order screen is neither: it is
a working surface with a cover, a shelf and a table on it, and holding it at a reading measure was
costing it the shelf. The prose measure itself has not moved, and the views that carry prose still
sit on it.

Sized 2 because the visual change is broad but the mechanism is narrow, and because the checking is
the expensive half: both widths, both themes, covers off, forced colors, and a hero button whose
click path must not gain a single `await`.




**BL-170: Give the library and progress views a summary before their rows**

- [x] Put a summary band above the rows on the three library and progress views
- [x] Group Everything read by when issues were read, with real headings and counts
- [x] Add cover thumbnails to library rows without introducing a new image size
- [x] Group Progress by series by state, and name the state in words rather than in colour
- [x] Let the three views use the wider layout the landing page and the reading screen already use
- [x] Mark completed, active, empty and hand-added states by something other than colour alone
- [x] Measure the result in a browser at both widths rather than deriving it from the stylesheet

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 1 is untouched because no image bytes
are hosted or stored, only cover URLs are used, and the thumbnails request the same variant the
reading rows already request, so no new image enters the cache. Constraint 3 is untouched because
nothing is uploaded and every figure is derived at render time from state already on the device,
with none of it stored. Constraint 4 is untouched because runtime dependencies stay at zero and the
new module adds none. Constraint 6 is untouched because the availability badge and its five states
are not touched at all. Constraint 11 is checked by the dash scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-21. Measured in Edge at 1280x900 and again at 2560x1080, against a seeded
fixture of 37 issues with 21 marked read across 7 series, 4 of them added by hand, and 3 read issues
belonging to no list. Every figure below is a before and after reading of that same fixture in the
same browser, taken from the running tree rather than derived from the stylesheet.

At 1280x900 the content column went from 876px to 964px on Everything read, Added by hand and
Progress by series. At 2560x1080 it went from 876px to 1296px on Everything read and on Progress by
series. Before this change the second measurement was identical to the first, because all three
views sat on the prose measure at every width. Horizontal overflow is 0px on every one of them at
both widths, before and after.

Everything read now groups its rows by when they were read, as Today, Yesterday, In the past week,
Earlier this month and then by month, each group a real heading with its count beside it. That took
the view from 0 headings to 9, which is nine places a reader can jump between on a screen that
offered none. Progress by series groups by state and names that state in words, taking it from 0 to
1. Added by hand stays ungrouped at 4 rows, for the reason two paragraphs below.

Cover thumbnails were added to the library rows at the same image variant the reading rows already
request: 0 to 21 covers on Everything read, and 0 to 4 on Added by hand. The summary bands did not
exist before at any width. They now read "21 issues read / 7 series / 3 in no list", "4 added by
hand / 2 read / 4 in no list", and "1 series / 7 of 8 tracked issues read / 0 series fully read".
The progress band says fully read rather than complete, because the app only knows about the issues
the reader has chosen to track, and a series can be finished in print while the tracker has one
issue of it.

Two fixes came after the rendered result was reviewed, and both are worth recording rather than
smoothing over. A chip repeating "In no list" was removed: the row's own meta line already says
those words, so a screen reader heard them twice, and on the hand-added view, where every row is in
no list by definition, the chip drew a column that distinguished nothing. And a derived grouping is
now drawn only above twelve rows, because below that it degrades into one heading per row. Measured
on the hand-added view with four entries, it produced four headings each printing a count of 1. The
progress groupings are deliberately exempt from that threshold, because there the group is the state
itself, and "Not started" is worth saying about a single series.

Sized 2 because the visual change is broad but the mechanism is narrow, and because the checking is
the expensive half: both widths, both themes, covers off, forced colors and reduced motion. Nothing
a reader has saved is touched. Every figure is computed from the existing state as the view renders,
and none of it is written back.

**BL-171: Make search the default way to add issues and group the other four paths**

- [x] Make the search panel always open rather than one collapsed disclosure among five
- [x] Move the other four paths under one "Other ways to add" section with a one line lead
- [x] Give each of those four a purpose line so a reader can choose a path without opening it
- [x] Head search first and drop the grouped headings a level so no heading level is skipped
- [x] Summarise each result set and say how many of it are already in your library
- [x] Mark a result already held, and keep that mark legible without colour
- [x] Name the destination reading order in the series and creator panes, not only in search
- [x] Give the loading messages their own notice kind so they carry no success tick

Implemented on 2026-08-21. The Add view offered five ways to add an issue as five equal collapsed
disclosures, search folded among them, so the fastest path for a reader who already knows a title
had no more prominence than importing a Markdown file. Search is now an always-open panel at the top
of the view, and the other four paths sit under one "Other ways to add" section with a one line lead
and a short purpose line on each summary, so a reader can tell what a path does before opening it.
The four leads read "Every issue of one series, oldest first.", "Every issue credited to one writer
or artist.", "A Markdown checklist or one title per line." and "Anything the 2025 metadata snapshot
does not have."

Verified in Microsoft Edge across the whole view: 38 checks, all passing. Heading levels went from a
run of equal disclosures to 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, with no level skipped, so the search panel and the
grouping read as peers and the four grouped paths one below. All 13 visible controls carry an
accessible name. Each of the five rail entries lands focus in its own control, and walking all five
in turn never left a second path open at once.

A result set now opens with a one line summary that a reader and a screen reader take the same words
from, for instance "12 results, 1 already in your library. Adding to My reading order.". That
sentence names the destination reading order in the search, series and creator panes alike; before
this change only the search pane named it, so two of the three left a reader guessing where an add
would land. A result already in the issue store carries an Already in your library marker. The held
count in that summary is derived at render time by one new pure function that reads the store and
counts distinct ids, with nothing uploaded or stored to produce it, so the promise that nothing
leaves the device is untouched. Under forced colours the marker stays a legible label with a tick
glyph rather than a colour, and the panels named in it keep a CanvasText border, checked in the Edge
high contrast mode.

The three loading messages moved to their own busy notice kind, so a message that means work is in
flight no longer wears the tick a success notice carries, and it shows no animation under
prefers-reduced-motion reduce. The results pane is still not a live region, so a screen reader is
not interrupted while rows move under it. Horizontal overflow is 0px at 640, 1280, 1920 and 2560 CSS
pixels, where 640 is what 200 per cent zoom reports. Lint reports 0 problems and the palette gate
exits 0. The one new function is covered by 8 tests, and a second test file guards the view's markup
and the repeated button classes.

Sized 2 because the change is broad in the view but narrow in mechanism, one pure reader of existing
state and a regrouping of markup that already existed, and because the checking is the expensive
half: both themes, forced colours, reduced motion and four widths. The availability model and its
five states are neither read nor changed here, and runtime dependencies stay at zero.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

**BL-172: Let the reader stop a long series or creator load once it has started**

- [ ] Add a cancel control to the series and creator adds so a running load can be stopped
- [ ] Leave a stopped add in a clean state, keeping the issues already fetched
- [ ] Follow the cancellation shape the reading view loaders already use, without moving them

Routed out of the research for the progressive disclosure work rather than built in it. Adding a
whole series fetches every page of that series in turn, and there is at present no way to stop it
once it is running: a reader who started the wrong series waits for it to finish or reloads the
page and loses the run. The app already has two loaders that can be cancelled, the cover hydrator
and the synopsis loader, so the pattern is known here. It is not reuse, though, because both of
those are wired into the reading view, not the Add view, and the series and creator runners have no
cancellation seam at all, so this is new capability rather than a wire from one view to another.

Scored V5, TC2, RE3 over Size3 for a WSJF of 3.33, and left Ready rather than started, because it is
a distinct piece of work from the disclosure change and the standing rule here is one feature to a
change. The measure of done is that a stopped add leaves the library exactly as a completed add of
the same issues would, minus the pages not yet fetched, with nothing half written.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

**BL-173: Show a cover thumbnail on each Add result row**

- [ ] Weigh a per-row cover request against the traffic it adds before building it
- [ ] If pursued, fetch each cover without blocking the row's own Add button
- [ ] Store only the cover URL, never image bytes, as every other view here does

Deliberately not done in the progressive disclosure work, and recorded so the omission reads as a
decision rather than an oversight. The search, series and creator endpoints are list endpoints, and
they return neither a cover nor a digitalId; only the per-issue endpoint carries those, which is the
whole reason hydration runs after every add rather than at list time. A thumbnail on an Add result
would therefore need a new per-row request pattern against the per-issue endpoint, one call a row,
which is a performance question about traffic and pacing rather than a styling one, and it belongs
in its own change with its own measurement.

Scored V3, TC1, RE2 over Size3 for a WSJF of 2.0, and left Ready. If it is taken up, constraint 1
governs it: the row would store the cover URL only and never the image bytes, exactly as the reading
and library rows already do, so no comic image enters a cache.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

**BL-174: Group the settings screen and give each control its own confirmation**

- [x] Group the settings view into Data safety, Personalization, Connectivity and Advanced
- [x] Put backup and restore first, inside Data safety, with the primary purple treatment
- [x] Move cached metadata out of the Metadata source card into its own card under Advanced
- [x] Give the metadata source control and the cache control each their own report pane
- [x] Carry a shape glyph on each of the four notice kinds so they read without colour
- [x] Keep every card title outranking its sub-heading, with no heading level skipped
- [x] Leave the danger zone card last, and reading progress and its storage key untouched

Implemented on 2026-08-21. The Backup and settings screen was a flat run of seven cards with no
grouping, so backup sat visually level with the cache size readout and nothing told a reader which
controls were safe to touch. The view is now four labelled groups, Data safety, Personalization,
Connectivity and Advanced, with backup and restore first inside Data safety and carrying the primary
purple treatment already used by the Add view's search panel. Cached metadata moved out of the
Metadata source card into its own card under Advanced, and the danger zone card stays last.

All three of the API-URL-refused, API-URL-saved and cache-cleared messages had been written into one
shared report pane that lived in the Backup card, so a confirmation for the metadata source control
appeared 905px above the button that caused it, in a different card and off screen, and a cache clear
silently overwrote a restore refusal the reader had not yet read. Two new report panes were added so
the metadata source control and the cache control each report into their own card, and the restore
pane now keeps only restore and export messages. Measured in Edge, the metadata source confirmation
moved from 905px above its button in another card to 38px below it in its own card, fully on screen,
and it stayed on screen at 200 per cent zoom. A refused restore now survives an unrelated cache
clear.

Under forced colours the notice kinds had been told apart by colour alone, which that mode discards,
so three of the four were indistinguishable from each other. Each kind now carries its own ::before
glyph, a tick for ok, a triangle for warn, a cross for error and a dot for busy, and all four keep a
1px border under forced colours. The finished-order empty state gained a simple glyph as well.
Measured in Edge, ordinary card titles render at 15.2px, the one primary card title at 18.4px, and
the view's only sub-heading, inside that primary card, at 13.6px, so where a title and a sub-heading
actually meet the title still outranks it. The heading levels run 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, 2,
3, 2 with no level skipped. The
settings view grew from 1,672px to 1,950px tall, 278px more, which is the honest cost of the four
group headings.

The four groups were expected to break a stated size claim about src/js/main.js and did not. The
only change to that file was repointing three message destinations from the shared pane to the two
new ones, which added and removed no lines, so it stayed at exactly 5,030 lines and every stated size
claim about it stayed true. Reading progress, its storage key and the recovery layer in
src/js/storage.js were not modified, nothing was uploaded, and no new storage key was introduced.

Verified with 7 new tests, taking the suite from 1,263 to 1,270, all passing. The repository browser
check passes 126 assertions across 14 scenarios, including the one that drives an unreadable saved
store against the salvage and start-fresh offers, and a 39-check acceptance run in Microsoft Edge
passes with 0 failures across both themes, forced colours, reduced motion and 200 per cent zoom.
Lint reports 0 problems, and the evidence anchors gate holds 993 citations with 0 drifted after 72
were re-aimed by this change, 42 of them by the source edits and 30 more by these records.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

**BL-175: Return focus to the control that opened a dialog**

- [x] Return focus to the control that opened a confirm dialog when it closes
- [x] Cover both routes out of the dialog, the Escape key and a Cancel click
- [x] Fix it in the dialog behaviour rather than in any one view's layout

Found while measuring the settings grouping, and deliberately left for its own change. When a confirm
dialog closes, focus does not return to the control that opened it: it lands on the view's h1 heading
instead, after both Escape and a Cancel click. Measured on this change's own base commit as well as
on its changed tree, the behaviour is identical on both, so it is pre-existing rather than introduced
here, and the settings change left dialog behaviour still by holding to the binding rules it already
had.

This is a WCAG 2.4.3 focus order concern: a keyboard or screen reader user who dismisses a dialog is
dropped at the top of the view rather than back where they were working. The fix belongs with dialog
behaviour, which is one shared seam, rather than with the settings layout, which is why it is filed
here rather than folded into BL-174. Scored V5, TC5, RE5 over Size2 for a WSJF of 7.5, and left Ready
under the standing rule of one feature to a change.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

**BL-176: Put type weight, size and corner radius on one shared scale and lift every target to 24 pixels**

- [x] Reduce the declared font weights outside the token blocks to a named, deliberate set
- [x] Remove the near duplicate rem sizes that no reader could tell apart
- [x] Put the corner radii on a small ladder so sibling controls stop disagreeing
- [x] Give every control a 24 pixel minimum height without changing what it does
- [x] Prove the consolidation is invisible rather than assuming it

The stylesheet had grown 13 declared font weights, 33 declared rem sizes and 17 declared corner
radii outside its token blocks. Colour and radius already had tokens; type never got them, so
values arrived one surface at a time and drifted. Two sibling buttons in the same hero carried 13
and 11 pixel corners. Six controls rendered under 24 pixels tall, which is the target size floor,
and two of them were the destructive buttons in the settings screen.

Weights now land on 400, 600, 700 and 800. The fourth survives on purpose: its three sites are the
large fallback numeral, the tile numeral and the tracked uppercase eyebrow, all display type where
800 is a deliberate choice and folding it into 700 would be seen. Radii land on 6, 8, 12, 14 and 20
pixels plus the pill and the token, taking the declared count from 17 to 11, and the two hero
buttons now agree. Sizes fall from 33 to 29.

The size map is deliberately smaller than a snap to a ladder, and the reason is the useful part of
this item. Bounding each value's own movement does not bound the movement between two values: two
sizes a hundredth of a rem apart can sit either side of a rung midpoint and be pushed in opposite
directions, which a nearest rung snap did to 120 pairs here. The map that shipped is the largest
subset under which no near pair is pushed apart. It was then cut again during implementation, when a
geometry census over 987 elements showed two of its rows shrinking section headings by 3.2 per cent
and cascading into 35 pixels of reflow. Those rows were withdrawn, and the bar that replaced them is
the stronger one: no declaration moves by more than a hundredth of a rem.

Verified by that census, which compares every element's position, size, weight, radius and line
height across all nine views and was itself checked by comparing two runs of the unchanged tree,
where it reported nothing changed. Afterwards every element's own box moves by under a pixel except
the six controls that were meant to grow, which land at 24 pixels exactly. Controls under 24 pixels
fall from 6 to 0 with covers on and off, horizontal overflow stays at 0 across nine views and five
widths, all 90 tab stops keep their focus ring, and no line in the diff changes a colour token, so
contrast is untouched in both themes by construction rather than by measurement.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

**BL-177: Give spacing a token scale, as colour and radius already have**

- [ ] Count what the spacing values actually are before proposing a scale
- [ ] Agree a small ladder and move the one-off values onto it
- [ ] Accept that this one reflows the page, and plan the visual check accordingly

Measured while consolidating type: 257 margin and padding declarations hold 51 distinct values, 19
of them used exactly once, and there is no spacing token anywhere. It is the same drift that type
had, in the one dimension that was never given tokens.

It is filed separately rather than folded into BL-176 because it cannot be done the same way.
Consolidating a spacing value moves boxes by construction, so the invisibility proof that governed
the type work is unavailable here and the change needs its own visual review. Doing it inside a pass
whose whole claim was that nothing moved would have made that claim untrue.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

**BL-178: Decide the type scale for the two size bands that cannot be consolidated invisibly**

- [ ] Decide what the small label band should be, rather than leaving six values in it
- [ ] Decide one size for the section heading band
- [ ] Treat it as a type decision, with a visual review, not as a defect fix

Two bands were left exactly as written by BL-176 because collapsing either resizes text a reader
would see. The small label band holds 0.86, 0.87, 0.875, 0.88, 0.89 and 0.9. The heading band holds
0.92, 0.94 and 0.95, and its 0.95 sites are all section headings: the section header, the open card
summary heading, the static card heading and its data view variant, and the library group heading.

An earlier draft did collapse the heading band and it was withdrawn on measurement. It shrank 17
rendered elements by 3.2 per cent, and shrinking every section heading is the wrong direction for a
pass whose purpose is accessibility. Choosing one size for these bands is a type decision worth
making deliberately, with a designer's eye on the result.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

**BL-179: Announce the two rail destinations that currently move focus in silence**

- [ ] Announce the destination on the two rail navigations that say nothing
- [ ] Keep the announcement consistent with the ones that already work

The application declares four live regions and uses them well in most places: importing a list,
marking an issue read, moving through the catalog and changing a setting all announce. Two of the
rail navigations do not, so a screen reader user moving there is given a new view and no word about
it.

Left out of BL-176 because adding an announcement is new behaviour rather than the removal of an
inconsistency, and that pass was scoped to changes it could prove nobody would see.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

**BL-180: Let a row in Everything read open the issue it names**

- [ ] Make a row reach the issue it names
- [ ] Keep the row a single target rather than several competing ones

Every row in Everything read is static text. It names an issue, the series, the date it was read and
the list it belongs to, and none of that is reachable: there is no button, no link and no key
handler on the row. A reader who spots something they want to revisit has to go and find it again by
another route.

Filed from the cohesion pass rather than fixed in it, because giving a row an action is a feature
and that pass was a defect removal.

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.




The original story text is preserved. Each story now carries its ID and disposition.

### EP-01, Epic 1: Curated reading-list catalog

**Goal:** Make multiple Marvel reading lists visible and easy to start.

- **P0: As a reader, I want to see a catalog of available reading lists so that I can
  choose something other than the Hickman Secret Wars list.** `BL-001` `Done`
  - The catalog includes the list name, a short description, approximate issue count,
    and the type of list.

- **P0: As a reader, I want to browse lists by category so that I can find events,
  character runs, creator runs, and eras relevant to me.** `BL-002` `Done`
  - Categories can be filtered without losing the list details.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to search the catalog by title or character so that I can
  quickly find a list I have in mind.** `BL-003` `Done`
  - Search results update clearly and show when there are no matches.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to understand whether a list is essential, complete, or
  tie-in focused so that I can choose the amount of reading I want.** `BL-004` `Done`
  - Each list displays its reading-depth label before import.

### EP-02, Epic 2: Expand Marvel event coverage

**Goal:** Provide useful non-Hickman examples and establish an expandable editorial
pipeline for event lists.

- **P0: As a reader, I want several major Marvel event lists available out of the box
  so that the app feels like a Marvel tracker rather than a single-saga tracker.** `BL-005` `Done`
  - The first release includes a balanced sample of events from different eras,
    such as House of M, Civil War, Secret Invasion, Annihilation, and King in Black.

- **P0: As a product owner, I want each curated list to record its source and version
  so that users can understand where the order came from and when it was updated.** `BL-006` `Done`
  - The list shows attribution and a last-updated date.

- **P1: As a reader, I want more than one version of an event order so that I can
  choose an essential reading path or a complete tie-in path.** `BL-007` `Shipped`
  - Variants are grouped under the same event and clearly named.
  - Three of the five events carry a pair. The other two say why they cannot: their main series
    does not open their order, so a main-series-only list would start in the middle of the story.

- **P1: As a maintainer, I want to add a new curated list without changing the main
  application logic so that the catalog can grow safely.** `BL-008` `Done`
  - A new list is defined through data and appears automatically in the catalog.

### EP-03, Epic 3: Import and create personal reading orders

**Goal:** Let users bring in lists that are not bundled with the app.

- **P0: As a reader, I want to paste a Markdown or plain-text reading order so that
  I can track a list from another guide.** `BL-009` `Done`
  - The app reports how many entries were imported, how many were unresolved, and
    never silently drops an entry.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to resolve an unmatched title by choosing from search
  results so that my imported list remains accurate.** `BL-010` `Done`
  - The app shows enough title, series, and date information to make a safe choice.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to create a list by adding series, creators, or individual
  issues so that I can build a custom reading path.** `BL-011` `Done`
  - Added issues keep their selected order and can be moved or removed.

- **P2: As a reader, I want to duplicate an existing list so that I can customize it
  without losing the original order.** `BL-012` `Done`
  - The copy has its own name and order while preserving shared read progress behavior.

### EP-04, Epic 4: Reading-list experience

**Goal:** Help users understand and complete a list with less effort.

- **P0: As a reader, I want to see which list I am currently following so that I do
  not mark progress in the wrong list.** `BL-013` `Done`
  - The active list is clearly identified in the navigation and reading view.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to see event progress by section or series so that I can
  understand where I am within a large crossover.** `BL-014` `Done`
  - Progress can be viewed for the list overall and for its constituent series.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to filter a list to unread, read, available, or pending
  issues so that I can focus on the next useful action.** `BL-015` `Done`
  - Filtering does not change the saved reading order.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to resume from the next unread issue so that I do not have
  to remember where I stopped.** `BL-016` `Done`
  - The app presents one clear next issue and advances after it is marked read.

- **P2: As a reader, I want optional notes on a list or issue so that I can record
  context, reactions, or reminders.** `BL-017` `Done`
  - Notes remain local and are included in backups.

### EP-05, Epic 5: Trustworthy metadata and availability

**Goal:** Make the app transparent about what it knows and what it cannot verify.

- **P0: As a reader, I want to know when an issue's metadata is incomplete so that I
  do not mistake a pending lookup for missing content.** `BL-018` `Done`
  - Pending, unknown, and confirmed metadata states are distinct.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to know whether an issue is expected to be on Marvel
  Unlimited so that I can plan my reading session.** `BL-019` `Done`
  - The wording makes clear when availability is an estimate rather than a guarantee.

- **P1: As a reader, I want newer issues to remain trackable even when they are absent
  from the metadata snapshot so that the tracker does not become obsolete.** `BL-020` `Done`
  - Manual entries can be read, reordered, exported, and backed up.

- **P2: As a maintainer, I want the app to detect changes in the metadata API contract
  so that upstream changes do not quietly break the experience.** `BL-021` `Done`
  - Contract checks identify missing or changed fields before a release.

### EP-06, Epic 6: Backup, portability, and ownership

**Goal:** Keep user progress safe while preserving the local-first design.

- **P0: As a reader, I want to export all my lists and progress so that I can recover
  from browser storage loss.** `BL-022` `Done`
  - A backup restores list names, order, issue data, and read state.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to move a list between browsers or computers so that my
  reading progress is not tied to one device.** `BL-023` `Done`
  - Exported data can be restored on another supported browser.

- **P1: As a reader, I want to export one list as Markdown so that I can share or
  review it outside the app.** `BL-024` `Done`
  - The export preserves order and read/unread state.

- **P2: As a reader, I want optional synchronization between my devices so that I do
  not have to manage backups manually.** `BL-025` `Forbidden, Constraint 3`
  - Sync is opt-in and does not change the local-only behavior for users who do not
    enable it.

### EP-07, Epic 7: Accessibility and usability

**Goal:** Make the expanded catalog and tracker usable by more readers.

- **P0: As a keyboard user, I want to browse, select, and manage reading lists without
  a mouse so that the app is fully usable with my preferred input method.** `BL-026` `Shipped`
  - Focus order, visible focus, and keyboard actions are consistent.

- **P1: As a screen-reader user, I want list changes and import results announced so
  that I know what happened without relying on visual updates.** `BL-027` `Partial`
  - Important actions have meaningful accessible labels and status messages.

- **P1: As a reader on a small screen, I want the catalog and reading view to remain
  easy to scan so that I can use the app beside Marvel Unlimited.** `BL-028` `Dropped`
  - Dropped by product decision. Marvel Unlimited's own iOS and Android apps already carry
    reading lists, so the phone and tablet job is met first-party. This tracker is a desktop
    companion to the web reader, which is where no list feature exists. See the parked entry
    for BL-028.

### EP-08: Readers who depend on contrast cannot reliably read the interface

**Outcome:** OC-1. Items: BL-029, BL-030, BL-031, BL-032, BL-049.

Four measured problems share one root: colour decisions were made without a contrast floor. The
accent fails white text, the read state dims whole rows below the floor, the hero renders text over
an image whose contrast cannot be known at author time, and there is no alternative to the dark
scheme. BL-049 was added later from the same root, and is a decision rather than a fix: the badge
borders are faint enough to fail the non-text floor, but it is genuinely unsettled whether that
floor applies to them.

### EP-09: Working through a long order is slower than the list is long

**Outcome:** OC-1. Items: BL-033.

Marking one issue read rebuilds the whole application. The cost is measured and scales with list
length, on the most repeated action in the product.

### EP-10: Readers cannot get back to a place in the app

**Outcome:** OC-2. Items: BL-036, BL-037, BL-038.

Nothing about where the reader is survives a reload or a Back press, and two views that would let
them find their own history were never built.

### EP-11: The app answers the same kind of action in different ways

**Outcome:** OC-2. Items: BL-034, BL-035.

Naming, confirming and failing are handled by native browser dialogs in some paths and by the
app's own notice system in others, and one destructive action can be undone while another cannot.

### EP-12: Changing the code is riskier than the change usually warrants

**Outcome:** OC-3. Items: BL-039, BL-040, BL-041, BL-042, BL-043, BL-044, BL-045, BL-046, BL-047.

224 tests exist and nothing runs them automatically. The three modules touching the browser have no
tests at all, every view lives in one 1,566 line file, and there is no linter, no changelog and no
release version to name a build by.

**BL-183: Keep dated evidence anchored to the repository state it recorded**

- [x] Recognise every dated tracking artifact structurally rather than by a list of current files
- [x] Resolve each committed citation line from the Git commit that last authored that line
- [x] Keep current documents, edited lines and new ignored artifacts on the active tree
- [x] Preserve historical extensionless targets through source-specific repository membership
- [x] Refuse shallow history, missing provenance, missing source targets and malformed range ends
- [x] Prove the behavior in disposable repositories without changing application dependencies

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 3 is untouched because the mechanism
reads local Git objects and uploads nothing. Constraint 4 is untouched because runtime dependencies
stay at zero and no development dependency was added. Constraint 11 is checked by the added-line
dash scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-21. Dated tracking records now select a target tree for each citation
occurrence from that document line's Git provenance. A record can therefore contain lines authored
in several commits, and each keeps the repository state it actually recorded. Current product
documents still use the working tree or named revision, while an edited or new historical line uses
the active tree until it has a real source commit.

The corpus remains structural and complete. The checker still walks every tracked file, also enrolls
new dated artifacts hidden by the tracking-root ignore rule, and derives extensionless membership
from the same source tree used for fingerprinting. It does not exclude historical filenames, search
for repeated head text, fall back to current content, or keep a list of affected citations.

Five semantic process tests cover mixed historical and current sources, multiple source commits in
one artifact, direct and nested date paths, working lines, deleted extensionless targets, malformed
ranges, full and shallow clones, missing historical targets, and named revisions. All five failed
against the live-only checker and all pass with provenance enabled. A sixth test pins the existing
full-history checkout and was observed failing when that checkout was made shallow.

Sized 3 because the behavior crosses document discovery, Git history, citation membership and target
reads, while preserving the existing lock identity and comparison model. The implementation caches
one blame result per dated artifact and each source plus path read, and the complete repository
corpus resolves in under ten seconds.

**BL-184: Turn the root project page into a focused reader landing page**

- [x] Keep the product description, screenshot, reader benefits, and qualified privacy disclosure
- [x] Keep the stable Windows download, source startup, exact origin, and safe upgrade path
- [x] Move detailed reader operations into a focused running guide
- [x] Move checks, data authoring, and release procedures into a focused maintainer guide
- [x] Route support, contribution, and governance documents to the new canonical sections
- [x] Keep the root project page at or below 250 lines

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 3 remains explicit in the root privacy
section, including every direct request the app makes. Constraint 4 remains intact because the two
guides add no runtime or development dependency. Constraint 5 is more prominent in the short run and
upgrade paths. Constraint 11 is checked by the added-line dash scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-21. The root project page fell from 849 lines to 118 while keeping the
reader-facing product story, privacy contract, stable Windows download, source startup, exact
`127.0.0.1:8787` origin, safe upgrade sequence, disclaimer, and license. Detailed startup,
installation, restart, port, and troubleshooting procedures now live in one running guide.
Repository checks, live API verification, browser and upgrade proof modes, workflow pin review, data
authoring, generated indexes, and merge-before-tag release mechanics now live in one maintainer
guide.

Sized 3 because the change moved four document roles without changing runtime behavior, then
reconnected support, contribution, governance, semantic tests, and evidence anchors to the new
ownership boundary.

**BL-189: Show every reading order on the landing page, and give each kind of reading its own screen**

- [x] Draw every bundled reading order on the landing page, with no cap and no second screen promised
- [x] Ask the browser to defer a cover the reader has not scrolled to
- [x] Put the era definitions in one table, so a boundary or a label is a one-line edit
- [x] Split the catalogue by kind of reading, and prove every order reaches exactly one screen
- [x] Render an order that matches no era rather than dropping it, and fail the build when one appears

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached. Constraint 1 is untouched because deferring a cover
changes when a URL is requested and never where the bytes go. Constraint 4 holds because nothing was
added to run 59 cards; the deferral is the browser's own attribute. Constraint 5 holds because the
two new screens are hash routes on the same origin. Constraint 11 is checked by the added-line dash
scan.

Implemented on 2026-08-22. The landing page had a grid of 12 and a button reading "See all 59
reading orders" that led to a screen drawing the same orders as rows. The look changed at exactly
the moment the reader asked for more of what they were already looking at, which is the complaint
this item is about. The grid now holds all 59 and the button is gone, so there is nothing left to
promise a second look.

Measured in Edge at 1280x900 with the cache disabled: 59 cards where 12 were drawn before, in three
groups under three headings, on a page 8,178 pixels tall. The landing page issued 12 cover requests
on first paint. With the deferral attribute taken back off, the same page issued 59. So the page
went from 12 orders to 59 while asking the network for exactly the same number of covers, and the
47 it no longer asks for are the ones nobody has scrolled to.

The cover deferral was a defect rather than a new idea. Every other image the app draws already
carried the attribute and the shelf card was the one that did not, so at 12 cards it cost 12 eager
requests and at 59 it would have cost 59.

The catalogue is three screens rather than one: events grouped by era, line-wide reading lists, and
character spotlights. Which screen an order lands on is decided by one table rather than by a
condition inside a render function, and so are the eras, their headings, their blurbs and the
modern-era boundary the landing page filters on. Adding an era is one row. The partition is held by
a test asserting the three screens sum to the story count and that no order is drawn on two of them
or on none, which matters more with three screens than it did with one because there are three
chances to drop something.

Every era declares real bounds at both ends. An open-ended first era would have swallowed a 1975
event into a bucket labelled for the 2000s, which is the heading-promises-what-it-cannot-show defect
this repository has now fixed three times. Closing them reintroduces the risk that an order matches
no era, so that case is handled twice over and deliberately: at runtime the order still renders, in
a section that draws only when it has rows and claims no year range because its contents share none;
in the test suite the same order fails the build and names itself, so the fix reads as "add an era
row". Two tests hold it from opposite sides, one asserting the section catches a stray and one
asserting it is empty on the shipped catalogue. The stray test was proven by adding an entry dated
outside every era, watching the build go red, and taking it out again.

Each era heading carries the span its own rows actually cover, appended as a sentence, so the first
era reads "Dated 2000 to 2007" rather than repeating its label back. That is the early warning: when
pre-2000 content arrives it will print a span reaching past the label before anybody notices the
heading is wrong.

Sized 5 because the landing page, the catalogue renderer, the routes, the markup and five test files
all moved together, and because the change is one restructuring rather than two: writing the section
machinery for the era grouping and then again for the three-way split would have been the same work
done twice.

**BL-190: Give Silver Age and Bronze Age reading their own screens**

- [ ] Add the two ages as rows in the same table the eras and the modern boundary already use
- [ ] Give each its own screen, empty state and heading, as the three catalogue screens have
- [ ] Keep the partition test covering every screen, so nothing reaches none of them

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The landing page is for the modern era, from 1998. That boundary is now data rather than a number
written into a filter, and pre-modern reading is meant to get its own screens rather than being
folded into the modern ones.

Deferred rather than built, because there is nothing to put on them. Not one bundled reading order
is dated before 2000: the 72 dated stories run 2000 to 2024, and the 7 undated ones are character
spotlights, which are curated across the whole timeline and are exempt from the boundary by design
rather than by oversight. So the 1998 boundary admits everything today and filters nothing, and two
screens built now would ship empty.

It is recorded here rather than left in a conversation because the boundary shipped without them,
and a boundary with no screen behind it is the kind of thing that reads later as an unfinished
thought. Building them is the one-line-per-row edit the table exists to make cheap, plus a screen
each. Until then an order dated before 2000 lands in the visible fallback section on the era screen
and reddens the build, so it cannot be lost while these screens do not exist.

**BL-191: Make the next stop on a reading path reachable when it is on another screen**

- [x] Carry the screen a stop is drawn on alongside the stop, resolved from the whole catalog
- [x] Turn "Next" into a link on exactly the hops that cross a screen, and leave the rest as text
- [x] Make the path's own name the link back to the first stop, under the same boundary
- [x] Clear the destination's search and facet chips on arrival, so the named row is really there
- [x] Hold the arrival with tests proven to fail without the two lines that carry the screen

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

Splitting the catalog across three screens broke something BL-152 had shipped. Its badge tells a
reader what to read next by name, and that name was reachable by scrolling because every stop sat on
one shelf. Measured against the shipped data, the one bundled path now crosses a screen at two of
its nine hops: from the character spotlights to the era screen at stop 1, and from the era screen to
the line-wide lists at stop 5. On those two the badge named a row the reader had no way to reach,
which is worse than saying nothing, because it is an instruction with no route.

A link on the hops that cross, and nothing on the seven that do not. On a hop that stays put the
next stop is a row further down the screen the reader is already on, and a link that lands them at
the top of it would leave them further from the row than they started. That is the same reason
BL-152 refused to print the previous stop, read forwards, and it holds "Next" to two links rather
than ten. The words are unchanged either way: nothing names the destination screen, because
the screen says that on arrival and the text budget on these screens is what BL-189 was for.

The same rule then answered the backward direction without a backward badge. A reader who lands on
a crossing row has no way back to the head of the path, because it is not the row above any more,
and BL-152's amendment records why "Previous: Essential Avengers" was costed and declined. The path
name is already printed on all ten rows, so it carries the link instead and no visible word is
added anywhere. Measured against the shipped data, that is 9 linked names against the 2 linked
"Next"s: none on the landing page or on the character spotlights, because both draw stop 1
themselves, 4 on the era screen and 5 on the line-wide lists. It is worth stating plainly that this
is more link surface than the option it beat, not less, on 9 rows against 2. What it does not spend
is text, which is what BL-189 measured and what the owner chose on.

Both links come out of one function, which returns nothing when the stop is drawn on the screen
already being read, so there is no second copy of the boundary and no second copy of the arrival.
Rendered in Edge at 1280x900, one row carries both: stop 5 on the era screen links its name back to
the spotlights and its "Next" forward to the line-wide lists, the only row in the app pointing at
two screens. It reads as a sentence rather than a control strip, because the two links are neither
buttoned nor adjacent, with the row's own separator and the grey word between them, and because the line is the
smallest text on the row. The honest cost is that it is the bluest line on the screen: 55 of its 77
characters are inside a link, against 19 of 56 on the rows either side of it, and nothing but the
word "Next" distinguishes the direction the two point in.

An accessible name carries what the visible text will not. A link announced as "The Modern
Avengers" says nothing about where it goes, so it is named `The Modern Avengers: Start at Essential
Avengers` through the same helper every other control here uses, which builds the name out of the
visible words rather than beside them so speech input still matches what is on screen. Nothing is
added to the screen, which was the whole basis of choosing this over the backward badge.

The dangerous part is not the link, it is what the reader finds. A screen that still holds a search
or a facet chip from an earlier visit can be showing rows without showing the one the link named.
Measured in Edge at 1280x900: typing `x-men` on the era screen leaves 23 of its 46 rows and drops
Avengers Disassembled, which is exactly where the first crossing lands. Arriving by a link clears
that screen's query and returns its facet to all, because arriving this way is a new intent and the
offer is good while only the leftover state is not. Withdrawing the link instead would make a
working control vanish for a reason no reader can see. After the fix, following the link from a
narrowed era screen gives an empty query, a hidden clear button, the `all` facet, 46 rows and the
target among them, with focus on the destination's heading and Back returning to the row that named
it.

What no render-time check could fix is a stop that no screen holds, so that is settled in the data
instead. A stop now carries the screen it is drawn on, resolved from the whole catalog by the same
two rules the renderers use, because a shelf's own renderer only sees its own share and could not
answer for a stop that is not its. Three tests in `test/catalog-shelves.test.js` hold it, and they
were proved red by removing exactly the two lines that carry it rather than by reverting the module:
three failures, each naming the line it defends, then 15 of 15 with the lines back.

One defect found and fixed here rather than filed, because BL-189 caused it. The conditional
sentence pointing at the "Start here" badge was a field on the events shelf, and once that screen
drew its sections from the era table instead, the field was never read: the sentence rendered on no
screen at all. It would have been on the wrong screen in any case, since retyping Essential Avengers
took the badge to the character spotlights. It is one sentence now, printed by whichever section
actually contains the first stop. Measured on the landing page, 4 of the 7 facet chips keep rows
while dropping the badged story, as do the searches `x-men`, `civil war` and `spider`, so the
gating it always had is doing real work.

**BL-192: Call the one act of adding a bundled order by one name, everywhere it is offered**

- [x] Bind the words once and let the landing card and the browse row both draw from that binding
- [x] Rename the rail's two browse destinations for what they hold rather than how they are built
- [x] Drop the three rail subtitles, which no renderer had drawn since the rail was rebuilt
- [x] Rename the two add paths whose labels described the mechanism instead of the result
- [x] Keep the accessible name carrying the order's own name, so a control read out of context still says which one

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The same act had two names. Pressing the button on a landing card added a bundled order to the
library and said "Add to library"; pressing the button on a browse row ran the same code and said
"Import". Measured in Edge at 1280x900, that was 59 cards saying one thing and 59 rows saying the
other, for one behaviour: the row's handler is a wrapper that delegates straight to the landing
card's, and the busy state both share already said "Adding". Two names for one act is EP-11 stated
exactly, and the reason it drifted is that the words were typed twice. They are one binding now, so
the next rename cannot reintroduce the split.

"Import" was also the wrong word for what happens. Nothing leaves the reader's machine and nothing
is read off it; a bundled order is already in the build and the button copies it into the library.
"Add to library" says that, and it is the word a reader who has never used a developer tool will
already know.

The rail was renamed on the same principle. "Browse by era" described how the screen is arranged and
"Line-wide reading lists" described how its contents were assembled, when what a reader wants to
know is what is on them: events in publishing order, and whole runs. They are Timeline and
Storylines. The route ids are untouched, so every bookmark and every Back entry still parses:
`src/js/lib/catalog.js:637-639` records why `catalog` in particular can never be renamed. On the add
side, "Add a whole series" became "Find a series", because the button that follows it searches and
finds and adds nothing on its own, and "Paste a reading order" became "Paste a reading list", which
is what every other surface in the app calls the thing.

An owner follow-up on 2026-08-22 made that name explicit across the whole interface: every heading,
control, empty state, preview and accessible label now calls the object a "Reading List", with both
words capitalized. Internal route and storage identifiers stay unchanged, so the terminology change
does not alter saved progress or existing addresses.

Three rail subtitles went with them. Each rail entry carried a second line of grey text under its
label, and they were dead in two senses: they restated the label, and the field behind them had no
renderer at all after the rail was rebuilt, so the table declared copy that reached no screen. The
field is gone rather than left declared, and the test that required it of every shelf no longer does.

**BL-193: Cut the standing text on the screens a reader chooses from**

- [x] Shorten the three browse subtitles, which repeated the blurbs the landing page already prints
- [x] Fold each row's provenance behind a disclosure instead of printing it on every row
- [x] Replace the three search buttons with an icon, and carry the word in the tooltip and the name
- [x] Delete the landing page's closing strip, which offered a second route to a rail entry
- [x] Give the era breaks a band of their own, so a long screen has a felt boundary

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The complaint that started this was the amount of text on the screens a reader chooses from, so the
work is measured in words rather than argued. Measured in Edge at 1280x900, on the shipped
catalogue: the Timeline screen fell from 2,833 visible words to 2,205 and from 100 paragraphs to 54,
Storylines from 692 to 611, the character spotlights from 1,128 to 1,031, and the add screen from 79
to 67. Nothing was deleted that is not still reachable.

Most of that is provenance. Every browse row printed who curated the order, which section of their
site it came from and when the snapshot was taken, which is 46 lines of small grey text on one
screen for a fact a reader checks once about one order, if ever. It is a disclosure now, closed by
default and headed "Source". A disclosure rather than the hover tooltip the request asked for,
because a tooltip reaches neither the keyboard nor a touch screen, and because Chromium opens a
closed disclosure for find-in-page, so the words stay findable while they are out of the way. Each
one is announced as the order it belongs to rather than as a bare "Source", since 46 controls with
one name is a list nobody can navigate.

The three page subtitles were the next largest. Each browse screen carried a sentence of up to 148
characters restating the blurb the landing page already prints over the same shelf, so a reader who
arrived from the landing page read the same claim twice. They are one short sentence each now, and
the landing blurbs are untouched, because that is the surface where a reader is still choosing which
screen to open.

The search buttons lost their words rather than their meaning. Each of the three sat immediately
beside a labelled field that already said what it searched, so the word on the button was the third
statement of it. The button is a magnifying glass with "Search" as its tooltip and a fuller phrase
as its accessible name, and it holds the 44px target the field beside it holds. This is the one
change here that adds nothing to the screen while removing something, so it is worth being plain
that an icon-only control is a trade: a reader who does not recognise the glyph has to hover it.

The landing page's closing strip is gone outright. It offered "Or start from scratch" and a button
that did exactly what the rail's "New empty list" entry does, one screen-height below the last card,
which is a second route to a destination already permanently on screen.

The era breaks went the other way and gained weight. Four of them divide 46 rows on the Timeline
screen, and they were set at the same size and nearly the same weight as the row titles under them,
so scrolling gave no felt boundary. Each is a band now, with its own fill, its own outline and an
accent edge. That is more paint, not less, and it is the point: the screens were not only wordy,
they were undifferentiated, and a reader scrolling past 46 rows needs to know when the period
changed.

Two things were left alone on purpose, both of them recorded here so the next pass does not read
them as oversights. The manual lookup hint and the address hint under it are privacy disclosures
rather than helper text, and four assertions hold their wording, so the hint that says nothing is
sent until you press the button stays exactly as it was. And the Marvel Unlimited address field was
asked to be removed on the grounds that a title is enough, which is true of everything the metadata
snapshot covers and false of the only case that form exists for: it is the mitigation for issues
published after the snapshot ends, and for those there is no identifier to resolve and the pasted
address is the only route to a working Read link. Removing it would have taken the one working path
out of the one place it is needed.

**BL-194: Stop one card's extra line from inflating the two cards beside it**

- [x] Decide whether the landing grid holds equal cards or ragged ones, and say which
- [x] Give the always-present blocks a fixed number of lines, if equal is the answer
- [x] Re-measure the spread and the blank space against the figures recorded here

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The landing grid stretches every card in a row to the tallest of them, and the card's footer is
pushed to the bottom by an automatic margin, so the difference lands as blank space inside the
shorter cards. Measured in Edge at 1280x900 with three columns, on the shipped catalogue: the cards
run from 273px to 398px, a 125px spread; a row holding a card with a reading-path sentence wasted
between 168px and 256px against 6px for a row holding none; and 1,152px of blank space sits across
the whole 59-card grid, which is more than one viewport of nothing. The variable blocks are the
path sentence on 10 cards of 59, the "ways to read this" line on 6, the beginner badge on 11, and
the title, which runs to one line on 46 and two on 13.

Two cheap fixes were tried and measured and both are rejected here rather than left as suggestions.
Clamping the path sentence to one line recovered 19px of the 125 and cut nine of the ten sentences
mid-word, one of them through the middle of a link, so it traded a small gain for real loss.
Reserving two lines each for the title and the description made it worse, taking the spread from
125px to 145px, because the shortest card was already using both and only the taller cards grew.
The remaining honest options are a fixed card height with the title and description clamped to a
set number of lines, or a grid that does not stretch at all, and choosing between them is a design
decision rather than a defect fix, which is why this is filed rather than folded into BL-193.

Owner direction added on 2026-08-22 widened this item to the two other landing-page surfaces with
the same visible cost. Saved reading orders must become a responsive grid of bounded tiles instead
of full-width rows, and the single featured suggestion must stop widening once its existing content
has enough room. The content and actions stay intact; this is a spatial correction, not another
copy-removal pass.

Shipped with ragged cards, which keeps every authored sentence and lets each card own the height its
content needs. Repeating the original Edge measurement at 1280x900 left the 59 cards between 273px
and 397px, but reduced the same blank-space measure from 1,152px to 113px. That remainder is the
one-pixel card edge counted on both sides after rounding; no shorter card is stretched to match a
taller neighbour.

The owner-directed additions use the same rule at two other scales. Three saved orders render as
three 384px tiles on a 2048px display and two at 1280px, each 163px tall in the measured fixture.
The first-run suggestion uses the whole 964px content width at 1280px, then stops at 1,152px when
the content column grows to 1,296px. It remains the featured choice without becoming a page-wide
empty band.

A second owner review of the 2048px result found the same slab under Continue reading and a
different misuse below Discover more: the Home category named Timeline was painted with the boxed
era-break treatment intended for periods inside the Timeline screen. The continuing-order panel
therefore takes the same 1,152px cap as the first-run suggestion, and Home category headings return
to plain headings. The real era breaks on the Timeline screen keep their background, outline and
accent edge.

The owner then removed the text beneath those headings rather than merely restyling its container.
Continue reading is enough context for a returning reader, and Timeline, Storylines and Character
spotlights are enough context for the three Home groups. Their explanatory blurbs remain on their
dedicated screens, where the reader has chosen that subject and the explanation orients the shelf.

A third owner review rejected the ragged-card decision after the difference remained conspicuous in
both the 2000s Timeline group and the Storylines group. The variable detail rows were the cause, not
the grid itself. Home now moves path position and beginner suitability onto compact cover labels and
moves the number of reading options into the preview action that already opens those options. Full
path identity and next-stop links remain on the dedicated browse screens rather than being repeated
on every Home card.

With those rows out of the card flow, equal tracks no longer create large empty interiors. Repeating
the production-catalog measurement in Edge puts all 59 cards at 273px at 1280x900 and again at
2048x900. The earlier 125px spread is now 0, and the blank-space measure is 118px, exactly the
two one-pixel card edges counted for each of 59 cards. The browser harness checks equal heights at
both widths, the compact visible labels, the complete assistive path wording and the option action.

The dedicated browse cards now follow the same spatial rule without dropping their path context.
Their full path name and next-stop wording sit behind a compact position disclosure beside Source.
Before that change, multi-card Timeline years carried spreads up to 81px; afterwards every card
within each year measures to the same height, and opening the disclosure restores the full wording
and links.

A fourth owner review returned to the first-run Home state. The sentence beneath its main heading
repeats context the featured choice and Reading Lists already provide, so it must be removed and
the heading shortened. The featured card also still leaves a broad unused area to the right of its
bounded description. The final composition will keep the readable line length while either using
that area for the decision controls or withdrawing the card edge from space its content does not
need.

The owner selected "Start Here" and a decision column. The feature keeps its cover and readable
summary on the left, while the commitment facts and both actions occupy the formerly empty right
side. Below 1,100px the decision column returns beneath the summary so neither part is squeezed.

**BL-195: Give each way of adding issues its own screen**

- [x] Declare a route for each of the five ways to add issues
- [x] Point the five rail entries at their own routes rather than at one view and a section id
- [x] Keep the existing address working, so a bookmark of the combined screen still resolves

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The rail lists five ways to add issues and all five address one view, opening a named section of it
rather than a screen of their own. That is why four of the five arrive collapsed, why the rail
cannot show which one you are on, and why Back from any of them leaves the same screen. Splitting
them is a routing change rather than a copy change: it needs an entry in the declared view list, its
own markup, a branch in the view switch and a rail entry for each, and the existing combined address
has to keep resolving or every bookmark of it breaks. It was asked for in the same request as
BL-192 and BL-193 and is held back from them deliberately, because a rename and a route split
landing in one change would make the route split impossible to review on its own.

Shipped as five real destinations: Search issues, Find a series, Browse a creator, Paste a reading
list and Add an issue by hand. The old combined address resolves to Search issues, so bookmarks and

**BL-196: Draw the timeline as a timeline, over the years the catalogue actually covers**

- [x] Derive the spine's range from the stories that landed rather than from a declared bound
- [x] Make the years navigable, so pressing one moves the screen to the stories in it
- [x] Say what an empty year inside the range means, and leave it visible rather than closing the gap

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The Timeline screen is a list in publishing order with five era bands over it, and the request is
for a spine a reader can scroll and press. The range asked for was 1998 to 2026. Measured over the
bundled catalogue, that is the wrong range and the measurement is the interesting part: the 66
events and all 72 dated stories run from 2000 to 2024. A declared 1998 to 2026 spine is 29 years, of
which 9, or 31 per cent, would be empty, including four years outside the catalogue's actual ends.
A derived range is 25 years with 5 empty, and all five are internal: 2001, 2002, 2003, 2015 and 2023.
That distinction is the whole design. An empty
year inside the range is honest information, that the catalogue skips a year, and it should stay
visible; an empty run at either end is a promise of coverage the app does not have. BL-189 already
derives the era bands from the stories that landed rather than from declared bounds, so the rule
exists and this reuses it.

Shipped as 21 years from 2000 through 2020, derived from the 46 events on the screen. The five empty
internal years remain visible as quiet gaps: 2001, 2002, 2003, 2015 and 2019. A year containing a
story is a 44px button. Pressing it clears a prior search or facet, rebuilds the complete shelf,
scrolls to the first story in that year and moves focus to its heading. Browser verification started
with an active `x-men` search, pressed 2000, and observed the query clear, all 46 cards return and
focus land on Maximum Security. Review then made that behavior durable in the Edge harness and
restored the visible focus ring on the destination heading. Empty years now keep full muted-text
contrast and expose their "no Reading Lists" wording as actual assistive text.

The browser harness is not run in CI, for the same reason the contract check is not: it drives an
installed browser that no build machine has. So it can fall behind the app without anything going

branch that changed no shelf code at all: 109 assertions pass and 10 fail in both runs, and the 10
are the same 10 by name, so the failures belong to the harness rather than to any change since.

What was observed rather than diagnosed: the harness's own stub stories render under the heading
"Not yet placed in an era", which is the fallback section that draws when a story matches no era's
declared bounds. That fallback is correct behaviour and BL-189 shipped it deliberately, so the
harness is asserting an arrangement the app stopped producing when the catalogue became three
screens. Four of the ten failures name a section or an ordering, one is a wait that times out
looking for a section that is not drawn, and the rest are counts derived from the same fixture. The
fix is to the fixture and the expectations, not to the app, but that is a claim to prove by making
the change rather than to inherit from this paragraph.

**BL-202: Turn the Timeline year strip into a vertical chronology**

- [x] Put era milestones, year markers and their cards on one continuous vertical axis
- [x] Keep one muted marker for every empty year without giving it an empty card row
- [x] Pin a populated year beside its cards and reflow it above the cards at narrow widths
- [x] Remove the separate year-jump control rather than duplicating the chronology
- [x] Keep year labels clear of their nodes and compact-sidebar icons visible while the list scrolls

Constraint gate: checked 1 to 11, none breached.

The owner intended the year spine to run vertically, with each group of cards occupying the space
beside its year. The horizontal strip consumed a full-width band, required a scrollbar on the wide
review viewport and stood apart from the content it described. Three concepts were compared before
implementation: literal equal-sized year slots, a sticky year navigation rail, and a continuous
spine whose populated years expand to fit their cards. The continuous spine was selected because it
keeps the chronology visible without manufacturing large empty intervals.

The selected design keeps the existing era headings as major milestones. Populated years own card
grids, every empty year remains as one muted tick, and the active populated year stays pinned until
the next year pushes it away. The scale is chronological rather than proportional: a year with many
cards grows to fit them. At 700px and below, the year moves above a one-column card list while the
line continues down the left edge. The owner explicitly removed fast year jumping rather than
replacing it with another picker.

Owner inspection found the year labels touching the circles beside them and the Windows scrollbar
covering navigation glyphs when the sidebar was collapsed. The labels now reserve the full node
width plus a visible gap. The compact rail keeps wheel, touch and keyboard scrolling but hides its
scrollbar chrome, while the expanded pane continues to show it.

Measured in Edge against the production catalogue at 2048x1500, the result draws 4 era milestones,
16 populated year groups and 5 empty-year ticks. The marker is sticky at desktop width and moves
above its card group at 620px. Compact path disclosures reduced the largest within-year card spread
from 81px to 0 while preserving the full path name, position and next-stop wording on expansion.
